div.head: WOMAN'S REALM.
div.p: WOMAN'S REALM.
DRESS-FASHION-HOME.
BEADS IN MILLINERY.

A fashion that cropped up last year of having beads as hat-trimming has now again been revived. Large jet cabochons are worked into passementerie with fine beads, and used as hatbands, if one may call them so, sometimes being wide enough to hide the crown all round. The brim is often bordered, says 'a Ghibc writer, with cut jet beads, a peculiarly becoming arrangement, the way in which the light catches them being propitious to the complexion. Again, it is the crown which is a-glitter with jet or garnet. Some- times it is a row of graduated beads like a necklace ,that trims the hat, either in making a circuit of the crown or forming a couple of loops about it. A red straw -hat for the Riviera has a string of black beads about the crown with a band of red velvet surrounding it. The brim is lined with finely-pleated black tulle, and a pair of black velvet streamers hang from one side.

div.head: SMART SHIRT BLOUSE.
div.p: SMART SHIRT BLOUSE.

Pictured in our illustration is a particu- larly smart and attractive shirt - blouse, suit- able for realisation in soft satin, taffetas, or crepe-de-chine. This blouse is quite plain down the middle of the front, where it fas- tens, the edging being cut in wide shallow scallops, and finished with a pleated frill of the material. In each scallop is a big silk- covered or embroidered button which pro- fesses to fasten the blouse; the real fasten- ing, however, consists of hooks and eyes which are concealed from view. On either side comes a group of five small tucks, then a plain space, and, finally, another group of

four tucks, the outermost of hid) projects slightly over the top of the sleeve. The sleeves are of a small leg-of-mutton slope, and are decorated with groups of horizontal tucks from the top to the bottom of the arm. A high tucked neckband finished by a frill completes the blouse.

div.head: JEWEL NOTES FROM PARIS
div.p: JEWEL NOTES FROM PARIS

From time immemorial the fondness of the average woman for jewellery has been a pp- verb, and really latter-day jewellery is so beautiful that one might almost be pardoned if one broke the tenth Commandment. It has remained, however, for the up-to-date . Parisi- enne to develop, perhaps, the prettiest caprice which has ever been connected with precious stones, says the Daily Graphic. For the latest dictate of fashion is that the stones worn must match the hue of the gown. Thus, with a frock of turquoise satin, souple tur- quoises set in diamonds are worn; with a gown of pervenche, sapphires, the blue variety, of course, with Parma mauve amethysts and diamonds. A gown of pink panne had a parure of rubies, and the effect was magnificent, it must be owned, in this in- stance. As it was, tot), in the case of a won- derful Directoire creation of palest sea-green chiffon over satin of the same shade, where the jewels worn were emeralds, set in dia- monds of extraordinary brilliance. USEFUL PETTICOAT.

The subject of our sketch is a neat and attractive petticoat of a useful and up-to- date shape. This design might be success- fully carried out in moirette, alpaca, taffetas, or soft satin, the last - mentioned beiug, of
course, much the m
Ist fast
i!onable of them

all. This petticoat fastens on the left side, and is darted to fit the figure quite accu- rately round the hips. The bottom of the skirt is finished by a closely-kilted frill, wide enough to come almost to the level of the knees, the frill being set on with a neat pip- ing of the material.

div.head: PRACTICAL CHARITY.
div.p: PRACTICAL CHARITY.

The Duchess of Sutherland is reported to have said in a speech the other day that everyone realised now the uselessness of charity. "The poor have got to find their own feet." One recognises the fine doctrine underlying the Duchess's remark, and ad- mires her for escaping from a class tradition, says "The Roamer" in the Lady. Yet the man who the same day gave £200,000 to the Unemployed Fund was offering warmer com- fort. A few meals and a few clothes given by the rich to the poor do not solve the terrible problem of poverty and the abject misery that it causes; but while the poor are "find- ing their own feet," the practical philanthro- pists do at least help them to find their feet • in boots.

div.head: TO-DAY'S RECIPE.
div.p: TO-DAY'S RECIPE.

FILLETED SOLE.—Skin and fillet two soles, put the bones to stew in a pan with a cupful of water and stook. • Reduce to half and strain. Skin and bone a whiting, pound it in a mortar, add four ounces of breadcrumbs —moistened wth two tablespoonfuls of cream —a finely-chopped shallot, ard a little flaked -lobster. Mix thoroughly, adding one and a• half ounce of butter; the yolks of three eggs, pepper, salt, and chopped parsley. Put all through a sieve. Spread one i:ide of each fillet of sole with this forcemeat, roll up, and wrap in buttered paper. Place in a buttered baking dish, sprinkle with a few drops of lemon juice, and put it in the oven for five minutes,' then add one • gill of white wine, baste well, and cook another ten minutes. Fry sonif croutons of bread, spread each with- a little of the remaining forcemeat, and bake a few minutes. Take the fillets, remove the paper, and put each upright on a crou- ton. Place a star cut out of a truffle on each, and serve with lobster sauce,

div.head: ECZEMA ON HANDS AND ARMS.
div.p: ECZEMA ON HANDS AND ARMS.
FLESH ROTTING FOR FIVE YEARS.
Another Etriking Cure by Zam-Buk.

A story of Zam-Bnk's gnat triumph • over a terrible and most stubborn skin disease has just been gleaned by a "Merthyr Express" reporter, from Mrs. Ann Barris, of 11, Solomon-street, Penydarren, Merthyr Tydvl. Mr. and Mrs. Harris are well-known and highly respected in the district, and are prominent members of the Noddfa Baptist Church. " One day, in the early part of 1902," said Mrs. Harris to the reporter, "an eruption suddenly appeared all over the back of my hands. The skin became red and pulpy. I went to a doctor, who told me I had ecema as bad as it vies possible to have it. I think I caught the disease by washing the head of a child who was suffering from scalp eczema. Both my hands wee covered with itching scabs, which were constantly peeling away, and forming again. If I touched the skin, matter and blood oozed cut fnely. I was absolutely help7ess to perform any household duties, and the itching went on day and night until I became worn-out with constant suffering and loss of sleep. The eczema nelt broke out on my arms, and became so bad on my hands that I thought they would le quite eaten away. My .flesh was so rotted with disease that my finger nails dropped off three times, and my fingers became so swollen that my wedding ring had to be filed off. I had treatment and ointment from five doctors ; and I used besides, all kinds of ordinary ointments, lotions, and medicine, for more than fire years, until at last I gave up in disgust and let the terrible disease take its course.

"About twelve months ago, my husband scratched his hand badly and was advised to try Zam-Buk. So quickly and thoroughly did the balm heal his band that I decided to try it for my bands and arms. A meeting of the above council was hcld in the J.L.P Rooms, Friars-green, on Tuesday evening. Mr. D. L. Owen presided over a fair atterdance which included Mr. E. Plinston, secretarr.

div.head: WAPPT NEW YEAR.
div.p: A WAPPT NEW YEAR.
Mr. D. L. OWEN at the commencernont wished all the members present a happy and prosperous new year.
MUSICIANS'
OR lEVA SCE.

A letter was read from the Musicians' Union, calling attention to the unjust competion suffered by the civilion bands at the hands of the military bands at the recent Olympic games at the Franco-British Exhibition. A great deal of discussion took place on the subject and a resolution was proposed by Mr.Tnomas seconded by Mr. RICHARDSON, that the Trades Council strongly condemned the unjust competion by the bands of the Government, which took the work from the civilian bands and thus caused them to fill the ranks of the unemployed. This was agreed to.

div.head: FEDERATION OF TRADES AND LABOUR COUNCILS.
div.p: FEDERATION OF TRADES AND LABOUR COUNCILS.

A letter was read by the SECIWARY, stating that a half yearly meeting would be held on June 30th at 3 o'clock, in the offices of the Co-operative Udion, Nicholas Croft, High-street, Mancbsster. The follow- ing resolution would be brought k•efore the meeting. "That this federation heartily supports Mr. Keir Hftrdies Bill to amend the Unemployed Workmen's Act, 1903, so as to enable the Distress Committees to pay wages out of public funds, and to confer upon the Special Committees all the powers of Distress Committees." It was decided to send Mr. Plumb as a delegate to this federntion.ana that the Council strongly support Mr. Heir Hardie's Bill. NATION NE ROUSING REFORM COUNCIL.

A letter was read from this Council stating that they were now paying special attention to the housing conditions of Lancashire towns, and that they would during the next few months, bare repotts prepared on the general housing conditions of several of them, Including Bolton, Blackburn, Burnley and Warrington.

TILE QUESTION OF UNEMPLOYMENT. Mr. J. HALEY, the Council's delegate to the Distress Committee, gave a report of the annual meeting, particulars of Nshich have already appeared in the "Examiner." Lie said there were about 500 unemployed In the town and the average man of those unemployed had four of a family which made 2,C00 persons pm- tically starving. They were not living; they were only existing. Some men en the Town Council apparently did not care whether they lived or died, is the works of utility suggested by the Distress Committee had not yet been started. He found that the widening of Knutsford- road and the building of the new wharf were to be included in the re-construction of Warrington Bridge, so it was not likely that the work would be commenced for a considerable time. . .

Mr. PLUMB moved that a vote of thanks be given to Mr. Haley for his report and his excellent work in the matter. Mr. HALEY : I do not like votes of thanl:s. I have (banks Enough Tam I Eee that people ara being relieved. A SKILLED LAPOUR SUB-COMMITTEE WANTED.

The CHAIM: AN asked why the Distress Committee did not cppoint a Skilled Labour Sub-committee,Ps Le considered the town needed one. Half the unemploy- ment in the town was through the lack of such a sub- committee. They had them in all large towns such as Liverpool ard MancLester and ho thought they should have one in Warrington.

div.head: DIAMOND & RUBY NECKLACE.
div.p: A DIAMOND & RUBY NECKLACE.
BY L.
T. MEADE.
Author of "Scamp and I," "Dad:ly's Boy," 'IA World of Girls," "The Way of a Woman," "An Adventuress," "Little Wife Hester," Sce.

Judge Algernon Greenfield arrived at his friend Peter Tracy's house on a certain Saturday. The assizes were to commence on the following Monday morning in the prosperous town of Brookville. He w:v3 to occupy the bench on this occasion, and Tracy had long ago asked him to make his house his headquarters.

Peter Tracy was a rich man and owned a lovely estate in the neighbourhood of Brookville. The time Ivas the middle of August, and the country was in its full summer splendour. When Gceentield stepped from the luxurious carriage which Tracy had sent to meet him at the railway stn.tion, and took the smooth young hand of his host's only daughter in his own, he could not help giving a sigh of pleasure. "Until Monday I can enjoy myself," he thought, "and need give no thought to crime and its attendant miseries." _ _

Evelyn raised her full, dark eyes, and smiled in his face. "It is nice to have you here again, Uncle Algernon," she said. She was no relation, but from her babyhood she had called him by the familiar name.

"And it is very nice to come, Evelyn," ho replied. "After the toils and noise and fuss of London, this place seems like Heaven. But haven't you some news to give me, or did that indefatigable little bird which flies over the world, to east and west, to north and south, whisper in my ear in vain ? " The girl blu,ibed very vividly. toll you ? " the asked.
"What did it

_ "Well, that I should soon have to put my hand in my pocket and present someone with a wedding present." Evelyn smiled, and then she sighed. "I am going to say a very tremona.ble thing," was her mat remark. "I hate wedding presents. I have had a great many, and the most expensive of all has put me into fearful trouble. I should like to tell you, only--" "Only what, Evelyn ? Why should you not let me share your anxieties? That is, if you really have any." "I have indeed. Only Christopher and father both said that I ought not to tell .you. It might be unfair; it might, in fact, prejudice you." "It sounds very serious and alarming, but pray tell me first if Christopher is here, and are you very much in love with him ? "
Christopher is here; he is coming down the walk to meet U 3. I will introduce him."

A good-looking man of about eight-and-twenty years of age now came forward. his name was Christopher Selkirk. He had loved Evelyn for years, and their marriage, which was to take place in a few months' time, was regarded by the friends on both sides as a singularly happy one. Judge Greenfield was pleased to meet the young man, and soon they were chatting together, Evelyn walking beside them, with her band laid lightly on the judge's arm. They approached a small summtr-house, and the three entered.

It was then that judge Greenfield for the first time remarked that his favourite's eyes, notwith- standing her real and great happiness, were full of subdued anxiety, and that her pretty face was paler than its wont. "What is this mystery, Evelyn ?" he said, pinching her ear. "You must tell me, whatever Mr. Selkitk happens to say to the contrary. You hive made some strange remarks with regard to wedding presents; one in particular has given you trouble. May I not hear ? " "Indeed you may, Uncle Algernon, even if you aro twenty times a judge." "You ought not to tell, Evelyn," said Selkirk, but Evelyn did not mind. "We are very unhappy about it," she said at once. "Oh! here comes father. Perhaps he will tell you. I—l just can't when it comes to the point." To the judge's consternation Evelyn burst into tears. Mr. Tracy, who had been absent when the judge arrived,.ryow hureied forward. "Delighted to-see you, my dear friend. Evelyn in tears! What about ? "

"You must tell Uncle Algernon," said Evelyn. "I am so miserable ; I miss her so much. I wish there were no such terrible things in the world as wedding gift,;." She left the summer-house, Selkirk immediately following. "Poor little girl," said Tracy when he found himself alone with his friend. "I did not want to tell yell, Greenfield, for you will have to judge the poor, miserable creature." "But you must tell me, my friend. Your dear little daughter mis3rable—so miserable that even in the presence of her betrothed she bursts into tears! What has happened 9 I shall not have an easy minute until I find out." "It is this—and the trouble is pretty big, although we try to make light of it. It has shaken Evelyn terribly. You must know that when her mother died, my little girl was not a year old. My dear wife's last words were to commit her to my care, and also to the care of a faithful nurse of the name of Rebecca Hickson. From that 'moment Rebecca was trusted as One would trust a member of one's own family. A mo-t affectionate faithful soul she proved. She was married at die time of my dear wife's death, and her on was our Evelyn's foster-brother. When ha was a baby he was allowed to be a good deal here, and he and Evelyn used to play and romp together. When he got older I paid for his schooling, and by-and-bye apprenticed him to a stone-reason. He was clever, and apparently an upright young fellow, and for a long time did well in his trade. But soon after his eighteenth birthday he took an extraordinary turn, got with wild, unscrupulous companions, and gave his mother a great deal of anxiety. Ho became heavily in debt, and the poor woman used up the savings of years to set him free from this incubus. In the end I persuaded her to let the young man go to America, arranged to pay his passage out, and gave him a little money to start afresh in another country. He went, and I hoped that I had seen the last of him, but about three months ago he returned unexpectedly. Evelyn told me, for Rebecca would not, herself, mention the fact. Evelyn saw him skulking about the place after dark, and evidently waiting to see his mother. I spoke to Rebecca on the subjee but to my amazement she denied that Jacob was back in England. Evelyn maintains stoutly, however, tat beyond doubt she saw the man. We did not give the circumstance a great many thoughts however, for my child was just then engaged to Selkirk, and we were all so full of this, and the preparation for her marriage, that even more important things than the return of Jacob Hickson would not have concerned us.

"For the last month Evelyn has been the recipient of some beautiful and valuable gifts.. Amongst other presents. Selkirk's mother, Lady Esther, sent the child a magnificent diamond and ruby necklace. The necklace was of immense value. It had been in the Selkilk family for generations, and was said to have been presented by Queen Elizabeth to the then reigning lady of the house on her marriage. Christopher is the eldest son, and will in due course inherit Selkirk Towers; Evelyn was there- love the eight person to receive the necklace. She was wildly delighted when she found herself the possessor of such a valuable trinket. It reached her by special messenger exactly four weeks ago. • "Well, Greenfield, you can judge of our horror, when I tell you that a week later the ornament was lost, evidently stolen ; how, or by whom we could nolat first imagine. Detectives could afford ie3 no clue, snd the fact remained that the neck- lace of incalculable value was no longer to be found. Lady Esther arrived on the scene in a fearful state of mind. All possible steps were ttlen to get a clue to the robbery, but without success, until just at the eleventh hour—namely, a week ago— when suspicion of undoubted character was shed 'upon the doings of that Fortunate. woman, Rebeeea Hickson. Lady Esther heard of this, and • insisted on the law As.king its course, with the result that Hickson is tow in prison charged with the theft. She 'will confess nothing. Her unscrupulous son nas been seen in the neighbourhood since the loss of the necklace. You will, of course, hor the (evidence later on, so perhaps it i 3 -unfair to tell you any more." "I am glad you have told me so much," inswered,Tuden Greenileld. "What a remarkable thing for a woman so faithful to be tempted to commit a theft of such enounity." "You Mast try to imagine that she is innocent until sou can prove her guilty," was Wracy's

remark. "I fear I have done wrong, and perhaps injured the unfortunate creature by telling you the story in advance." "What you have said will make no difference in my judgment," said Greenfield. "You under- stand that a judge has so to train his mind that he addresses the jury simply on the evidence given at the time of the trial. My wish would be to clear the poor woman. I see that Evelyn is unhappy." "Unhappy! She is wretched. She was so devoted to her old nurse. She has gone to see her once or twice, and has come back in a frantic state of grief." "And what about Selkirk himself ? Does ho mind the loss ? "
"He does for his mother's sake; but he is the sort of man who thinks nothing whatever of jewels. In fact, he hates diess' and can't imagine why Evelyn should burden herself with a trousseau."

-"Then he can know nothing about it?" "What do you mean? Why should he hare anything to do with it?" "Nothing whatever, only in a matter of this kind one likes to look round and see where a possible loophole can appear. Is your poor servant, this Rebecca Hickson, well defended?"

"Yes, I saw to that myself. I am paying all the expenses of her trial, and have got a first- rate K. C. from town to unlertake her case." "That is all right. What is his name?" "Percival. You will meet him at dinner this evening:"

NotW-ithstamding her anxiety, Evelyn Tracy did hr utmost to make the evening a pleasant one f )1. her dear old friend, Judge Greenfield. When h: came into the drawing-room she sat by his s'de, and when he begged her to sing for him s'ie did so, but he could not help noticing how troubled were her eyes, although the subject of tie necklace was not again alluded to. Among the guests was Lady Esther Selkirk, a proud and imperious-looking woman. She said a word to Judge Greenfield as they were parting for the night. "I have learnt that you are acquainted with the fact that the valuable necklace, so long an heir- loom in our family, has been stolen," was her r mark.

Judge Greenfield bowed. • "I am glad you know beforehand. Had no one else mentioned it, I should have done so. I trust you, by some means known only to yourself, will get that wretched woman, who is now in prison, to confess her crime, and so lead to the recovery of the necklace; for that she has stolen it I have no doubt."
Nothing further was said with regard to the that on the following day, and Greenfield was glad of it, although he himself could not keep it out of his mind.

On Monday the assizes began, and many eases were tried before this well-known judge. It was on the third day that Rebecca Hickson appeared before his lordship for judgment. ' The circumstantial evidence-. against her was very conclusive. She was known to be badly in want of money, owing to the fact that her son had impoverished her and used up all her savings. The tradesmen in the town came forward as witnesses against her. To one she owed as much as twenty-five pounds, and to the other as much as fifty pounds. Her wages were repre- sented by thirty pounds a-year, and these enormous debts were therefore quite unreason- able for a woman in her position. The items on the bills all proved that every penny the wretched woman had spent had been given to her son to provide him with clothes and luxuries of different kinds. He had beyond doubt been seen in the country quite a week before the disappearance of the necklace. Not only had poor Evelyn been obliged with a bursting heart to swear to the fact, but several other people in the neighbour- hood had seen him. One man, the under- gardener at Brookville Priory, had even been present during an interview between mother and son. On going home to his cottage after dusk, he had seen Rebecca, whose face was well known to everyone on the estate, standing by a five- barred gate talking to a good-looking young man many years her junior. Mummery recognised him at once as Rebecca's son, and, impelled by curiosity, waited a stone's-throw off, wondering what was up. Neither mother nor son knew that anyone was listening, and the first words that fell on Mummery's ears were the following: "I must have the money. If you can't help me it is all up. What does a hundred pounds matter to rich people like the Tracys ? Why, my dear little foster-sister, Miss Evelyn, could get it for me without the slightest difficulty. She has but to ask the squire and the deed is done."

These words were uttered very roughly and in a menacing tone, and the poor woman could only sob bitterly in reply, and finally declare that nothing would induce her to trouble her darling Miss Evelyn. After that, the conversation continued in broken whispers; but Mummery heard the two appointing a rendezvous for the follohing evening. His curiosity was much excited, and he made up his mind to eavesdrop again. He then saw Mrs. Hrr ieksotake parcel- from her pocket and thrust it into her son's hands. "There," she said. "I'd rather die than give it to you. You don't know NA ha t this means to me, but I can't see you go under. Go away now at once. You daren't sell it hero where it's known. Go, you must, and don't ever come back again. This is the most I can do for you." "It is enough," Jacob Hickson answered, and then he kissed his mother and disappeared, crunching sonie fallen timber under his feet as he walked .away. Before the next evening Mummery had heard, as had all the employees on the estate, of the loss of the diamond and ruby necklace. Hp immediately thought of Rebecca and the mysterious parcel, but did not say anything about it until Lady Esther appeared on the scene and offered a substantial reward to anyone who -would lead to its discovery. Now, .!'innunely was poor and in debt himself, and theAlty pounds which he would certainly receive.' ftom Lady Esther was too good to lose. He consulted his wife and she agreed. with him, and the result was that the two appeared on a certain morning at Brookville Priory and asked for an interview with Lady Esther Selkirk and Mr. Tracy. Lady Esther was triumphant and terribly excited. Tracy was pained beyond words. But the imperious old lady had her way, and that very night Rebecca Hickson was lodged in prison to wait her trial before the magistrate.

_ The poor woman professed the utmost amaze- ment and her absolute innocence, but could not be got to say what she had given her son. For a long time she denied that he was in the country, but finding herself brought to book on this point, she finally acknowledged that he had come home in great difficulties, and that she had been forced to r'help him, but in what way she would not divulge. The whole of this story was, of course,.• repeated in court, and very black was tho evidence against Rebeeca. Owing to a rush of small trials, hers came on very late in the day, and in consequence the judge could not deliver his charge to the jury until the following morning. It was Thursday of Assize week when Rebecca Hickson's case came on, and that night the necklace was the talk of everyone at Tracy's table. Selkirk, in particular was much excited, and took the part of Rebecca Hickson in a very hot and almost intemperate fashion. "My dear boy," said Lady Esther, "your attitude is quite ridiculous. There isn't a doubt of the woman's guilt. Ido trust, my lord," she added, tundug to Greenfield, "that you will do your utmost to bring the woman to confession. I must get that necklace back." "I greatly fear it has been broken up and sold long before this," stdd Tracy. "You will probably have your revenge, Lady Esther, but I do not think you will ever see the necklace a gain. " "A good riddance! I hate the thing," mumbled Selkirk under his breath. • After dinner he and Evelyn went out. The ; night was a perfect one, the sky cloudless. The August full moon floated majestically in the . heavens.

"lam so miserable," said Evelyn, "that I scarcely know what to do. I shall never, never he happy again with my dear old nurse locked up in prison." j "I do wish she would confess," said Selkirk. , "Her obstinate silence with regard to the parcel she gave her son tells so much against her.'

"f went on my ku ols to her," said Evelyn. i"She clasped my hands and kissed me over and over, and kept on repeating: • 1 am innocent, my darling. I know I shall have to go to prison, but I won't tell—no, I won't. You must trust me, Miss Evelyn. I never took the neck- lace, but I know things are black against me. Still, I won't tell.'" As Evelyn spoke she burst into tears. Selkirk

did Nis best to comfort her, but he felt r:ry gloomy and depressed himself. The two talked for a little longer, and then Selkirk went off to bed, confessing that he had a bad headache and could not sit up any longer. He was subject to these attacks, which were generally of a very severe character. Evelyn went up to her own room, for she did not care to meet anyone else of the party. There was a wide, low balcony outside her windows, and the night being breathlessly hot, she went to sit there. The moonlight fell all over her slender, white-robed figure, and also on the gravel path which wound away into the thick shrubbery just beyond. One by one the lights were put out down- stairs, and the rest of the family retired to their respective rooms. Still Evelyn sat with her hands clasped before her, her eyes Thoking out into the distance. To go to bed was impossible. She could but remain where she was and think of the future. No longer was that future a happy one to the affectionate girl. She leved her nurse almost as much as though the poor woman had been in very truth the mother whose duties she had so nobly undertaken. Evelyn thought of her in all the long years of the past— her tenderness, her deep affection, her faithful love.

"This will kill her," thought the girl. "If she dies, and by this means, I shall never know a happy hour. Oh! why do girls get wedding presents? How miserable I am. Of course, my darling is innocent. But there is a mystery which she cannot explain:" Just then Evelyn was conscious of a slight stir in the house. It was the soft tread of a footfall. It passed her door, going downstairs and then being lost to sound. Evelyn's first idea was to follow it, but she did not do so. She stood up, however, on the balcony, for the sound which was no longer perceptible within the house, was now heard outside, and to her amazement, her almost incredulous astonishment, she saw Selkirk walking in a slow and uncertain fashion up the winding path which led to the shrubberies. He did not look behind him, but walked forward something as a drunken man would walk. He wore a dressing-gown with a belt round his waist, but no hat On his head.

Suddenly Evelyn clasped her hands to her heart as she recalled that Lady Esther had said that Christopher was addicted to sleep walking as a child, and he, himself, had confessed that he had not altogether lost the habit, but that under pressure of excitement, or in deep and unusual anxiety, it was apt to return to him. Imme- diately the girl resolved to follow him, to keep him, as she expressed it, from danger. She swiftly left the balcony, entered her room, and flew downstairs. She found a side entranco slightly ajar—no doubt Selkirk had let himself into the open air by this means. In a very short time she had gained his side and now walked softly by him, her white dress bru.hing his legs. He did not take the slightest notice of her. His eyes were wide open, and had the expression in them which anyone who watches a sleep-walker knows well.

By-and-bye he got into the very heart of tha wood, which joined on to the shrubbery. It was pine wood, and along the straight branches of the trees the moonlight shed a glittering and uncertain radiance. The white light lay in bars on the ground, and sometimes Selkirk and Evelyn were in shadow and sometimes in niu:it" brilliant light. _ _ _ _ _

Suddenly-Christopher stopped, and Evelyn saw that he had lowered • his gaze and wag looking down on the ground. The next instant, to her amazement, he went on his knees and began pushing away a lot of fallen leaves and dibris, smoothing the ground as he exposed it with the• palms of his hands. He then took a large clasp- knife from his pocket, unfastened a big blade, and began to dig up the earth. Evelyn watched him in breathless suspense. Ho dug up the earth for a space of several inches, and then thrust down his hand, uttered a sudden exclamation, and drew forth the glittering and lost necklace. He thrust it.at once into his pocket, and turned to go back to the house as quickly as he could. Evelyn followed him. She was trembling all over. She knew the danger of waking him, and had no intention of doing -so. She saw him safely back to the house, and even guided his footsteps as he tottered upstairs. She went with him as far as the door of his. room, saw him open it and go in, and then went to her own. The greater part of the remainder of that night the poor girl spent on her knees asking Providence what she was to do, and tremblingly thanking Heaven for her poor old nurse's escape. Early in the morning she went out, having first despatched a note to her lover asking him to join her without -a moment's delay. Ile came down- stairs, looking pale and anxious. "What is it, my darling ?" he said. "What h the matter? I have had a had night, and my head is still troubling me." "I must tell you something, Christopher," said Evelyn then. "And at once," she added, "for Judge Greenfield must be in possession of my information before he goes into court." ' She then told Christopher exactly what macl happened. He looked at her with his eyes full of incredulity. "The necklace is at this moment in the pocket of your dressing-gown," she said. "Come ui with me, and we will find it." Seeing was indeed believing, and the unhappy man had to confess that on the night the necklace was supposed to have been stolen, he had been suffering from the same sort of eppressive head- ache and had gone to bed to dream very badly. Beyond doubt he had taken the necklace and buried it in the wood in his dream.

The rest of the story is soon told. Of course, Rebecca was cleared, and when Selkirk app&ared in court and told his story, which he did in a- very manly, effective way, the excitement and interest and enthusiasm rose almost to furore. In fact, the decorum of the court was ve7 y nearly jeopardised. Rebeccffilwas at 011C3 acquitted, and thzlt night she slept in her old nursery, Evelyn insisting on sharing her couch. It. was just before the young girl dropped asleep that she bogged of Nurse Hickson to tell her what she had really given to Jacob. Amid tears which she could scarcely restrain, the old woman at last unburdened herself. It was the watch and chain left to her by her late mistress, and which she valued more than any-- thing else in life. "If you had ever known, Miss Evelyn, that I had given it to him I felt that I'd die," was her remark, "and in truth it seemed to me worth going to prison to keep it a‘secret. But I tell you now, my darling, for I seem driven to it." "And I forgive you with all my heart," said Evelyn, "and you shall have another watch end. chain from me on my wedding-day. But I know," added the girl, speaking in low tones, ."that if my mother could be aware of it, she would be very angry with you for running sueli an awful risk in order to keep such a secret."
THE END.I

div.p: LOCAL ODDFELLOWSIIIP.
Bro. Freeman Elected District Grand Master.

- _ The annual meeting of the Warrington District of the Indepe .dent Order of Oddfellows (Manchester Unity) was held on Saturday at the Pelican Hotel, when there were present Prov. brand laster Lot. Brooks, Prov. Deputy Grand Master G.F. Freeman, W. Holbrook, P.P.G.NI. Frank Webster (corresponding secretary) P.G. Thomas Wadsworth (district treasurer) and numerous delegates from the Lodges. The accounts and auditor's report for the year were Pissed and showed the worth of the district to be £3,479 19s. 10d., and a membership of 1,999. Sana 0. Ashton (Cadishead) was appointed auditor. P.P.G.M.T.P. Bradshaw and P.G. Walter Dennett Wore appointed lodge-book examiners. P.P.G.M. T. P. Bradshaw, P.P.G.M. William Holbrook, I.P.G.M. Lot Brooks and P.D.G.M. T. P. Forbes were appointed as delegates to the meeting of the Lancashire and Adjacent Districts' Conference to be held at Liverpool in February next. P.G. A. E. Spann (" Constitution "), P.P.G.M. Alban 13"10 (" Olive Branch "), and P.O. 11. Lawrence (" Prince of Wales "), were nominated as delegates to the annual Alovahle Conference to be held at Bradford in Whit-week. The selection will take place on the 10th April next. Prov. Depu.ty Grand Master G. F. Freeman ("Prince of Wales " Lodge), was unanimously appointed Grand Master of the District for the year.—P.G. Thomas P. Forbes (" Olive Branch ") and P.O. A. E. Burdett (" Constitution ") were nominated for Deputy Grand Master and the poll resulted in P.G. Thomas P, Forbes being elected.—P.P.G.A. James Massey ("Prince of Wales ") was appointed examining. and relieving officer, and grand tyler.—P.G. George Higharn was appointed sick visitor.

it wa-s—tiWtnimonsly resolved that the retiring Grand Master (P.P.G.M. div.head: ATTEMPTED SUICIDE AT STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: ATTEMPTED SUICIDE AT STOCKTON HEATH.

At the Warrington Occasional Court, on Tuesday, "before Mr. G. Pilling, Alfred Rickhuss, a spade maker, Was charged with attempting to take his life by cutting his throat with a knife at Stockton Heath on December 22nd, Ann Probed, a widow living at 43, Heath-street, Stockton Heatb,said that the prisoner had been a lodger at her house for about three months.He had often-com- Plained about his throat. On the Sunday preceding December 22nd, witness heard prisoner using very foul language in the presence of her children, and she then told him he would have to find fresh lodgings. The next two days witness was out washing, and about seven o'clock on the Tuesday evening her son James came and told her something about the prisoner. She went home and found a policeman and a doctor present. James Probert, aged 13, said he came home from work -on Tuesday, December 22nd, and after his tea he called to the prisoner to come downstairs or he would bring a policeman. When asked by Mr. Pilling why he sold this, the boy replied • that his mother wanted to get rid of the p risoner. The prisoner said, "I cannot come down my throat is cut. Go and bring a policeman and a doctor." Witness ran for Police-Constable Barber. P.C. Barber stated that upon receiving information from the last witness, he went to the house and found the prisoner in bed, end the bed clothes were saturated with blood. The prisoner told him that he had cut his thought because he had been suffering with it for a long time. He added that he would find the knife under the bed. Witness rendered first aid, and sent for Dr. Taylor, Who after examining the prisoner had him removed to the Warrington Inflrmary.On the 28th December,witness visited the infirmary and charged the prisoner with the offence,but he made no reply. • Prisoner stated that he had been drinking and that he did not know what he had done until he came round. Asked by Mr. Pilling if she would take prisoner back, Mrs. Probert replied that she was not willing to do so. Sergeant Barlow said the man had been working at the Stockton Heath Spade Works, but he had been dis- charged on eccount of inattention to his dirties, but they were willing to take him on again if it would help him in any way. Prisoner was a man with very sulky habits and his fellow workmen could not get on with him. Prisoner promised to behave himself in future, and it was decided to adjourn the case for a week in order to communicate with his relatives in Wolverhampton.
