div.head: SENSATIONAL PROSECUTION
div.p: SENSATIONAL PROSECUTION
SERIOUS CHARGES AGAINST M. LOUIS HMI-DILL.
Alleg,ed Forging of Inui33s.
mamma TO TIE ASSIZEiI

Great public interest centred in the prozyeedings at the Warrington Police Ciurt on Tuesday when the magisterial investigation of the charg,,'!s against Mr. Louis llenshall, Runnymede, Sto:diton He at), for 23 years connected with the firm of Messrs. R. A.. .Naylor, Ltd., timber merchants, Howley, was carnmence.i. The case occupied from 10.15 in the morni,:g to 4.39 in the afternoon (r,ith an hour's adjournment for InocheDa) and do ring the whole of that time the Conrt was crowded. Mr. Ilenshall was committed to take his trial at the Liverpool A..sizes on three charges of flrging invoices and it was announced that further allegations would be gone into to-day (Saturday.) The magistrates on the Bench were : —Mr. H. Roberts (in the chair) Aldermen Bolton and Smethurst, Coun- cillors Wilkinsonl and Evans, Messrs. W. Richardson, J. W. Hayward, H. Thornton' W. Roberts, C. Jackson Holmes, A. J. Jolley and W. Furness. Mr. Gordon Hewart, barrister, Manchester (instructed i by Messrs. Tatham, WorthingOn and Cu., solicitors, Manchester), conducted the prosecution and Mr. Henshall was represented by Mr. Rigby Swift and Mr. ' Morris, barristers, Liverpool (instruz.ted by Mr. T. S. Steel, solicitor, Warrington).
THE FIRST CHARGE. A GARDENING ACCOUNT.

The first charge against the prisoner was that of having during the month of October 1903, forged an invoice to R A. Naylor, Limited, from George Tandy, nurseryman, Latchford. ' Mr. Hewitt said it would be within the recollection of the Court that prisoner was arrested on a warrant granted on December 13th, and he appeared before the Court on the following day. There had been since that time successive remands and for the moment he did not propose to complete the charge of larceny upan which the prisoner was arrested—he would do that at a 1 dor stage—but he now proposed to offer evidence upon a charge of forgery. It appeared that in the later part of 1906 Mr. Tandy did some gardener's work for the prisoner privately at his house 61 Walton and sent in to Mr. flonshall an account for £l5 2s. The firm of R. A. Naylor, Limited, had nothing whatever to do with the work or with the account. Thereupon Mr. Henshall whose relation to the invoices he (Mr. Hewart) explained at the first hearing, made out an entirely new invoice from Mr. Tandy to R. A. Naylor, Limited, purporting to be fcr labour done and materials supplied by Mr. Tandy to the company, for the same amount-245 21. Then the prisoner, purporting to act in accord- ance with his duties an analysing the "invoices inwards" department, analysed the invoice to the department of "foreign timber" and it was so entered and treated in the company's books. Prisoner thus obtained a cheque drawn upan the company's account in the regular manner for £l5 2s. and by means of that cheque he paid his own personal indebtedness to Mr. Tandy. The receipt was handed back to the company and it was entered up as a payment of the company in respect of an account owing by them to Mr. Tandy. The prosecution would produce the false invoice which the prisoner prepared and substituted for his own invoice and that, he (Mr. llewart) sub nitted, was a clear case of forgery. He WAS gl id that the prisoner was defended by Mr. Rigby a wilt and Mr. Morris who would do everything that could be done on his behalf.

div.head: EVIDENCE.
div.p: THE EVIDENCE.

George Tandy, nurseryman, &c., The Ackers, Latch- ford, stated that from October 22nd, 1906 to December 23rd, 1996 he did sortie private gardening work at the prisoner's house at Lower Walton. The work consisted of entirely re-modelling the garden,plauting shrubs, Bcc. He produced his day book recording the job. He sent in a bill to the prisoner for £l5 2s. Oa January Bth, 1907, prisoner brought him a cheqqa for that amotint (produced) and witness endotsed it. The receipt pro- duced was also signed by witness. No part of the work, that he was aware of, was dons for the firm of B. A. Naylor, Ltd. Tne invoice produced, made out, to the firm, waa not authorised by him. By Mr. Swift: He knew sir. Elenshall was a director of Slessrs. Naylor's, bat he did not know what his financial relations with the firm wore. The bill he sent in to the prisoner was, among other things, for " materials supplied." Re-exirninoi by lit. Tiewart : The bill he sent in was for "renovating and re-modelling garden."

div.head: APPLICATION TO SEE THE-BOO:S.
div.p: APPLICATION TO SEE THE-BOO:S.

Mr. Swift said the prosecution had very fairly given him sufficient partlcular3 to direct his mind to five or six specific instances they were going to make charges abaut. At present, however, he hai not had the oppor- tunity of investigating Messrs. Naylor's books and it would be necessary, before Mr. Flenshall could disclose his full defence and develop it upon the lines he desired, that he should have an opportunity of investigating the books with regard to the different items. Therefore he (Mr. Swift) did not want the Bench to think that in the very limited crost-examination to which he should subject the witnesses, he was covering itavthing like the whole of the ground which must be covered before anybody could decide whether there was any justifica- tion for the charges made. It was not likely that the whole of the evidence would be completed that day, and if they could have an investigation of the books before the next adjournment it might save a further one. The investigation could be made by a chartered accountant, if they deemed it necessary after hearing the evidence that day. Mr. Rowed said that if Mr. S sift seriously intended to make such an application it would perhaps be well if it were renewed later on. [le could only say that it struck him as being a most unusual application. Mr. Swift said he did not make it at present as an application ; he threw it out as a suggestion. lie was quite sure that before the Bench decided whether or not there was a case to be sent for trial by a jury, they would give him every facility in disclosing the prisoner's case, if he deemed it right to do so. As the case for the prosecutien developed it might appear even to him that he was wrong in making the request ; at present he thought it would be essential to 5,33 the books in order that the defence might be properly conducted. .

Mr. Gewalt : My only observation upon that, at this stage, is this: My learned friend might be ablt. to see but my eyesight does not enable ma to see how an examination of our books may be necessary in order to explain why the prison9r, having received an account for the renovation of his garden, should debit us with it as foreign timber. Mr. Swift: My friend and I look at it from different points of view. Consultation then took place as to the most suitable date for the adjournment, the Chairman suggesting that it would probably be advisable that the same Bench should deal with the case right through, as far as practicable. Eventually to-day (Saturday) was decided up3n. ACCOINTANT'S IN VESTIG ATIO N.

Walter Mather, chartered accountant, Higher Broughton (with Messrs. D %rid Sinith,Garnett and Co., Manchester), said he had inspected the books of R. A. Naylor, Ltd., and the invoice from Mr. Tansy Ind been passed throulh the purchase analysis book and credited to NIT.. Tandy's accannt in the parchs.aa ledger. An entry had been made in the company's cash book of a payment to Mr. Tandy of a like amount and posted to his account in the purchase ledger. At the foot of the account produced was written "foreign timber." The passing through of the invoice was debited to "foreign timber." Prisoner himself had a ledger account with the company but there was no entry in that account of the item in question. There was no entry,so far as hecould discover, indicating that the work was done for the prisoner. By Mr. Swift: tie could not say whether the ledger account showed any money owing to Mr. Henshall on January Bth, 1907. He did not know whether there was anything else entered in the "foreign timber" accounts besides timber. Ho believed the accounts headed "foreign timber" were the accounts of a department of the business known as tho foreign timber department. He did not know, without referring to the books, whether the accounts contained items which were not the sale or purchase of timber. It was clear that the invoice pro- duced was not all for timher. The words " foreign timber " were merely an indioation to the book-keeper lof the account to which the item had to be placed. He did not know anything about Mr. Heushall's relations with the company. There were a number of different I departments to which accounts had to be allocated in I the analysis. SECRETARY CROSS-EXAMINED.

John Edwards, cashier and a director of Nfessrs. R. A. Naylor, Ltd., residing at The !follies, I.4ymm, stated that the invoice for £45 2s. against the compaoy was in the prisoner's handwriting. The cheque for that amount was drawn in the usual way upon the company's account at Parr's Bank Ltd., and was sirtned by Nil-. Jain Naylor, and also by witness. no worth a foreign timber " on the invoice meant that it must be decited to the foreign timber department. It was the prisoner's duty to indicate on the invoices to which department they were to be debited. His duty in that respect did not neces- sarily extend to all invoices but only to the general accounts of the co npany apart from the larger timber purchases. The alleged forged invoice had been kept in the possession of the company amongst the usual invoices and was dealt with throughout as a regular account of the company. The ch.opie was honoured by the bank and paid by the firm. By Mr. Swift: It might have happened that if an invoice was lost a rough invoice, similar to the one produced in this case, was made oat by some-one in authority in order to secure payment. Am I right in saying that betore any accounts were

I paid they all came before the directors ?—No. Did the directors take any interest in the accounts? —They had particulars of the payments. And the invoices on which the payments were made? —Not always. Do you really mean to tell us that the directors did not see the invoices ?—Not in all cases. Did they in the majority of the cases ?—No, they did not. I suggest to you that this invoice, with all the others, before it was paid would go before a directors' meet- ing ?—No. Who would see it before it was paid ?--Me. Henshall. Who else ?—The book keeper. Who else ?—f don't know of anyone else, necessarily. 133 you moan to say it would be left 'entirely to Mr. Henshall and the bookkeeper to say whether an account for £l5 should 63 paid ?e-At that time, yes. And who signed the chorine ? —Mr. John Neylsr and myself. - 191.1 yon ask whet it was for ?—No. Did Mr. John Naylor ?—I cannot sty. Did you see the ineoie3 ?-1. did not. . Was it on the file when you went and looked for it? —I did not look at the Ale. Where did you get the invoice from ?-ost of the °raillery invoices of the company. At the time you drew the cheque, do you think if you had gone to look yeti would have found the iavoice among the ordinary invoices of the compeny ?—I cannot say. Have you any reason for supposing you would not?— I cannot say. You can surely sty whether you have any reason for supposing you would not find it there ?—I don't know whether I would find it there or not. If you had found it there you could have seen it was in Mr. Hanshall's writing ?—Yes. 'You knew his writing quite well ?—Yes. And so did the book keeper ?—Yee. Everybody in Naylo-i'S place of business who SW it would know whose handwriting it was ?—I cannot say that. Everybody who had anything to do with the office would know it?—Probably. There is no attempt in any way to disguise it ?—No. I dare say you knew that in October, 1906, Mr. Ti enshall was making alterations at his house at ' Walton ?—I knew ho had been making alterations but whether that is the exact time I cannot say. I Had Naylor's got the slightest business going on at 1 Walton in October, 1936 ?—Not that I know of. Mr. Henshall, you know, has been with Naylor's for aboul 28 years ?—Yes, about the same length of time as myself. The company was formed in December, 1995. Do you know what the financial relations between Mr. ilenshall and R. A. Naylor's were at that time ?—No. Mr. Naylor and Mr. llenshell took 2,000 shares in the company and I dare say you know Mr. Henshall actually ' paid cash for 1,000 of those ?—Yes. He had been working in this business for 23 years ? Am I wrong in saying that Mr. Henshall was the Most prominout man in the business for a good part of hat time Y—l won't say he was the most prominent. From the business point of view ?-I.le was a promi- nent man. Mr. R. A. Naylor in the later years of his life did not do very much work at the businese ? —No. Did Mr. John Naylor do much—Yes. Did he get about as much as Mr. Heashall ?—He did not go about as much. . You know that Hr. Flenshall was also joined in the guarantee to the bank ?—Yes. And how much was due on that in January 1937 ?—I don't know. You are a director and cashier of this company?—Yes And the secretary ?—Yes. And you have come here to be cross-examined about its affairs to-day ?—Yes. You seem signally ignorant. Do you mean to say you don't know what the amount of the overdraft at the bank was in January 1907 Y—l do not. And you don't know how much Mr. flenshall along with the other directors was liaqle for on that account? —I am not aware that there wan an overdraft. Was there a guarantee ?—There was not. . Then why did you not tell us so? When was there a guarantee 2—ln 1908. Did Mr. Henshall join in the guarantee ?—Yes. How much is he liable for on that now ?—I don't know. Did you join in it ?—Yes. How much are you liable for ?—I don't know. , How much would you be liable for if you were called upon to pay ?—I cannot say. Anybody who looked at the invoice coral see it was not for foreign timber ?—Yes. Have you known on other occasions personal accounts of' the directors to be debited to departments ?—Yes, with the name of the director attached. Have you known personal accounts of directors to he debited to departments without the name of the director being attached ?—I have no recollection of it. If there are such, the books will disclose them F-- Yes. And the books will show whether or not Mr. Henshall in sending this account to be debited to the foreign timber department was following an ordinary custom or 'emetics in the business ?—They should do. Don't you know as a matter of fact, whether it was irregular or not, he was following the ordinary custom? —Yes. Mr. Hewett interposed with the remark that the ambiguity of the question was obvious.lf Mr. Swift was going to ask whether it was the ordinary custom that the account should be debited in that way he should put the invoice to the witness. It was one thing to say that the invoice which was analysed to foreign timber should ho passed through in that way; it was a totally different thing to say that a director, having received a private account from Mr. Tandy, should make out an account of another kind and passe that through. Mr. Swift: I don't think there is any ambiguity. (To witness.) Try and follow what lam suggesting— that it was an ordinary thing for directors' personal accounts to be debited to different departmental accounts.—No. Now you say" No," I will remirei you of what you said to us a minute ago. You say it was an ordinary tbingovith the director's name attached.— It was done occasionally. I suggest to you again that the course Mr. Henshall followed with regard to this particular account was a course which had been followed in other instauctes by other directors with regard to , their own personal accounts.—No. , I suppose any of the directors knew that Tandy was not a foreign timber merchant ?—I don't know whether the directors knew. Ido not know him at all. You would not expect to find Naylor's buying foreign timber from a man at Latchford ?—No. Is it not quite obvious that everybody connected with the company, seeing that account would knew perfectly well that it was a private matterlof Mr. Henshall's ? I don't know that they would.' They would not know it was a private matter of Mr. Henshall's. Re-examined by Mr. Hewart, witness said the com- pany ens incorporated on December 33th, 1905, and prisoner was a director from the outset. He was com- pletely trusted until quite recently—that was until the investigations which led to those proceedings. Witness had also been a director from the outset. Mr. Hewart : Have you ever known a case before this in which a director having received a personal account has then made out an account against the company in some respect corresponding to that personal account and has then passed i tovi thout his name attached at all, to a department of the company ?—Never. Was il*. John Naylor commonly called "Mr. John " at the works ?—Yes sir. . PRISONER'S REHARKATILE LI3TTER. Look at the fetter (produced.) In whose handwriting is it ?—The prisoner's. Mr. Tlewart then read the letter as follows :—" Dear Mr. John,—Please excuse my writing you, but Tam at home with nothing but my thoughts for company, and I have during the last few days suffered the pains of , remorse and reflection upon my misdoings, and it is a grief to me to know that I must have greived and dis- appointed you, and to realise that I have forfeited my right to your respect and losing my honour. There has filtered to borne all manner of statements, and my wife is in an agony of distress, and it makes my p inishment none the less to know I have been the cause of bring- ing terrible trouble into my domestic life. Alone I ; could endure the penalty. I railed at the office this morning ([6th December' 1908), hoping I could have the privilege of a few words with yon'. I think if you understood the conditions just now you would extend some measure of sympathy. The suspense of waiting makes it difficult for me to know what to do for the best. The cloud overhanging me must affect my future, though T nun desirous of making every amend to recover my self-respect." The Chief Constable said he charged the prisoner that morning in the terms in which he had been charged by the Clerk. He (witness) had in his possession at the time the document which prisoner eras charged with forging. Prisoner said " May Ise@ it ?" He then looked at it nnd said " Yes, that's right." In his (witness's) opinion all he meant was that the invoice was in his handwriting. • "A BOMBSHELL." . ! Mr. Swift said that as other charges were to follow ,it would be more convenient for the Bench to hear 'them all, and then he (Mr. Swift) would say what he had to say on behalf of the prisoner. Mr. Hewart submitted that if Mr. Swift wished to call any witnesses on the charge, now was the proper time. A statement on a point of law was a different matter, but the witnesses should come now. Mr. Swift said there was no reason in the world that he knew of why the Bench should not adjourn their decision.in that case wail they had heard the othersoand why he should not adjourn his part of the case until they had heard the complete prosecution. When a man in Mr. lionshall's position was charged with an offence of that kind, it was usual for every facility to be given to him for conducting his defence. The Clerk : If Mr. Swift wishes to call witnesses specially on this case he should call them now. Mr. Swift s till that it the other cases had no more substance than the present one he might agree to fight that out to the bitter end and call all the esidence be bad got but if there was something coming along on which he must go for trial, it was no use fighting that. If he bad to go to the Assizes at all, he would go on everything. Mr. Hewed said that if the prisoner was to remain

silent and refrain from calling any evidence until the COSOIITTED FOR FRIAL. whole of the cases for the prosecution had been heard The magistrates deliberated in private and on their by the Court and was then to have the option of return the Chairman announced that they had decided giving evidence upon all or any of then, it was quite that the prisoner must go for trial at the Assizes on the obvious that he would be in a much better position to charge. deal with the evidence as a whole than he would be if Having been cautioned in the usnal Way,Mr. llenshall he had to deal with one charge, Tillibut quite know- replied: " lam not guilty. I never intended to defraud lag what the evidenupen the sulisequent charges was, the company of a penny." Mr. Seift : Then my friend supports my applica- A discussion then took place on the question of bail, tiou. I never in my life heard it suggested that the Mr. Elevvart contending that it should only be con- Crowa did not do its best to lilt the accused person in sidered when all the charges had been disclosed. the best possible position. 11Iy friend helps me to put Mr. Swift said Mr. Ilenshall was arrested on December ray client in the best pAition, and he is entitled to be 18th, and he had appeared at the Court regularly. in it. Nobody suggested that he did not intend to come and

Mr. Howart : My Meters vehemence of manner shows that he perfectly understands my meaning. Mr. Swift.: lam shocked at the suggestion of the Crown seeking to take an advantage of a prisoner. Mr. Howart : There is no suegestion of the kind. Mr. Swift.: It cannot mean auvthing else. Mr. Hewed : I have never heard it said that a prisoner is entitled to hear the full evidence regarding every chtrge against him before he decides what explanation he is going, to offer as to one. Mr. SA-if : I never before knew charges to be taken piecemeal like these, without the whole story ' being opened. I have invariably hoard the case opened against the prisoner, everything alleged against him that can be alleged,end the witnesses called against him, and then the prisoner is called upon to make his answer. Mr. Hewart My friend was not here on the first dty when I outlined the scope of the charges. Sir. Swift : I cannot fight an outline. I want con- crete cases before I can deal with them. Mr. Hewart said that if the Bench were of opinion that it would be in the interests of the prisoner to have all the charges against him thoroughly disclosed before he offered evidence or made any statement with regard to any one of them, and if they considered that was an advantage the prisener was entitled to have, he (Mr. Hewart) would offer no objection. Mr. Swift: Teat is, if the Bench decide against my friend, he won't object. (Laughter). Mr. Hewett : Oh, no. I say that before the decision is given. My friend is not entitled to make that remark. The Chairman gild the Bench thought the prosecation should submit sach cases as could be dealt with that day, and the defence should be called upon for the defence to those charges that day. The Clerk said the question of bail would then arise. Mr. Hewarte My instructions are at the close of this hearing to resist any application for bail. Mr. Swift: That is a very startling proposition. I don't understand it. Supposing Mr. Henshall were to be committed for trial to-day on every one of these charges.— The Chairman: It is hardly fair to ask us to express an opinion on the question of bail now. Mr. Swift: lain only commenting on my friend's bomb-shell and trying to prick it. • Mr. Hewart : I don't know what pricking a bomb- shell means—(laughter)--but I was merely answering the suggestions of my friend. Eventually Mr. Swift said that having regard to all the circumstances he thought it would be most con- venient for him to deal with the charges one at a time , but he asked the Bench to do the same and to decide whether or not Mr. Henshall was to be committed for trial in that case before any others were gone into. SPEEMI FOR TIE DEFENCE. Mr. Swift, in hi a address for the defence, said he hoped and believed that the justices would banish from their minds the fact, that there were other charges to be brought against the prisoner, and deal solely with the present case as though it were an isolated instance. First he would ask the Bench to consider the man against whom the charge was made. Of all the prominent officials of R. A. Naylor, Limited, only Mr. Edwards, who seemed to be happily ignorant of most things that had been going on, had been put into the witness box. Mr. John Naylor, the most prominent and most active member of the board of direetors, had not been put into the box end all that Mr. Edwards could tell them about grAlenshall was that for 23 years he had been taking an active part in the business—long before it was turned into a limited company ; that until they started investigating the books when, he (Mr. Swift) supposed somebody made some suggestions against Mr. Elerishall and they found this instance amongst some others, he was a roan who enjoyed the fullest con- fidence of everybody with whom he was brought into contact. What was the evidence against Mr. Henshall? There was absolutely no dispnte about it as far as it went, and his (Mr. Swift's) only complaint was that it did not go far enough. The prosecution had selected a gentleman to give evidence who did not know enough about the transactions, and the gentleman who did know, Mr. John Naylor, had not been put into the box. Mr. Henshall, having had work done at his own house, received an invoice. That invoice had disappeared. The prosecution had not got it ; it might still be among Mr. ffensholi's papers or gone altogether, he did not know, hut until they came there that morning they knew nothing about the invoice. Mr. Henshall put the invoice in his own handwriting—he did not pretend to make it an invoice from Tandy—and everybody who saw it knew that for some reason or other he had written the invoice. The prosecution alleged that there must be something improper about that. According to Mr. Edwards, however, there were occasions—he (lid not say they were many—when invoices were lost or torn or, for some reason, were not in a fit condition to be put on the file or go before the directors, and the person in authority instead of taking the trouble to get another, copied the invoice from memory on a slip of paper. The invoice Mr. Henshall made out was for "work done and materials supplied at Walton." Every director and every clerk in the office knew that Walton meant Mr. Hensl•all's house. Mn Henshall's openly handed the invoice to the book-keeper and wrote upon it, "Debit this to foreign timber." There was the absence of the first essentials of forgery—concealment and disguise. Everything was open and straight- fortiard. The prosecution had not called a solitary individual to say this was not open and straightforward, and yet they asked the Bench to say that because the document had been put to the foreign timber account instead of being debited against Mr flenshall private account., Mn, Haushall had sacrified the position he had • so long and honourably held and had become a common forger with intent to defraud. They had a reasonable explanation of how the invoice ewe to be entered in the foreign timher account.. He was not going to say it was a regular or proper way or doing business for directors personal accounts to be debited to departmental expenses. There was a great deal of difference between improper methods of hook-keeping and forgery or larceny. Mr. Henshall was only doing what it was admitted by Mr. Edwards other directors did, with the exception that the others attached their names, and he could not tell whether there were not some acceunte in which that bad not been done. This explanation did not make the thing right and proper. It showed great laxity in the book-keeping and great irregularity on the past of Mr. Flenshalt arid other directors, but there was the greatest difference in the world between irregularity and forgery and between bad book-keeping and fraud, lie suggested tnat the prosecution had net put the case in a way that justified the Bench in sending prisoner for trial. The prosecution did not evee produce the book showing the foreign timber account. They simply put forward Mr. Edwards, who knew nothing. He did not know what the relations between Mr. flenshall and Naylor's and Mr. ilenshall and the bank were. Why hadn't Mr. John Naylor and the people who dealt with the books come? ! Because they did know something. They would have to admit irregularities in the book-keeping that had been going on since the compsily started. Mr. Ifewart : I don't waut to interrupt— Mr. Swift : Considering that you don't want • to interrupt, you interrupt very frequently. Mr. liewart : My friend is entitled to make any argument ha likes on the evidence offered, but he is not entitled, if he is not going to call evidence, to make statements purporting to be statements of fact, unless he is going to prove thorn. Mr. Swift said he was permitted to comment on the absence of people and suggest reasons, and he was suggesting Mr. Naylor had not gone into the witness box because he would have bad to have admitted that he knew the things he (Mr. Swift) had put to Mr. Edwards and which Mr. Edwards did not know. It could not be said he (Mr. Swift) had shirked that issue. He hari.cross-examined.the only witness the prosecution had called, and had Widited from him the very depths of his ignorance, and it was not his fault the prosecution bad kept out (if the box people who did know something. He suggested that the fact that they had kept them out went to show that whet lie was putting to Mr. Edwards was indeed true, and these irregularities had been com- mitted by everybody. The Chairman : You suggest that other directors have bad their personal accounts charged up to depart- mental accounts, the only difference between them and the case of Mr. Henshall being that in their case they had their names attached ? Mr. Swift: Yes, that is what I suggest. Mr. Edwards said lie does not know cases,—and I cannot point them out—where names have not been added. It is quite clear there is absolutely no frend, although I agree there is gross irregularity. Mr. Se ift concluded by asking the Bench to come to the conclusion that they were not going to send a man of Mr.llensliall'e position or of any other pesition for trial on a charge of such gravity on the 'evidence which had been offered. The prosecution had failed to make out their case and the charge ought to be dismissed.

it was iidiious to suggest that he should not have bail. The. Chairman said the Bench had decided to allow bail on the same terms as previously in that case, on the understanding that when the whole of the cases were heard, if the serious nature of them produced any change of opinion,the Bench would be unfettered in their action as to granting orarefusing bail at that stage. The Court then adjanrned for lunoheon. MORI?. C:IARGES. On resuming the prisoner was charged with having in or about the month of April, 1907, knowingly and falsely forged and conntarfeited a certain writing purporting to be an invoice dated 30th March, 1907, from J. S. Garland to R. A. Naylor, Ltd., with intend to defraud ; also with having, in or about August, b 1903, I falsely forged and counterfeited another writing par- parting to be an invoice from Willia:n Stubbs to R. A. j Naylor. ! Mr. Ifewart in explaining the first charge said Mr. Garland was an ironmonger carrying on business in Bridge-street. On the 30th March, 1997, he rendered to the company on account of £lO 03. id. for goods properly delivered by Messrs. Garland to the company. • The prisoner at that time had a personal account with j Mr. Garland and he was at that time indebted to Mr. ! Garland in the sum of something over £ll5. The invoice j from Garland's to the comp tny of £lO Os. id. came into ! the hands of the prisoner, who thereupon added below the account as it then steed a further item "Corrugated j sheets as per contract, £115," making the total invoice £125 Os. Id. Having done that the prisoner obtaieed ; from the cashier of the company a cheque for £ll5, and he paid it to Mr. Garland on account of his own indebtedness to Mr. Garland. The cheque was honoured and paid, and the money, therefore, came from the moneys of the company, and Heushall returned the receipt for £ll5 to the company as if the payment had properly been made on account of the company's own indebtedness. From that time onwards the prisoner made no attempt to repay any part of the £ll5 until the beginning of the investigation which led to the present. proceedings—and,he was told, not even then with regard to that particular amount. The second case, continued Mr. Tlervart, was a some- what similar one except that in this case it was not altering a genuine invoice, but the making of a wholly false one. Whether it be making or altering an invoice it was forgery. The prisoner had an account with the \Varrington Motor Carriage Company, Limited, in Sankey-street, and on the 18th August last year be owed them a sum of £24 ss. 41 for motor covers and repairs to covers. That was entirely a personal account. Having received from the Carriage Company an invoice for that sum he made out an entirely new invoice "William Strilahs. Sankey-street, Warrington, in account with R. A. Naylor' for sundry fittings, iron bars, £24 ss. 41," precisely the amount of his own personal indebtedness. Thereupon the prisoner, dealing with the new invoice he had made, and purporting to. deal with it in the coarse of his duties, analysed it as belonging to the joinery department of It. A. Naylor and he marked the account "Joinery, £24 55. 4d." He obtained a cheque from the cashier of the company for .C 24 deducting ss. 4d. as discsunt and with that cheque for £24, which he personally took to the Carriage Company, he paid oft his own personal account of £24 ss. 4d. At that time the system in vogue in the company's business with regard to receipts was that they had endorsements which constituted a receipt— the endorsement on the cheque furnished the receipt to the company, and the cheque was returned in due course to the company by way of a receipt. He (Mr. Hewart) submitted that on these facts also there was a clear case of forgery. With regard to the first of the • two charges, continued Mr. Hewed, where £ll5 was added, purporting to be for corrugated sheets, as per contract, the prisoner analyzed the invoice in the usual way, and he marked it as far as the £ll5 was concerned I "outside contract," and it was so entered in the books ' of the company. MR. GARLAND CALLED. Ernest S. Garland, builder and furnishing ironmonger, Bridge-street, Warriuton' stated that in March 1907 he had an account against Messrs. R. A. Naylor Ltd. for various goods supplied, the total of which was £lO Os. Id. Ho sent in an account for that sum (pro- duced).There were nowadded to that account the words "corrugated sheets, as per contract,'£lls." Witness did not add those words, nor was the handwriting that of anyone in his employ. He did not authorise anybody to make that additioa. The cheque (produced) for £ll5 was duly received by witness from the firm of R. A. Naylor, Ltd., endorsed by him and cashed. Witness had a ledger account with R. A. Naylor Ltd., and also one with the prisoner' In May 1907 prisoner owed him on his own personal account a sum exceeding £ll5 —the exact amount of his indebtedness on May 6th was between £3OO and £4OO. There was no particular item of £ll5 but .there was one of £lll for miscellaneous goods. The amount of the indebtedness of R. A. Naylor Ltd. to him when he sent in the invoice of March 30th was only £lO Os. id. On May 7th they owed him between £2O and £3O. By Mr. Morris: The miscellaneous goods supplied to Mr. Henshall were things connected with motor cars. The rest of his iudebtedness was the cost of a motor car which cost approximately £5OO. Mr. Henshall had paid him part of that account, partly by his own cheques and partly by exchange. He was not sure whether he received the £ll5 cheque with a letter. He supposed the cheque represented payment on account of the car, As far as he was concerned,whether it was paid for by Messrs. Naylor's cheque or the prisoner's was a matter for private arrangement. He believed he had seen the prisoner and that he had said he would let him have a cheque —whose cheque he did not say. Witness did not credit R. A. Naylor's account with any part of the cheque. Mr. Henshall and he often had convegsations together and witness took it that the cheque was for Mr. Ifenshall's account. He understood there was an arrangement between Mr. Hensliall and the firm that they should each pay a proportion of the account. He knew the car was used for Messrs. Naylor's business purposes. Messrs. Naylor had paid him accounts for motor accessories, but whether the firm had owned motor cars during that time he could not say. He did not think Mr. John Naylor had had any dealings with him for motors or accessories. By Mr. thwart : When he received the £ll5 cheque he did not. knew an item had been added to the account for "corrugated sheets as per contract." The account was not returned to him. Having received the cheque for £ll5 he applied it in reduction of prisoner's indebetdness. lie never pressed Mr. Henshall to pay his account. When prisoner said lie would send a cheque on witness bad no doubt that he meant it to be for the reduction of Mr. Heushnll's account.: Messrs. Naylor in paying accounts usually sent a cheque in full settlement and not on account. They did not owe him anything for corrugated sheets on March 30th or May 6th. Mr. lienshall was a personal friend of his and lived next door. Prisoner had no interest in witness's business. He said he knew the car was used for the purposes of the company not, because he had seen the car used for the purposes of the company but because he had seen the car previously owned by Mr. Henshall so used. William Henry Lazenby, Ackers lane, Lntchford, book', keeper in the employ of Messrs. Garland, produced al receipt signed by himself for the cheque in question.l The body of the invoice for £lO Os. Id. to Messrs. R. A.. Naylor, Limited, was in witness's handwriting but the line " corrugated sheets as per contract, £115" was not raten by him. By Mr. Morris : He received the 'cheque from Mr. Garland. He had never seen a letter relating to it and did not know how it came. MOTOR REPAIRS TRANSACTION. Robert Unwin Stubbs, secretary and manager of the Warrington Motor Carriage Company-, Ltd., and as justice of the peace for Cheshire, said his company had an account with Messrs. It. A. Naylor, Ltd. and origin- , ally had one with the prisoner which was kept distinct and separate from the company's. On June 300, 1903, prisoner came to the shop and gave an order to witness personally for new covers to motor car tyres and the re-treading of an old one. He assumed that the car belonged to Mr. Henshall, hut could not say so psi. tively. The work was done and an account for £l9 83. 10d. was sent in to Mr. Henshall. As the account was not paid another account was sent, with sundry additions, making £2l Or. 4.1. A cheque for £24 drawn on Messrs. R. A. Naylor's account was subse- quently received in payment of the account and cashed, prisoner's account being credited with that sum. At the date the cheque was made payable the amount owing by Messrs. R. A. Naylor Ltd., was £5 12s. id. By Mr. Morris: Mr. Ilenshall had not had many transact ions with the firm.lfe had paid for other work in cash. Meszas. Naylor Ltd.'s account for the year end- ing July 1903 was under £3O; this being for work done to motor cars and sundries supplied. When they did repairs, they were carried out on •Messrs. Naylor's premises. Prances E. Lawton, book-keeper in the employ of the Motor Carriage Co., I.td., said the car to st hich the repairs had to be made was Mr. Henshall's. The cheque for £24 was handed to her by Mr. ilenshall, who said it was in settlement of the account. She was going to make out a receipt but prisoner mild it was not necessary as the endorsement of the cheque constituted a receipt. She credited the cheque to Mr. ilenshall's account. Edward Howard, Latchford Without, clerk in the employ of Messrs. It. A. Naylor, I.td., said the invoices (produced) to Mr. Ilenshall personally were found in a package on a shelf behind a door in the stores depart- melt. It was most unusual for any package to be there. He believed the discovery was made on the afternoon of the day of prisoner's suspension. By Mr. Morris ;. lie found the package by accident.. It might have been put there with the intention of being taken away ; he did not suggest it was hidden. The package also contained some books relating to the timher trade. The cheque in payment of the account was made out by Mr. Edwards, the secretary.
The Premier Cocoa at Popular Prices.

John Edwards, director and cashier of Messrs. E. A. Naylor, Ltd., stated that the addition re "corrugated sheets" to Messrs. Garland's account was in Mr. Henshall's handwriting. The analysis of the invoice written across it indicated to what department it had to charged. The company's analysis book showed that the account was analysed according to prisoner's instruc. tions and £ll5 was debited to "outside contracts." The cheque was signed by witness and Mr. John Naylor. It was drawn in the usual form of a cheque to be. psid on the firm's account. The company's ledger account showed a payment of £ll5 to Messrs. Garland on May 6th. The cheque was drawn by witness and the receipt came into his possession. The invoice purport- ing to be one of William Stubbs in account with Messrs. Naylor was in Mr. Henshall's handwriting. It was marked "joinery" which meant that it had to be debited to that department. The alleged counterfeit invoice was found amongst the invoices of the company and it was entered in the books as if it had been for joinery work done for the company. The cheque for I £2l in payment of the account was made out by witness ' and had been passed through the company's bankers. By Mr. Morris : lie found ',oth UtO iIIVOiCe4 on the Company's account 111Js. Tao . motor car that Messrr. Naylor Ltd. had was in October, 1933. Several of the directors had cars of their own. The accounts would not come before witness after analysis. The item analysed "motor cars"on one of the accounts was charged to Nlr.John Naylor as there was no "motor car" department. He did not know of any cases where things had been booked under any head of analysis and 11 had really been paid on the private acconnt of a 'director. Mr. Henshall passed the invoices and when they had been passed by him they were finished with. By Mr. Hewart : There was no secrecy about the debiting of the "motor car " amount to Mr. John Naylor at the end of the year. It was the accepted method. Walter Nattier, chartered accountant, said he had gone through the books of the company with regard to the transaction with Messrs. Garland. He found entries of the kind deposed to by Mr.Eilwards and corroborated' his evidence as to the method of dealing with the transaction. He had examined the account of the prisoner with the company and did not find anything in it relating to the payment of £ll5 to Messrs. Garland. The burden had been borne by the company. With regard to the account with the Warrington Motor Carriage Company he found the invoice for £l4 had passed through tho company's books in the regular way and had been paid by them. There was nothing relating to the item in prisoner's private account with the company. The Chief Constable stated that he charged the prisoner with the two alleged offences and he made no reply. __

Morris said these cases werevery similar in details to the one on which prisoner had already been committiA for trial and it would be idle for him to ask the Bench not to send the prisoner for trial on those CrtSeS as well.
Prisoner Ns-I,s then committed for trial at the Liver- pool Assizes on these charges. Having been cautioned, he replied "Not guilty." TRH QUESTION OF BAIL. FURTHER SERIOUS CHARGES.

Mr. iTewart, addressing the Bench on the question of bail, said he thought it was within their knowledge that information had been laid on the part of Mr. R. A. No.vlor'3 executors, by Mr. Edwatds, of two cases of larceny, one of £5OO and the other of £409. Mr. Morris : I thought we were to deal with these cases as they arose. My friend is speaking of something I know nothing about and I really protest. The Chairman: Are you ready with any further charges now? Mr. Hewart said he was, and probably one case would last another hour and a half.

I To meet the convenience of counsel on both sides it I was decidad to adjourn until to.day. IMr.llewart said the three forgery charges were complete_ lie mentioned the information laid that day because the I usual sequel was the issuing of a warrant, but as 1 prisoner was in custody on other charges they did not propose to take that course, and those cases would come on in their turn. He understood there were other charges to come. lie submitted for the serious con- sideration of the Bench, these facts when they were taking into consideration the question of bail. lie did not want to make any emphatic observations on the point but he was instructed—and he was not surprised to be instructed—to oppose bail. ' Mr. Morris said Air. tiewart had told them of some- thing he had never heard of before, in introducing the charges to be made by the executors. The Clerk : It was mentioned the tlrst day by Mr. Hewart that there would probably be charges on Lehalf of the executors.

Mr. Morris, continuing, said Mr. Tfeashall was on substantial bail, amounting to £2,090, and had shown every indication of his willingness to come and meet the charges. There was not the slightest ground for saying he would not come forward. It was important that ho should be allowed bail because they wanted his assistance to go into these matters. He suggested it would be a cruel hardship at the request of a private firm prosecuting in this way to deprive a man of his liberty. The magistrates discussed the matter in private for about ten minutes and on their return into Court the Chairman said : I am hound to say that I am only expres.;ing the views of my colleagues by stating that, in view of the very grave nature of the charges which have beon made, the Bench have had considerable difficulty in deciding whether bail should be granted or not. We have, however, decided to grant it on the distinct understanding. of course, that it is in addition to the bail already provided for; that ,is to say,, that if Mr. fienshall is bound we propose another £1,030 and two sureties of £503 each.

Mr. Morris : That means two persons other than those we have already. The Clerk : The same persons will do. This makes the total bail ..£4,0:10. Two additionll sureties were forthcoming aril Mr. Henshall was liberated about seven o'clock.

WE.LEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL.—The children attending this school were entertained at the annual tea party last evening week. Tea was followed by a bright little service for the younger children in the church,conducted by the Rev. T. Gladding and Mr. Jarman. Mr. John E. Richardson, of Warrintton, presided over the enter- tainment which began at 6.30, and referred to the fact that his father, the late Mr. Edwin Richardson, left to his executors the sum of .£25 to be given either to the Sunday school or the church, whichever made the first move for extension. The workers of the recent bazaar having allocated £5O from the bazaar profits to a school enlargement fund, he (Mr. Ri3hardson) as one of the executors had very great pleasure in placing the £25 to the credit of the ne.v building fund at once, so making a nucleus of £75 to bnin with. The programme con- sisted of the items given by the children at the previous evening's congregational tea meeting, with certain additions. Special praise is clue to the Misses Lillie Ward and Bertha London who were responsible for the training of the youthful performers. The prizes were distributed by Mrs. Wright. Alderman Bennett proposed a comprebonsive vote of thanks,Nhich was seconded by Mr. F. Wright, and cheers were given by the children for all who had helped to make the tea party so successful.

The old idea of the two WHAT THE Houses of Parliament was LORDS ARE that they should work DOING. tegether for the same ends, and that, in fact, oRe should complete the work of the other, instead of, as under existing conditions, destroying it. Lord'l Commissioner FIENNES, discoursing on this subject in the Commonwealth period, said: "This constitution of a chief magistrate and two Houses of Parliament is not a pageantry ; but a real and well-measured advantage to itself and to the Commonwealth, and is so consonant to reason that it is the very emblem and idea of reason itself, which reasoneth and discourseth by a medium between two cxtremes." Hardly any language could be less applicable to the present relationship of the two Houses of Parliament. The House of Lords resembles nothing so little as a medium between two extremes. With the exception of about fifty of its Members, it is as much a party organ as it could be if it were a mere Conservative association. It is now thirty years or more since the late LORD SELBORNR described it as committee of the Carlton Club. It now deserves that descrip- tion more than ever before, though the party arrangements are made, not in a corn mittee-room in Pall Mall, but in the drawing-room of Lansdowne House.
We inquired yesterdlry se to- BEHOLD THOsE the progrees of the Warring-- MARKS! ton Bridge scheme, and were

informed' that it: was- i&ic nubibus. This is an old store cupboard for highly— contentious proposals, but we really thought that the new scheme had escaped from custody,. and that it was now hindered only by a question of 61 feet or 80 feet in width. Is has been noticed that, certain significant marks have been painted ofl. the river walls on either side the bridge, and thee& are taken as optical illustrations of the difference between the suggested widths. But if the marks, are any real indication of the position of the new bridge, then now is a suitable time to protest.. Taking an imaginary line from bank to, bank and mark to mark it is clear that the bridge is to be swung round to the west,. and will swallow up Bridge lon. Like a photo grapher selecting his picture and getting the centre, the person responsible for these significant:paint marks seems to have determined to include the public-house. If the line had been taken a little to the eat of the present bridge it would have cleared this expensive licensed property even at 80, feet, and would have brought. linutsford-road and Bridge-street into something likes straight course. The ratepayers must take care to see and insist that when the bridge scheme re-Appears in tangible I form it shall not be burdened with unnecessary I and extraneout. expenditure.

After two Sessions of pro- TORIES IN OFFICE. gressive Liberal administra- tion in the Parliamentary Debating Society the Tories have at last succeeded to the fruits of office—and have shown their characteristic fondness for the same by appointing nearly every member of their party under the Government. S.) far as numbers go the new Ministry and Officers of the Crown make quite a formidable array, but in the eyes of the Opposition their solidity merely represents a target of such dimensions that it can hardly be missed by the most haphazard shot. Such lights of local Toryism as Alderman Bennetc,Councillor Fulton Smith and Councillor Broadhurst have been imported—free from tariff restriction—and now adorn the Ministry. Lively times are obviously in prospect, for the new Government is pledged to Tariff Reform and its leaders will have to stand a heavy battering from the Free Trade forces opposite and all around. The "King's Speech " has already drawn the enemy's fire, and the Tory substitute for Home Rule, in the shape of a Royal Residence in Ireland is likely to be the subject of caustic criticism. Ireland has had enough of King's and castles as the member for Kilkenny S. observed with reason. The Tories also promise to place Old Age Pensions "on a more satisfactory basis." Their efforts in this direction should be interesting, seeing how signally they have failed in the past to do any more than promise pensions. The new Session opens with the brightest prospects from a debat- ing point of view, but the resignation of the Liberal leader is a great blow to the progressive forces. Mr. Upson made such a staunch and vigorous Premier, that as Leader of the Opposition he would have been par excellence. Can he not be persuaded to re-consider the position

There is danger that the work of the House of Lords durirg the lifetime of the present Parlia- ment may be insufficiectly appreciated. On that ground we congratulate the editors of the "Liberal Year-Book" on having compiled an exact statement of the case. During the year 1906—within, that is to say, a few months of the General Election— the Lords either wrecked, rejected, or mutilated six bills. These were not insignificant measures. They were, for some part, of the first importance, including Mr. BIERELL'S Education Bill, the Plural Voting Bill, and the Agricul- tural Holdings Bill. The carnage of the following year was rather less extensive. One bill had to be withdrawn, another was rejected and a third was subject to mutilation. The with drawn bill, which dealt with Small Holdings in Scotland, was again sent up to the Lords during the present year, and was then rejected outright. Another Scottish bill, dealing with Land Valuation, was hopelessly wrecked. The Miners' Eight Hours Bill was converted into an E Half Hours Bill; and, as harilv anybody can fail to remember, the Licensing Bill was thrown out almost without formalities, and as the result of a vote taken, not in the House of Lords, but at the residence of Lord LANSDOWNE. In three years, that is to say, the Peers have either destroyed or eviscerated thirteen of the most important and well-considered measures of the Government. That is a bigger bag than it has ever before made in a period so brief. The House of Lords is not likely to do in any three years of its existence as much good as it has prevented during the three years which have elapsed since the General Election. _ -

For Rll the legislative proposals which it has put forward, the present Government, if not an express mandate, has at least as signal an expres- sion of public approval as is possible under our electoral system. Each of the measures destroyed or mutilated by the House of Lords was a well- understood portion of the party programme. The House of Lords has not been opposing itself to hastily-conceived legislation, or to a Government of adventure. It has deliberately placed itself in opposition to measures demanded by the people through the medium of the largest majority ever sent to the House of Commons. It thus,of course creates an intolerable situation. There can be no government by the people for the people so long as the Peers, pretending to understand the public Imind better than the majority of the electors, ' deliberately override the House of Commons in the interests of a defeated party. We are, con- sequently, on the eve of a struggle with the House of Lords which must be more momentous in its issues than those of 1832. And for our own part we have not the least uneasiness as to the result. The power of the House of Lords will be broken once for all.

SPIRITUALISTIC absurdities inseparable front- TARIFF REFJIIII. the working of a system of protective tariffs we have heard nothing to equal a story which comes from Australia. It has arisen out of what is called a " materializatiou "in Spiritualistic circles. Certain material things are claimed to have been produced by Spiritualistic agencies out of nothing. These " goods " if they were imported would be subject to a duty and the collector of customs in Victoria Mr. Smart, seems to have an idea that the goods in question have not paid duty. We do not know if his opinion is that th 3 goods have been smuggled, or whether he accepts the claim of the Spiritualists that they have been " materialized by agencies from another world. If this be the case the question is whether this other world should be treated in the same manner as countries in this mundane sphere, and whether such imports are subject to duty ? The further question is in what way can the spiritual visitors be called foreigners and be made to pay the duty? It is difficult enough to get the foreigner to pay on this side of death, but it seems almost impossible to present a bill to another world and have any hope that the liability will be met. A further problem arises as to whether the spirit world should be treated on the preferential basis ; could it any sense be called one of our Colonies ? If preference were given to such imports could we claim that our exports to the land of shadows should receive preference when as disembodied spirits we pass into the unknown? We give it up and refer the question to the President of the Warrington branch of the Tariff Rform League who has previously evidenced a good working knowledge of the chimerical.

caent's Old Age Pensions Act. Authoritative information shows that the total number of old age pensions paid in the first week of January is 501,263, and even if the 7,000 cases which have been appealed to the Local Government Board are all decided in favour of the applicants, the number will still be considerably fewer than the original estimate made by the Government. The Chancellor of the Exchequer calculated that the total number of pensioners would not exceed -570,000, and it is now clear that he was well within the mark. Of course, in the current year a good many people will reach the age of seventy and become entitled to a pension ; but, on the other band, a certain proportion of the existing pen- sioners will die. It is, however, pretty clear that so long as the age is retained at seventy the total number will not exceed the official estimate of 570,000. The actual cost of the scheme will not be more than £6,500,000, instead of £8,000,000 which some people have predicted. The Old-Age Pension Act has brought a great deal of heavy ' work on the President of the Local Government Board. In all, about 7,000 appeals were made to the Local Government Board, and of these Mr. Burns personally ermined no fewer than 3,000.
"The Times" is doing all THE "TIMES" it can to belittle the CAUGHT TRIPPING, speeches of Free Trade

stalwarts, and to further the cause of Tariff Reform. ut when it con- descends to use logic and argument,the Thunderer is apt to get into a knot with its idea of extract- ing national prosperity from a scientific system of protective tariffs, and in its leading article it was caught tripping only the other day. The article was on "The Prospect of Tariff Reform,"and contained the following significant passage, which we have italicised for Free Trade consumption : Undoubtedly the moderate protection of such of our great national industries as have suffered, and are suffering now, from the unfair corn.- petition of well-protected rivals will do much to lessen the burden of unemployment under which the country is groaning. Undoubtedly the broadening of the basis of revenue is to our welfare from even the most insular point of view. But it is well at the same time to bear in mind that the adoption of a moderate degree of pro- tection will lead inevitably to demands for succour from many industries which on broad national grounds may not deserve support, and that the very distress which may hasten the advent of a tariff may also tend to appeals for its abuse. It is somethitig to have Tariff Reform frankly revealed as Protection, even if you print it pro- tection. But the " Times "is quite right as to what will happen when the protective tariff comes to be framed. The various trades will look upon the Tariff as a pie in which they are entitled all to share, for a slice of which they will all " cry aloud." We have frequently observed that some of the most fervent apostles of Tariff Reform are exceedingly alive to the fact that the imposition of a protective tariff to suit their particular trade would mean money in their pockets. flow it would suit the people in other . trades who were not specially legislate for, they do not appear to have considered. It is quite certain that there would not be enough plums in the " pie " to go round. And the workingman I would probably only get the plum-stones!

Warrington Workman's Death. An inquest was held at the Warrington Police , Station on Thursday, by Mr. A. Jones, deputy coroner lon the body of Stephen Boardman (37), of Oxford- ! street, who died in the Infirmary on Monday night. Mr. R. Evans, solicitor, represented the firm of Messrs. Joseph Crosfield and Sons, Ltd., and Mr. Ashworth, Factory Inspector was also present. The evidence of Thomas A. Wilkinson, metal planer, 55 Orford-Avenue showed that Boardman was employed lat 'Messrs. Crosfield's, Limited, in the engineering department. On Monday, December 28th, he was engaged on a drilling machine when his arm was I crushed in the machinery. He attempted to throw a. bolt into the tool-box, but missed his aim, and, in • order to avoid a stoppage of the machinery, be endeavoured to remove the bolt, with the result that , his arm was caught above the elbow. He was taken ; to the Infirmary, where he remained as an in-patient, and died from heart failure, set up by the accident.— The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death," and expressed the opinion that it was a dangerous practice for the workmen to use the receptacle ! mentioned for tools.

div.p: NOTES AND NOTIONS. THE POLITICS OF THE WEEK.
The Meet is not going to the dogs, but the dogs are going to the Fleet. Lord Charles Beresford has given a bull pup to each of the battleships of the Channel Fleet.
* * * One of the New Year's greetings to the President of the Local Government Board (Hr. John Burnd), came from the daughter of Charles Kingsley in the form of a set of her father's works.

* * * It is surprising how cheaply good substantial meals can be provided. We hear that the dinners supplied to poor school children of Warrington by the Educa- tion Committee—and the quality and quantity of the fare are all that could be desired—are estimated to cost Id. per head. This is, of course, is exclusive of administration charges.

* * * Eager as they have been to receive their bonnty, many of the old age pensioners have been equally anxious to show their gratitude, and many instances of self-denial have been reported. We are pleased to chronicle a local case. In one of the offertory plates at the Golborne-street Baptist Church last Sunday evening was found an envelope which contained 53 and the following nnte : "I wish to give my first old age pension to the Lord's work carried on at Golborne-street:'

* The British Museum attains its one hundred and fiftieth birthday to-day. It has passed through many vicissitudes since it was officially opened on January 15th, 1759,in the great red brick building Chen known as Montagu House, Bloomsbury. The old mansion has now completely disappeared, its gardens have vanished, and, in their place stands the imposing edifice known all over the world for its collection of priceless treasures. But still it is far too small for the requirementa of the age, and will have to be extended in the near future.

* lir..Fred Stott seems to be absorbing politics with characteristic rapidity in his newly adopted country. In another column we print an article from his pen on the New Zealand elections, and the prominence of the licensing question there. Local veto is in actual Operation and twelve states have voted the requisite majority of votes to secure the Closing of about 140 hotels. No-License is becoming increasingly popular with the people, and especially with the enfranchised New Zealand women. We are glad to learn that the action of the House of Lords in throwing out the English Licensing Bill had its effect in far-away New Zealand and was used as an illustration of the power wielded by the liquor monopoly in effete old England.

The Rev. J. D. Jones,' of Bournemouth, will enter in May upon his duties as chairman of the Congrega- tional Union at' the comparatively early age at forty- three. Only two others, both ministers of the same church, have, we gather from the "British Weekly," occupied this Position at an earlier age —Dr. R. W. Dale, chairman in 1869, was thirty-nine, and the Rev. J. H. Jowett, chairman in 1903, was forty-two. More- over, no other Congregational church,save Carr's-lane, ean boast of having had three successive ministers upon whom this honour has been conferred —the Rev. Dr. Angell James, Dr. Dale's predecessor, having been chairman in 1838. There are at present living four- teen ex-chairmen, of whom Dr. Guinness Rogers occupied the chair as far back as 1874; the Rev. W. Cuthbertson (now at Dawlish) in 1879; and Dr. Fairbaitn in 1883.

[FROM OUR -LONDON CORRIESPORDMITT.] After the truce of the Christmas holidays, the cam- paign of political speech-making has reopened briskly. Mr. Haldane and Mr. Winston Churchill have been the principal speakers on the Liberal side,and Mr. Austen Chamberlain and Mr. F. E. Smith have been present- ing the case of the Opposition. The Departmental Committee on the law relating to inebriates have issued their report, and the Trade Returns show a large decrease both in exp nis and imports of the year but with some recovery in the past month. Though Tariff Reformers are tumbling head-over-heels in their eagerness to make capital out of this decrease, our export trade only stands as it was in 1906. Now, Mr. Chamberlain, speaking in 1903, referred to 1902 as one of the best years that we had ever known. From 1902, up to and including 1906, the 1 over-seas trade showed a continuous increase. So that this year just past, to which Tariff Reformers are pointing as an awful example of the effect of Free Trade, would have been, if the boom of 1937 had not intervened, one of the best that we had ever known, judged, that is, by their own partial and often, fallacious test of over-seas trade. The acceptance by Sir Hudson Kearley of the important post of Chair- man of the new Port of London Board, which, with much public spirit, he has decided to hold without 'salary, admits Mr. H. J. Tennant into the Ministry as ! Parliamentary Secretary to the Board of Trade. Mr. Tennant, who was at one time private secretary to Mr. , Asquith, has long been known as an expert in the ' problems of the conditions of labour. ' EARLY VICTORIAN CRITICISM. On Thursday, the 7th, Mr. Haldane replied to the 'Early Victorian criticism' of the House of Lords upon the Government policy of home defence. The ideas expressed in the debate initiated by Lord IRoberts were not, Mr. Haldane pointed out, the ideas of the yonnger soldiers, either here or in any other country, who have a foremost place in reputation for military organization. Lord Roberts has spoken of a surprise attack by a force of 200,000 men. Stich an , army could not, with our preponderance of naval I power, get across the North Sea And out of that total only about 150,000 would be fighting men. In a few weeks we shall have in this country about j 118,000 highly trained Rogulars, with a reserve of Regulars, including the Special Reserve, of about 200,000 men. Four divisions could now be mobilised 'by touching a button,' and the weapons, men and etores are all ready for the mobilisation of all six Idivisions. In nine months the Territorial Army has reached the figure of 207,000, out of a total establish- ment of 313,000. COMPULSORY SERVICE AND AN OVER-SEAS AMY.- -

Speaking on Monday tO a meeting of employers of labour in furtherance of the Tearitorial scheme, Mr. Haldane drew attention to an aspect of the military problem in this country which is constantly over- looked by all those who advocate compulsory service in some form or other The geographical conditions of the British Empire oblige us to maintain a larger over-seas army than any other Power. But it 18 impossible to get men to enlist for seven years in over- seas service except on a voluntary basis. Germany had far greater difficulty than we in finding troops to proceed to South-West Africa, where her campaign, a much less task than ours, was not brought any quicker to a conclusion. If we were to raise a home army by compulsion, the enthusiasm which prompts men to volunteer in sufficient numbers for seven years' service over-seas would be destroyed. THE STIMULUS OF FREE TRA.DE.

* * * Mr. W. 11. J. Jenkins has been entertaining the Warrington Society with a graphic account of his -early experiences, under the title of" The Romance of Youth." This ishis picturesque description of a trip across the Bay of Biscay. The Bay of Biscay I It's all very well for poets to write and songsters to sing, uproarious ditties about it. "There she lay! all that day in the Bay of Biscay. 0 !" In all probability the rhymers have never been there. Those dwellers in more ethereal regions who in the calm serenity of their studies think—" Of heav'n and earth. Thy twin design, To set my spirit free," should seek the wild freedom of the tossing brine. There she Icy! did she! Oh! you poets! You have much to answer for, pandering as you do to youth's insati- able desire for greater freedom. There she lay ! Ah I If, she had only lain still, it would have been a merciful consideration ! But alas! when the bow of a ship is gracefully pointed skyward, and the Internal economy persists in grovelling to the !mighty deep! Then the poetry of life is lost in heaving sighs! • All- things comes to an end. Miseries included.

* * * Mr. W. P. Westell, F.L S., gives in the "Animals' Friend," an interesting account of bird and plant life at the Garden City at Letchworth: There are (he says) fine-wooded areas at Norton Floward Park, and Letchworth old village, but a paradise, or sanctuary, for our bird friends is Norton Common. It is about seventy-eight acres in extent, and consists of magnificent privet, haw- thorn, elder, wild rose, bramble, buckthorn, blackthorn, a few firs, and other large trees, &c. There is a profusion of grasses, and over GOO species of wild plants have so far been identified. There are fine open spaces and secluded walks and glades. The wild fruits this autumn have been phenomenal, and the birds have had a royal feast indeed. The Garden. City Company employ a keeper to look after the Common, which is said to he "simply alive with birds," and very little, if any, spoliation of nests, wild flowers, Sr.c., appears to take place. May -the number of such " paradises" increase and multiply! Some dly, we may have them in our immediate neighbourhood.

* * The great work of social reform already accom- plished by the Government was pithily and eloquently described by Mr. Winston Churchill in his speech at Birmingham on Wednesday evening. The President of the Board of Trade said : " Although we have sustained checks and vexa- tions from circumstances beyond our control, which have prented us settling as we otherwise would have done the problems of licensing and of educa- tion, no lover of progress, no true friend to democracy who compares the Statute Book as it stands to day with ite state in 1905 need feel that he has laboured in vain. (Cheers.,) No one can say that we have been powerless in the past. The - trades unionist, as he surveys the progress of his organisation, the miner as the cage brings him to the surface of the grt,und, the aged pensioner— (cheers)—when he visits the post office with his cheque-book, the Irish Catholic as he sees the ranges of a University career thrown open, the child who is protected in his home and in the street., the peasant and the small holder who desires to acquii-e a share of the soil he tills, the youthful offender in the prison, the citizen as he takes his seat on the county bench, the servant who is injured, in domestic service—all these give the lie to that. All can boar witness to the workings of a tireless, social, and humanitarian activity, which, directed by knowledge and backed by power, tends steadily to make our country a better place for the many without at the same time making it a bad place for the few."

At East Linton, Haddingtonshire, Mr. Haldane dealt with the question of Tariff Reform from the double point of view of its effect upon the system of taxation, and its effect upon industrial efficiency. To collect revenue by its means of protective duties on imports, he showed, would be to surrender the two principal objects which a wise statesmanship would pursue in financial administration. For the most economical method of revenue-raising it would sub- stitute the most wasteful. And it would directly contravene the principle that taxation should be imposed according to the ability of the people to bear it. It would place the heaviest burden on the weakest shoulders. The poorer a man was, the greater would be the relative proportion which he was called upon to contribute to the revenue. There could be no doubt of the influence created by Protection and Free Trade respectively upon the life and spirit of industry. Free Trade was stimulating, Protection enervating. Under Free Trade the country was putting its energy and wealth to the most effective uses. Protection was designed to cocker-up those who fell behind the times, who did not acquaint themselves with modern methods, and did not put their backs into the struggle. "PILING TAX UPON TAX."

In a speech at Liverpool, which mainly consisted of " gibes and flaunts and sneers," Mr. F. E. Smith let fall the strange and bewildering remark that "one could not imagine any really great Statesman piling tax upon tax while the Empire rocked in the balance. One certainly was under the impression that the chief quarrel of the critics of the Opposition with the last Budget was because the Chancellor of the Exchequer, instead. " piling tax upon tax," remitted rather more than half of the duty upon sugar. It is the Tariff Reformers who desire to pile tax upon tax." They propose to "broaden the ba,sis of taxation" until the number of commodities upon which an impost is levied will be as large as it was in the days before the younger Pitt began the task of simplification in a system that was baffling by its complexity, and stupendous in the opportunities which it afforded for evasion. Free Trade finance has always aimed at restricting taxation within the limits of absolute necessity, so as to obtain the greatest amount of revenue and the least possible interference with industry and commerce.

div.head: NASTY DILEIDIA.
div.p: A NASTY DILEIDIA.

The Tariff Reform programme is like a bulging and ill-packed parcel, from which, whenever an attempt is made to secure it in one place, articles tumble out at another. Tariff Reform undertakes to achieve a large number of inconsistent aims. Every argument advanced to prove that it will achieve any one of them is far more convincing against its claim to achieve some other. Thus Austen Chamberlain, after claim- ing for Tariff Reform, in one speech, that it would revive British agriculture, has immediately gone on to claim, in another speech, that it will open new markets to British manufactures. The first claim is founded on the assumption that Colonial wheat and meat will not take the place of the foreign wheat and meat excluded by the operation of a tariff. The second claim is founded on the assumption that the Colonies will remove restrictions on our manufactures provided that their agricultural produce is allo.wei to take the place ot the foreign imports excluded by a tariff. Tariff Reform is laying itself out to delude either the British or the Colonial agriculturist. That is what Ur. Joseph Chamberlain's followers —or should we say Mr. Balfonr's ? —call " drawing closer the bonds of Empire."

THE TREATMENT OF INEBRIETY. _ The Departmental Committee on the operation or the law relating to inebriety has made a number of recommendations for the amendment of the Inebriates Act, 1898, and the provision of accommodation for detention and treatment. They recommend that magistrates should have discretionary power to send to reformatories all persons adjudged to be inebriates who commit offences which can now be dealt with summarily by committal to pris in, and that power should be given to a relative, friend, or guardian voluntarily appointed, to petition a judicial authority for a compulsory order of guardianship or committal to a retreat. The State itself, or in combination with County and Borough Councils, should provide for the accommodation and maintenance in retreats for inebriates who cannot be suitably provided for, either at their own cost or at the cost of their friends or relatives. The powers flow exercised with respect to retreats by local authorities should be in the hands of the Secretary of State. Any future Act applicable to drunkards should apply to drug-takers also.

Presentation to Mr. Harry Rogers, Mr. Harry Rogers, who recently left the Electricity Department of the. Warrington Corporation after seven years' service in the mains department, in order to take up business on his own account as an electrical engineer and contractor, was yesterday afternoon the recipient of a present from the employees of the department. The gift took the form of a handsome silver cigarette case hearing the following inscription : "Presented to Harry Rogers by the employees of the Warrington Corporation Electricity Department." "Mr. F. V. L. Mathias made the presentation in the presence of large gathering of employees, amongst those present being Mr. H. B. Jackson (chief assistant) and !dlr. Jordan (mains engineer). In handing Mr. Rogers the cigarette case, Mr. Mathias wished him every success in his work. Mr. Rogers suitably leknow- lodged the gift.

Roller Skating in Warrington. . One of the brightest entertainments seen at the Parr Hall for some time has been presented this week by Mr. Matt. Kilduff's Dandy Militaires, and has afforded great pleasure to all who have taken the opportunity of witnessing it. Mr. Kilduff is one of our own townsmen who has gained a high reputation as an entertainer, and has succeeded in getting together a company of very capable artistes. The show ; is merry and interesting as well as reffned, and the variety of the programme is such that there is not a dull moment faun beginning to end. Mr. Kilduff himself submits some excellent humorous songs and his child mimicry is exceptionally clever. The other members of the company are : —Mr. J. Sutton (accompanist and entertainer), Mr. Jack/ Hodson (mixture comedian), Mr. Reuben Hill (light comedian), Mr. Dann Cameron (baritone vocalist), Miss Florence Holroyd (contralto comedienne), and Miss Maude , Hastings (soprano vocalist.) Each performance includes a very laughable sketch and closes with , up-to-data animated pictures.
