With the object of stimulating interest in the War- rington Musical Festival, which will be held at the Parr Hall on February sth and 6th, a social, to which members of the committee, their wives and lady I friends were invited, was held at the Winmarleigh I Cafe on Saturday evening. Mr. E. Lloyd Jones (chairman of the committee) presided over a good attendance and the function proved highly successful and enjoyable. The programme included songs by Mr. A. Greenough and Mr. J. W. Willett, selections by the Apollo Quartette Party (Messrs. R. W. Cook, D. Gittens, J. Critchley and W. Woodcock) and humorous songs by Mr. Frank Hickman. It was I reported by the Secretary (Mr. R. W. Cook) that the ! entries were coming in most satisfactorily and that the success of the festival from the musical stand- point was assured. The Chairman announced a fact of particular interest to Warrington people —that the two local male voice choirs have decided to take I part in the second choral contest —and he also ; expressed his gratification that the committee bad secured the services of two such eminent adjudicators as Mr. S. Coleridge Taylor and Mr. Harry Evans. The hon. treasurer (Mr. Frank Hickman) reported that he had received numerous promises of subscrip- tions to a guarantee fund and the lope was expressed that the townspeople generally would rally to the I support of a festival which cannot but do a great deal lof good in fostering and increasing the love of music in the town and district. Warrington Man Killed at Wigan. Mr. Parker, deputy coroner, held an inquest at Lower Standish, Wigan, on Monday, touching the death of Thomas Folliard, of 39, Liwer Standish Ground, Wigan, and late of Warrington, a fireman employed at the Standish Chemical Works, near Wigan, on Friday afternoon.—Mr. T. E. Knowles, on behalf of Ur. Thomas S. Steel, represented the rolatives of the deceased ; Mr. Gaffey, of Wigan, represented the Chemical Works, and Inspector Clarke, factory inspector, was also present. —John 11°1Hard, Waning- ton, brother of the deceased, gave evidence of identifi- cation, stating that his brother was 33 years oi age. —ln answer to Mr. Knowles, witness said his brother had been employed at the Standish Chemical Works for he last 13 months. Prior to commencing work in Wigan, eceased had been employed at the Paddington hernical Works, Warrington, for twelve years. Witness further stated that deceased's mother, who resided at Ballyharness, Ireland, was dependent on the earnings of the deceased. —The evidence of Arthur Benson, works manager, was to the effect that deceased was found fast in the shaft of the engine, dead. Apparently while he was oiling the machinery or brushing up, his clothing bad caught in the machinery.—ln reply to Mr. Knowles, witness stated that there were no guards on this part of the engine. The factory inspector had suggested a guard. —Dr. Edward Colston Williams stated that deceased was crushed to death between the shaft and the engine.— ' Mr. Got:trey expressed regret at the accident on behalf of the firm.—Mr. Knowles said that on behalf of the relatives he accepted the company's sympathy and he hoped it would take a practical form. —The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death."

Harry Faulkner, Dostock-street, was charged at the Borough Police Court on Honday morning with being suspected of coming from land whereon he had been in search of game, also with carrying a Laded gun, nets and powder suspected of being used while in search of game. He pleaded not guilty.—P.C. Reddington stated that at 11.30 a m.on Monday the 4th inst. lie met the defendant in Selby-street. Noticing that his pockets were very bulky and knowing that he was an associate of poachers he stopped him and searched him, and found in his possession 12 purse nets, a ferret, a quantity of powder in a flask, four cartridges of No. 4 &lot, generally used for shooting rabbits, and a small dead bird.. Witness took posses- sion of the articles and told defendant that he would be reported. Defendant's clothes and boots were covered with mud, indicating that he had been on wet land.—Defendant stated that he could prove that he had only been ratting on the riverside.—Charlee Hughes and Edward Jones, two workmen, stated that they were on the riverside at half-past 11 o'clock on the morning in question, and saw the defendant in the act of ratting. Jones stated that men went along the river bank shooting gulls and other birds.-11r. White (magistrates' clerk) :1f a rabbit came along they would shoot that too. (Laughter.) Jones could not testify to that. Defendant stated that he had killed as many as 13 rats in one night.—The Chief Constable stated that the purse nets were quite unsuited to rat catch- ing as the meshes were too large and they could only be used for rabbit catching.—After much deliberation the bench decided to give the defendant the benefit of the doubt and dismissed the case, the Chairman (the klayor) rehlarkincy that if defendant appeared before them again for the same offence he would be severely' dealt with. A Pair of " DOULTON " ORNAMENTS make a choice and acceptable present. Stock ranges from si. to £5 per pair.—J. S. GARLAND, 51, Bridge-street, Warrington.—Advt. Robbing Graves. Florence Williams, a middle-aged woman, last from Wigan was charged on a warrant at the Borough Police Court on llonday, with stealing flowers horn graves in the Warrington Cemetery on the 2nd November.—The Chief Constable stated that about 11 a.m. on the date named, the prisoner was seen by an employee of the Corporation, to be standing by the side of her father's grave. She afterwards went to a grave close by, and took some flowers from a wreath, and then went to another and plucked some chrysan- themums that were growing upon it. The employee went up to her and asked her if she had any authority to pluck the flowers and she told him that a Mrs. Cartwright bad given her possession to take the flowers. She was taken to the Itegistraar's office, and he telephoned for the police. Detective Meacock t.ook the prisoner's name and address and told her she would be reported. Prisoner, however, failed to present herself at the court on the morning of the summons and a warrant was taken out for her arrest. She was arrested by Detective Nfeacack on Sunday night last.—Prisoner stated that she was ill and cDuld not answer the summons.—The Chief Constable stated that he was in a position to deny this as she told Detective Meacock that she had no money to pay the fine so she went to Wigan. Detective Meacock deposed to going to the Cemetery on the 2nd of November and taking the woman's name and address and also to apprehending her in Wilson Patten-street at a quarter past eight o'clock on Sunday night. Prisoner became very violent when the charge was being read out to her.—Prisoner: "Yes, because you pinched me. You had bad drink I could smell it." The Chief Constable stated that Meacock was perfectly sober and that the woman bad been making accusations to many people. _Prisoner, who had been several times previously before the court, was ordered to pay ss. and costs or seven days.—Prisoner, "I'll go down, then."

The Warrington Charities Committee which recently carried through a most successful competition in aid of the funds of the Warrington Infirmary and Warrington District Nursing Association held a business meeting at the Lion Hotel on WednesdAy evening. The Com- mittee includes representatives of the following organizations :—Nnrsinn. Association,Tufirmary, Liberal Club, Conservative Club', Cycling Club, Arpley Tennis Club, Musical Society, Commercial Traveller's Associa.- tion, St. Paul's Association, Warrington Football Club. Warrington Football Association, Warrington Anglers' A,sociation, Warrington and District Teachers' Associa- tion. Alderman Smethurst presided and there were also present :—lfessrs. Geo. Walker, J. P. lluxtable, J. H. J. Hampson, J. Fargher and H. Hope (hon. secretary). The SECRETARY reported on the result of the recent competition in which prizes totalling 10 were offered. The amount received from the sale of tickets, which were distributed in Warrington' Lymm Grappenhall, Thelwall,Croft,Winwick, Sankey, Newton and Earlestown was £94 11s. Ild.' and after payment of expenses there was a balance in band of £79 15s. lid. The committee set out with the intention of raising £BO so that they had practically achieved that object. Their intention was to raise funds by old or new methods and the draw was arranged to keep the eemmittee together until spring when they hoped to hold old English sports. Their intention was in the future, when they got a fair sum in hand, to help all deserving local charities, irrespective of their nature. Messrs. J. P. Hurtable and I. Bowen were appointed auditors.

Mr. GEORGE WALKER said the committee's idea was that as many annual events as possible should he held so that the townspeople would come to setapart certain days for the promotion of certain objects. The Foot- ball Club had been approached with a view to granting the use of the Wilderspool ground for old English sports on Whit-Monday and he thought there was a fair promise of the request being acceded to. They had the co-operation of all the clubs in the town in some form or other. With regird to the distribution of the money raised by the draw they all • recognized the yeoman services rendered by Mr. Hope and knew the keen interest he took in the Nursing Association. Ho (Mr. Walker), however, thought that the committee should show its recognition of the magnitude of the work of the Infirmary and the heavy expense involved by giving that institution the larger proportion. Mr. HAmesoN said he believed the Infirmary would he indebted to the extent of £BOO or £9OO on the ordinary maintenance account. Mr. HOPE said the committee was formed to help the Nursing Association and as the draw was their first venture he thought they conid not do less than give that institution one-half. In future they could give it one-fourth or one-fifth of the amount they raised. When the comehittee was formed the Nursing Association was very heavily in debt,but thanks to Alderman Smethurst's efforts and to Mr. Johnson's handsome donation the debt had been wiped out to the end of June. They had, however_, still a very heavy year to face. ThS CHAIRMAN said Mr. Roberts had sent out a special appeal and he believed that would be well responded to. Eventually it was decided to grant the Infirmary £4O and the Nursing Association £36, retaining the balance for working expenses. • Mr. IlAmrsoN moved a vote of thanks to Mr. Hope who, be said, had thrown his heart into the work. The success of the draw was undoubtedly duo to his enthusi- astic labours. Mr. WALKER seconded and the CHAIRMAN supported the motion, wihch was cordially agreed to. Mr. fropE said that all he had done had been for the love of the thing. He had had a strong committee behind him and they had worked manfully. A vote of thanks to the Chairman concluded the meeting.

div.head: 1 SANITARY INSPECTORS' ASSOCIATION.
div.p: 1 SANITARY INSPECTORS' ASSOCIATION.
Meeting at Warrington.

IThe fourth meeting of the session of the North- ; western District of the Sanitary Inspectors' Association was held at the Town Hall, Warrington, on Saturday, when 35 representatives from various towns in Lancashire and Yorkshire were present. In the afternoon the members visited the Beamont Council Schools and the premises of Messrs. Toole and Sons, Ltd., horse slaughters and fat boilers, Longford, who were recently amalgamated with the English Product Co. The visitors were conducted by Mr. W. T. Flood, chief sanitary inspector for Warring- ton, and subsequently, at the invitation of the Health Committee, the members were entertained to tea at the Town Hall. The general meeting was afterwards held in the Council Chamber, when the chair was taken by Mr. J. H. Cannel!, of Wtterloo, who was supported by Mr. John T. Quinton (hon. centre secretary) and Mr. W. T. Flood. The CHAIRMAN congratulated Mr. QJinton on his appointment as chairman of the Central Executive , Council. WARRINGTON'S PROGRESS—PAPER BY MR.FLOOD. Mr. FLOOO read a paper on the "Sanitary Administration in Warrington,' and remarked that in 1774 the number of houses in the town was between 1,600 and 1,700 and the population about 8,000. In 1872 Dr. Ballard (a Local Government Board Inspector) lissued a report on the sanitary conlition of the town and the prevalence of fever. The average width of the 1 old streets of the town was then about 12 feet, and with the abundance of courts and yards crowded with small dwellings between one street and another, free circula- tion of air about the dwellings was scarcely attainable. The water supply was also deficient and bad in quality. The Warrington Corporation Lighting and Improvement Act of 1879 was the first step for definite improvement, and contained sections for opening out ill-ventilated co,irts. paving of courts and yards, and the compulsory notification of infectious disease and powers for , removal. By the Warrington Extension and Water Act, 1890, the local authority were empowered Ito purchase the waterworks, and since then several extensions had been made at the pumping stations, and now they had a good supply both in quantity and quality for domestic pur- poses. Another Act in 1899 considerably improved the power with which they were previously vested. In 1908 fifty houses had been dealt with under the Housing of the Working Classes Act. Mr. Flood also dealt with the sewage system. The area of the borough was ,115 acres, and the estimated population in 1908 was 72,000. They had no public abattoir or special meat inspector, but when he told thorn that about 16 tons of diseased and unsound meat, fish, and vegetables had been dealt with during the year 1908, ho was sure they would agree with him that the work was not wanting in attention. With regard to the tuberculosis question, their difficulties with the butchers was got over by an insur- ance scheme which was adopted by the butchers several years ago, and had proved very satisfactory. Warring- ton being a manufacturing town, the smoke nuisance took up acensiderable portion of their time, but the chief offenders were the iron and wire manufacturers, who were practically exempt under Section 334 of the Public Health Act, 1875. Messrs. QUINTON (Liverpool), WILSON (Stockport), DEARN (Liverpool), and the CHAIRMAN also took part in the discussion. _ _

Mr. FLOOD, in reply, said he and the members of the Council regretted that the sewage of the town wz.s turned into the river, but a new and complete sewage system would cost a great deal of money, and the rates were rather high at present. Mr. QUINTON draw the attention of the members to the recent report of a committee with regard to the Truck Act, and alluded to the clause with regard to fines mid the system of paying people with small articles and money combined, lie also alluded to the clause" that the law as to the sale of food unfit for human consumption should be extended so as to apply to the case of an employer supplying, or having on his premises for supplying, to his workers, food unfit for human consumption." A resolution to support the recommendations was carried.

FORMER WARRINGTON CURATE DEAD, An Interesting Career.

The death took place on Thursday, of the Rev. Arthur Alexander Bridgman, vicar of Lozayre, Ra.nsey, at the advanced age of 95. Previous to entering the Church he held an appoint- ment in the Navy, and served on ILH. Thunderer in 1840. Ile was at the bombardment of St. Jean d'Acre, of which he was the sole survivor of the officers of the Thunderer, and for his services he was presented with medals by the British and Turkish Governments. He was curate of Warrington after leaving the Navy; then vicar of Padgate, and in 1879 was appointed vicar of Lezayre. He was a keen politician and an excellent linguist. He was largely instrumental in introducing the Poor-Law into the parishes of the Island.

Cantata at Golborne-street Church. At the Golborne.street Baptist Church on Thursday evening, in aid of the extension funds, the cantata "Esther the Beautiful Queen" was given by the Legh-street Primitive Methodist choir. There was a) good attendance, the pastor (Rev. R. E. Letheren presiding, and the music was rendered in a most devotional and efficient manner, which evidenced careful training. Mr. H. Billingham gave the connective readings, Mr. A. Spruce conducted, and Mr. A. W. Clatworthy acted as accompanist. The principal parts were creditably taken by the follow- ing: —Esther, the Q nem, Miss A.Bridge ; Ahasuorns the King, Air. G. Gough; Haman Overseer, Air. J. W Warburton ; Prophetess, Miss L. Snelling; Mordecai; , Mr. W Tynan; First Maid of Honour, Miss E.Taylor, Zeresh, Harnan's Wife, Miss L. Plinston ; High Priest, Mr. J. Phillips.

Merriment is the keynote of the eatertainment at the Palace and Hippodrome this week. The famouaSix Brothers Luck produce their latest extravaganza entitled" Lift-em's Ltd ," wh;ch is chock full of fun of the screaming variety. For those who like this kind of entertainment it was quite a treat, and there :vie no lack of laughter from the audience. In our view, however, the Luck Brothers might easily produce an act possessing greater merit and giving scope for genuine ability. The Three Transfielda produce a novel turn in the role of lady instrumentalists. Their combined playing on the zylophone, bells, etc., was very good and found hearty appreciation in all parts of the house. One-legged men seam to ha gravitating to the music halls in pairs. The Sovereigns are the third couple we have seen quite recently, and they rank with the best one-legged equilbrists and jumpers. Some of their feats would have earned rounds of applause if performed on the average number of legs. The way they did a hop jump over a high table and eight chairs in line was really wonderful. Lisboa and Barker are comedians in the dude and duffer line, but they have a good deal to learn before they can be classed " Al." Harvey's American Boys and Girls are responsible for some attractive items in rairth,song, and story. Miss Daisy Dennis sings very daintily about " Bessie and her Big Brown Bear," and the - dancing of the troupe forms an additional attractive item. As.comediennes, Cherry Lass and Hilda Mascott render songs and dances in pleasing style. The orchestral selections and the biograph pictures maintain their customary high class.

div.head: APPLETON RIFLE CLUB.
div.p: APPLETON RIFLE CLUB.
Annual Meeting.

The annual meeting of the Appleton Rifle Club was held at the Hall Cafe, Stockton Heath, on Monday evening under the presidency of Mr. T. J. Grocott. A letter was read from Mr. Louis A. Voisey resigning the office of treasurer as he could not devote the necessary time to the work.

div.head: FINANCIAL STATEMENT.
div.p: FINANCIAL STATEMENT.

In their report the committee stated that the accounts showed that the financialcondition of the club was very satisfactory and that the debt Ind been cleared off. No depreciation had been written off the first costs of the formation of the club, but a slight addition hid been made to the assets shown by reason of the outlay of small additional sums expended in the purchase of a new rifle and other requisites. The balance surplus for last year was .£l7 18s. 11d., which showed a slight decrease as compared with 1907, when it was £lB 198. 7d. The working expenses for 1938 had been £3B 10s. 51, as compared with £3l 12s. 81 in 1907. The club had now 83 members as against 80 at the end of 1907. The range was available for club use on the afternoons of Thursday and Saturday during the five months from May to September (inclusive), during which time about fifty-five members tooke advantage of the facilities for shooting which were offered.

div.head: ANNUAL REPORT.
div.p: ANNUAL REPORT.

Mr. Arthur Down, in the course of his interesting annual report, commented upon the satisfactory financial position of the club. Although they had nothing in hand at the bank, the debt of £7l 13s. 7d. had been wiped off and their account was now clear. He con- tinued : There are now 83 members of the chib-73 civilians and 14 who are members of ff. M. Forces. Although the number is steadily increasing we have not yet reached 100, but I hope we may do so this year. The experiences of the last two yea-s have fully justified the changes that were made at the annual and committee meetings, which were held on May 4th, 1937, when the amount of ordinary members' subscriptions was reduced from 10s. to 55., and the entrance fees on competition days were reduced from is. to 6d. About 55 members have visited the range during the past season and 39 of them competed in the monthly prize competitions. Out of these 39, 2?. beortme prize- ' winners. The total numbar of prizes awarded wits 47. Arrangements were made last year with the Colonel and'officers of the Warrington Territorials for them to use the range on the evenings ef Monday, Tuesday and Friday in each week during the club shooting season, in addition to the whole of Saturday, Jane 6th. rho Warrington branch of the National Service League had the use of the range on eleven dates. In addition to these fixtures they had four extra "shoots." The N.S.L. mostly used their own rifles, but brought 2040, rounds of miniature ammunition from the chn. The Stockton Heath Company of the Church Lads' Brigade had ten evenings allotted to them. They used the club rifles and purchased 1,047 rounds of ammanition from us. Only lads of sixteen years of age or over were allowed to shoot-16 being the minimum age for club members. Mr. Down concluded by announcing that he was reluctantly compelled to relinuish the secretaryship owing to his increased engsgornents and responsibilities.
The report waa adopted on the propNitio3 of gr. F. V4rbnrtoo, seoonded by 14fr. Page.

He pointed out Vast the site of the now Council school was on the north side of the road mil building opera- tions had already coraml-nced. The gas mains would soon be required to be laid in the road for purpose; in conneotion with the school, and a. gas supply was particularly essential in view of the fact that evening classes, cookery classes &.e., would be held at' the school. That being so and as the road was a public thoroughfare,the Com- mittee ought to erect the lamps very soon and not wait, as was their custom with new streets, until they felt the expenditure was justified by the erection of honses. The difileelt; would he with regard to r4O-ver Walton, as the parish bouadary intersected the new road about half way up, and Lower Walton might net look at the matter from the same standpoint as Stockton Heath. lie would, however, paint out that it would be some- what of an inducement to intending builders to erect houses more quickly on the land if the road were lighted.—After discussion, the suggestion was approved by the Committee. ST. TtroMAVBAND OF FloPE.—Wednesday will long be remembered as a red letter day by the members of the above society, as it was the occasion of a most successful Christmas party. An excellent tea was pro- vided at 6 p.m., to which 1:30 members sat down, and was presided over by Mrs. Taylor and Mrs. Whiteman and the Misses Astol,Ceine, Fawcett. Howard, Hallows, Knight, XL Howard, Hughes, Cliffe, Smith and Turner. —After tea Mr. Hallows told them how he had been troubled and wondered how he was to provide the Christmas party, as their funds were low, when, as some would say by chance, he met a gentleman on whom they had no claim. This gentleman asked him about the society, and thee said he should like to show his appreciation of the work by giving them a good tea. The offer was thankfully accepted, an.' so they were met there that evening through the kindness and generosity of Alr. Frank Houghton, of Broom Cottage. (Cheers). He felt sure that kind act would long he rernembered.—Mince pies and bon-bons were handed round. The first being dis- p.osed of, the second were quickly woven into a fairy like scene with paper caps and Other articles during which the donor entered the room and was most enthu- siastically received by the little folk with whom he, together with the Vicar, was soon at home and entering into their joys. A little after 7 o'clock,the sound of the bugle by Mr. J. Sankey announced the arrival of Father Christmas. lie was preceded by a band of trnmpeters, followed by two fairies. Then came Father Christmas in state encircled by a blaze of coloured light and fpl- lowed by a number of girls dressed in white, carrying the toys which Father Christmas had come to present. The scene at this point was most realistic. Three rockets were sent up in honour of his visit, after which he distributed the presents, and as these consisted chiefly of Musical toys, a merry bedlam soon reigned. When quietness had been somewhat restored amongst the excited but happy party, votes of thanks, on the motion of Mr. Hallows seconded by Mr. Whiteman, were passed to Mr. Houghton, the Vicar, Father Christmas, and all who had taken pirt in the evening's enjoyment. Oranges were presented to the happy little people as they left for home.

ANCIENT ORDER OF FORESTERS. The quarterly meeting of the Warrington District of the A.O.F. was held at the Horns Inn, Farnworth, on Saturday last, when the chair was occupied by the District Chief Ranger Bro. James Walsh, supported by D.S.C.R. Bro. 3. Grayson, D.T. Councillor P. Peacock, D.S. Bro. J. Davies, Bros. Clayton,Chrirues, Healey and others.—The quarterly accounts were re-ad and passed, and the satisfactory progress of the District and the continued accumulation of its funds were unanimously accepted by the delegates as matters for much con- gratulation.—The usual business having been gone through, it was decided to again hold a picnic and bowling main early in the coming summer.—References were made to the loss which Forestry had sustained in the demise of P.H.C.R. Bro. Hulse, of Chester, and the D.C.R. gave a report of his visit with Bro. Maybury to the funeral as representatives of the Distriet.—After the meeting the party adjourned to enjoy an excellent tea supplied by the hostess, Mrs. Twiffg, and this was succeeded by s short smoking concert at which Bros. John Stockton, J. Hamer, Roylance, Wilding and Janus made the company their debtors by giving them a most enjoyable evening.

John Jackson, D.G.M. presided, and was assisted by Rev. George Shaw, D.D.G.MI.—Bro. E. Allen, D.C.S., read the balance sheet, which was of rt satisfactory nature, and showed the total benefits which had been paid during 1903 were £1,063 16s. 3d , increa-43 over 1907 of £143 13s. 4d. The total worth of the funds now was £3,060 16s. 81—After the usual business of the District was gone through, election of officers for the ensuing year took place, when the following Brothers were elected :—Bro. George Shaw, D.G3f., Bro. A. T. Clay, D.D.G.11.., junior auditor Bro. George Rushton ; Bro. E. Allen and Bro. Robert Perdue were re-elected as D.C.S. and D.T. Bro. R. Pooley was elected as the Warrington Equalized District nominee at the next A.I.D. of the Order as Grand Secretary, and Bro. E. Allen for a position on the Board of General Committee. The pleasing event of the evening was a presentation of a belutifully framed emblem of the Order to Bro. Ilonc.,,hton on the completion of his term of office as P.D.G.If. Bro. John Jackson made the presentation and spoke in high terms of the creditable manner in which Bro. Houghton had worked for the benefit of the Order. Bro. Allen and Bro. Perdue also spoke and referred to the bad health Bro. Houghton had gone through and hoped he would live long to look upon the picture. Bro. Houghton responded in suitable terms and with great emotion. Bro. John Jackson installed the new oqicers, after which a vote of thanks brought a most pleasant and business-like meeting.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH.

GannEN SocrwrY.—The annual meeting of the Stockton Heath Garden Society was held in the Halt Gab, on Tuesday evening, Mr. C. Plinston presiding over a good attendanoe.—The committee's annual report, read by the hon. secretary (Mr. A. Fawcett) showed that the membership of the Sooietystands at 6;1 (45 of these being in the juvenile section), an increase of 140.—The financial statement indicated that the receipts from the bulb show were £1 I6s. 41. and the expenditure 211 Bs. 41.; August ,show, receipts £BB Os. 81., expenditure £127 2s. lid.; chrysanthemum show, receipts £.5 14s. 11d., expenditure £l4 3s. 31. The Society started the new year with a clean sheet, so far as the financial position was concerned.—Sir Gilbert Greenall, Birt., was elected president; the vice-presidents were re-elected with the addition of Mr. Vote B. div.head: CROSS-COUNTRY RUNNING.
div.p: CROSS-COUNTRY RUNNING.

RYTANDS v. WARRINGTON Wr3LETAN3. The above race took place from the headquarters of the first-named club on Saturday. Great interest was centred in tho fixture as this was regarded as the tip bit of the season and both clubs were well represented. Trial waslail by seven. of the wirework's team, over about CI miles of heavy country. A muster of 50 runners compisinz 27 Rylands and 23 Wesleyans, faced the starter and a great race for supremacy ensued. From the start .T. Massey, of the visitors, went to the front with a groat sprint, but was not allowed to keep this position long for Thorniley of the Wesleyans Hackett, Wilding, Skelland and Harding of the Wire- pullers came to the front and made most of the running to within about three miles from home, when C. A. Harding of the home team, shot to the front and gradu- ally increasing his lead ran out on easy winner. He was warmly greeted by a large conconre of spectators who • had assembled to witness the finish of the race. The order of the finish was as follows :—Rylands, C. A. Harding 1 E. Sklland 3. T. Wilding 4, A. Whitmore 7 T. Warburton 11, total 23 points ; Wesleyans, W. Thorniley 2, S. l‘lillett 5, 11. Gill (1, J. Battersby 8, J. Massey 9, total, 30 points. The Wireworks team thus gained- a victory by 4 points. To-day the Wirepullers are at home fora Cross Country Handicap.

" Aspects of Chivalry In English Literature." . The above was the title of a th iiightful and very interesting paper given before the rueinb?:rs cf the Literary and Philosophical Society on Monday even- ing by Miss Waring, of Latchford. Mr. A. J. Jolley (president) occupied the chair. The essayist started at the beginning of English literature and traced the development of chivalry to women down to to-day. In Anglo-Saxon times, she said, there was practically nothing in the way of chivalry. There was no English literature to speak of until rifer the Conquest, because the English were so oppressed ; but 'in the mean- time the literature of chivalry was going up in France under the Trouveres and Troubadours. The ideals of chivalry, so voluminously, vet so vaguely defined in much middle English literature, were siunmed up clearly and tersely in a passage of Uorte d'Arthur." This was what Arthur's knights swore :—" Never to do outrage, nor murder, and always to flee treason. Also by no mean to be cruel, but to give mercy unto him that asketh mercy, upon pain of forfeiture of their worship and lordship of King Arthur for evermore; and always to do ladies, damsels, and gentlewomen succour upon pain of death." The chivalrous ideals of the Middle Ages were revived in Henry ATM's reign. They reached their height again in the reign of Elizabeth. It was the greatest age of chivalry both in though and action. Chivalrous ideals died away during the reign of the Stuarts. In the reign of Queen Anne they again had in literature types of courtly gentle- men such as Sir Roger de Coverley, and soon after Richardson gave to the world the recognized pattern. of gallantry and courtesy, Sir Charles Grandison. In Fielding and &millet there was no exalted picture of womanhood. In Goldsmith woman was treated as an amiable absurdity. Towards the end of the century, howet-er, there were unmistakable signs of the dawn- ing of a happier era for women. On the whole there was no theme so insistently brought forward in the 19th century as the chivalry that ought to be and was not shown to womanhood. The fundamental difference between the chivalry of the Middle Ages and that of the present day was that the past demanded honour for woman of noble birth, and the present demanded it for all.—A vote of thanks was accorded to Miss Waring at the close.

div.head: OPIUM-TAKING IN MANY LANDS.
div.p: OPIUM-TAKING IN MANY LANDS.
PERiL OF OLD " MOH-CURES."
Science Reveals a Uniqle Novelty.

Opium undermines the bodily health, whether taken io the old English form, or eaten as in Turkey, or smoked as in the Far East. Old-fasbioned cough-mixtures/ere not only danger- ous, but useless in Oeiign, because it is a physiological i7;possibility for aoy liptid medicine to enter the lungs. At the back of the nvatii are tyro tubes, one the gullet along which all food is conveyed to the stomach ; and the other, consisting of the throat and windpipe, organs used solely to take the breath of !ife to the lungs and send the bad "air" out. Between the stomach and the lungs no passage whatever exists. Hence to get" at the root of throat and lung troubles it becomes necessary to alter the form of the medicine itself. The accomplishment of this in Peps and the freedom of the Peps medicine from 'opium gives this remedy its unique character and its extraordinary success. A Peps tabiet, divested of its preserving silver wrapper, is placed on the tongne and as it dissolves certain rare medicinal fumes are given elf which can then be breathed quite easily down the throat and windpipe into the lungs. These delicate air-passages which have been ito itated by frequent coughing and got clogged with phlegm are soothed, cleared, and strengthened; the lungs are inrigorated, and all germs likely to provoke inflammation and disease are destroyed or expelled. A few Peps tablets before going to sleep, and occasionally during tiro day, will end the most hacking cough, make one's breathing easy, and bring comfort to the chest. A t the same time there is the happy consciousness that no dangerous and nerve- depressing drugs like opium, morphia, chloral, or • menthol are being taken into the system, but, instead, only the purest and most novel breathe-able essences that were ever concentrated and locked up in a handy, compact tablet. Peps lureg new hope to chest sufferere, for cases are on record showing that neither age nor the long-standing nature of the trouble is any barrier to relief and cure.

div.head: SCIENCE NOTES AND NEWS.
div.p: SCIENCE NOTES AND NEWS.
PURE IRON RESEMBLES PLATINUM.

Chemically pure iron has never been ob- tained until recently; it has been found almost impossible to remove the last traces of impurities, especially of sulphur. But a Ger- man chemist, Dr. H. lircusler, has finally, by a long series of ingenious processes, partly chemical and partly electrical, succeeded in isolating the pure metal, the properties of .which he reports to differ greatly from those of the impure iron that we know. Iron pre- pared by Kreusler's process resembles platinum.

div.head: HUGE MASONRY ARCII.
div.p: HUGE MASONRY ARCII.

The second larg2st mar3onry arch in the world has, according to the Engineering New.. been built on a new railway in Austria. This arch is the largest span of _ a bridge over the Isonzo liver, and is 278 f t. Gin., having a rise ,of 78ft. The arch is of cut stone founded cn re-enforced concrete footings, backing into solid rock. It is Oft. Gin. thick at the crown. The largest masonry arch in the world is at Platten, Germany, having a span of 2051 t., and the hitherto second largest at Luxemborg, with 277 ft. 6in. span.

div.head: DEATH BY ELECTROCUTION.
div.p: DEATH BY ELECTROCUTION.

What Professor John H. Larkin regards as an important discovery in pathology was Made during the inquest on a man who was kiikd by a live wire. The autopsy shewed that death had been caused by an air On- bolism (plugging of an artery) in a vein cf the right side of the heart, causing suffocation. Titis was caused by the electrolysis of the blood, which resulted in a disintegration of the corpuscles. Heretofore, death in the case of electrocuted persons has -been attributed to the rupturing of the "veins of the spinal cord, the brain, and the lungs.

div.head: LUPUS AND THE SUN.
div.p: LUPUS AND THE SUN.

That chronic disease of the skin known as lupu.s—a diease which assumes various forms, sometimes of an ulcerated nature—has been found by Dr. Holier to be curable by the rays of the sun at a high altitude. The p7.lients are exposed almost naked, --Ind the effects. are excellent. It would seem that the p:gmentaiicn—sunburn—which results from exposure to the sun is of great importance in rendering the penetration of the rays more complete. Dr. Balzer also reports a case of lupus of the nose which has been cured by exposure to the rays of the sun at sea -level. A high altitude is, however, preferable, for there the chemical rays of the sun are mort active and the heat rays less so.

div.head: ILLUMINATED SIGNS WITHOUT "LIGHT."
div.p: ILLUMINATED SIGNS WITHOUT "LIGHT."

Illuminated signs without sources of light form the, curious invention, of a French engi- neer, who uses stray light rays, and makes it possible to appropriate our neighbour's light- inz without stealing current from his electric mains. The diffused light from street lamps, brilliant shop windows, and ordinary daylight may be utilised. The rays are collected by reflecting mirrors and glass prisms, and cg..n- centrated in a box behind the transparent sign, which may be at considerable distance away. The sign glows so brilliantly that it is difficult to realise that there is not a p)werial arc lamp directly behind it.

div.head: SHAPES OF EgGS,
div.p: THE SHAPES OF EgGS,

Professor D'Arcy Thompson gave before) the Zoological Society of London a mathe- matical dissertation on the differences in the shapes of eggs. A few eggs, like those of the owl and the tortoise, are spherical, or nearly so; a few, like the grebe's or the cormor- ant's, are elliptical, with symmetrical ends; the great majority, like the hen's, are ovoid, or blunter at one end than the other. The hen's egg is always laid blunt end foremost. P,ggs which are the most unsymmetrical are also eggs of large size relatively to the parent bird. The yolks of eggs are spherical, what- ever the form of the entire egg may he. This Professor Thompson shewed to be due to their being enclosed in a fluid, the " white," which makes the pressure everywhere on the surface of the yolk practically constant.

div.head: RADIOACTIVITY EVERYWHERE.
div.p: RADIOACTIVITY EVERYWHERE.

RA:searches now lead absolutely to the con- clusion that radioactivity is not confined to the so-called radioactive elements, radium, uranium; thorium, and others, but is a general property of matter, says Popular Science Siftings. Not only the heavier metals, Ouch as lead, zinc, silver, hut various other substances, namely, aluminium, copper, tin-foil, air from soil, spray at the foot of waterfalls, mud, tap-water, petroleum, freshly-fallen rain and snow, metal surfaces on which light waves of skort wave length impinge' and flames,, have all been found to give off a penetrating radiation. It seems probable that radicactiVity is a general .pro- perty of matter. Results already obtained demonstrate conclusively that it is a factor in the normal environment of living things, and its effect on the life processes of plants be- comes, therefore, a matter of incomparable interest and importance.

div.head: DEATH BY DROWNING.
div.p: DEATH BY DROWNING.

A French doctor has reported observations made by him bearing on the phenomena -which precede death by sudden immersion. The first stage of deep inspirations lasts about ten seconds, followed by a reaction caused by the resistance to the entrance of water into the bronchioles. This lasts for o minute, and sis succeeded by arrest of respira• lion and lees of consciousness. Finally, the scene closes with four or five respiratory .eaorte.. The last immersion e.anAes an inane,.

rise in the Wood preceure with slowtr.g of the heart beats. The action of the heart remains slow but strong. till death ,eusues. The pressure gradually lessens, but -rises just before death to fall to zero immediately after- wards. The heart sometimes continues to beat feebly for about twenty minutes. The re- sult is the eame in animals which have been tmcheotornised; the period of respiratory re- sistance is therefore due to the respiratory muscles, and not to spasm of the glottis.

div.head: FLOATING TELESCOPE.
div.p: A FLOATING TELESCOPE.

A telescope that floats in a tank of water instead of being mounted on a solid pier has been installed at the Harvard Observatory. The instrument is of the reflecting type, and is the largest of its kind in the world, the object .mirror being sft. across. The instru- riint proper •is mounted. on a water-tight cylindrical steel float, which is buoyed up by water in a concrete tank only slightly larger Clan the cyl:nthr!, and shaped to fit it. The cylinder is inclinc.l, and serves as the polar axi3 of the, t el-3seope. It does not float freely in the tank, but has a delicate pivot at each end to hold and guide it. The water, however,

se that none cf it rests on the pivots. All movements of the telescope are regulated by electric Motors. The great fines mirror is eo armnged that it can enzily be removed and resilVered whenever it grows dim, although its I,v3i,elit is. about two tcms. The whole in- strument is mounted in the open air, but the image. is reflected to an eyepiece in an ad- joining, building, where the observer site. The telescope is expected to reveal stars of the fieV,2:lt ent h or e!ghteenth magnitude— possibly. even fainter ones and work may thus be done with it that would be -impossible with any other instrument.

div.head: AN EARLY CARNIVOROUS REPTILE.
div.p: AN EARLY CARNIVOROUS REPTILE.

The simplest of the early carnivorous rep- til!s were aquatic, living in the waters of the great rivers, or perhaps even in the ocean, says a writer in Popular Science Siftings. The body wns long and slender' and the tail was exceptionally-, so, in Correlation with tho swimming habit. Aside from the more tech- nical points, the interest in the development of the primitive rePtiles centres in certain chang,?s of the teeth and the dorsal spines of the vertcbrm. In one of the simplest forms, Pelicsaurus, the teeth have the form of simple cones of nearly equal size in all parts ol the jaw; sikh a dentition indicates that it preyed upon small animals, which it seized and sy.-a!lowed whole, after the manner of makes anci many lizaals. Inc aorsat spines are low, and do not project beyond the skin. The animal probably resembled very c10f....e1y the living monitor of the Nile.

div.head: FACTS AND FANCIES.
div.p: FACTS AND FANCIES.
PRIVILEGES OF PEERS.

According to tho Law Times, the legislative rights of a member of the Peerage are sus- pended only during bankruptcy under the statute of 1871. These rights cannot under any other circumstances be forfeited, cancelled, or limited. A Peer cannot surrender or lose his nobility but by death or attainder. A Peer con- victed of felony by his Peers can sit in the House of Lords and take part in its discussions without let or hindrance, 'whereas a Member of the House of Commons on conviction of felony ceases to be a Member. A Member of the House of Commons can be expelled for miscon- duct within its walls or without. A Peer is un- affected in his Parliamentary status by any mis- conduct, however heinous, as his fellow Peers have no power whatever to expel him. There is, no doubt, an instance in the reign of Edward IV. of the degradation of a Peer by Act of Par- liament on account of his poverty. Blackstone says this is a singular instance, which seems at the same time, by having happened, to "shew how tender the Parliament hath been in exert- ing so high a power."

div.head: HIGHEST BLAZE ON RECORD,
div.p: HIGHEST BLAZE ON RECORD,

What was undoubtedly one of the highest fires in the world's history occurred when the wire- less telegraph station at the top of the Eiffel Tower, 900 ft. above the streets of Paris, was burnt out with a loss of £4,000. The fire could not, of course, be reached by lines of hose, so firemen ascended from the street in the hope of extinguishing the blaze with chemicals.) By the time they reached the top the delicate apparatus had been ruined.
A HONDURAS WEDDING.

A wedding in Honduras begins in the bride's house at precisely -eight o'clock p.m. The rela- tives and friends of both families are present, the men smoking endless cigars till tho atmo- sphere—lit up with Japanese lanterns and heavy with the scent of orange and pomegranate—is fairly blue. A band plays, and at last the bridal party takes its stand at the head of the sala, the bride always in white, with veil and train, orange blossoms, prayer-book, end rosary, the groom in the regulation tail-coat, white tie, gloves, &c. The civil ceremony is then carefully gone through, and then, this done, the cure per- forms a small part of the Church Service. Then the cure goes away, leaving the business but half completed. All night long music, feasting, and dancing continue. At four in the morning tha cathedral bells peal, the merriment ceases, and the bride and bridegroom set out in pro- cession. At the cathedral door the priests meet them, and the bride extends her small white hand, into which the groom places thirteen coins, repeating the phrase equivalent to the English, "With all my worldly goods I thee endow."

div.head: Do FISHES T,u.x?
div.p: Do FISHES T,u.x?

It is an old problem whether fish can talk. When landed by the fisherman many of the finny tribe make involuntary sounds. The noises most noticeable to the ordinary fisherman may be caused by a blow on the head or a prick from a sharp-pointed in.strument. But there are others which are entirely voluntary, and proceed from different parts of the body, according to the species of the fish. Some them the mackerel, with which most experiments have been made—articulate by moving the superior and inferior motor muscles of the pharynx (be- hind the mouth); others emit distinct sounds from the vertebrae (spine), which are extremely sensitive, and some bring all their internal organs into play at will, until the air around them is a babel of sounds.

div.head: OVER – SEA BY RAIL.
div.p: OVER - SEA BY RAIL.

The Florida Keys Railway runs from the mainland, for a distance of 124 miles, over what is practically open sea. Imagine a string of tiny islets, stretching, like the broken-qt piers of some titanic bridge, right out into the great salt ocean, and you have the Florida Keys. Most of them are only a few rods in exi.ent. Here and there is one that reckons its area in acres; while four or five amongst them are really islands, rather than islels, covering several square miles. Big or little, however, they serve merely as stations for the railway, which runs over and upon the open sea with the open sea on either side of it. Moreover, tho viaducts and embank- ments that carry the trains, although immensely strong, are so narrow and steep that the passen- gers look out upon ocean only. There is no land whatever in sight during the greater part of the trip. Rockefeller, the Standard Oil King, had a great deal to do with starting the concern.

div.head: MISCELLANY.
div.p: MISCELLANY.
Little. words, not eloquent speeches, little deeds, not miracles nor battles, nor one great heroic or mighty martyrdom, makes up the Christian life.
Every day brings a moral crisis, no matter how small, to each soul, to be decided one way or the other. We cannot get away from the eternal conflict of good and evil, within ourselves.
"There is an unseen battlefield In every human breast Where two opposing forces meet And where they seldom rest."
Nothing is lost so surely as that which we dared not risk.

If a virtuous man be ever so poor or un- fortunate in the world, still his virtue is his own reward and will comfort him under his afflictions. The quiet and satisfaction of his conscience make him cheerful by day and sleep Gound by nights; he can be alone with pleasure and is • not afraid of his own thoughts. Besides this, he is esteemed and respected, for even the most wicked people themselves cannot help admiring and respect- ing virtue in others.

Over my heart in the days that are flown, No love like mother love ever has shown; No other worship abides and endures— Faithful, unse;fish, and patient like yours; None like a mother can charm away pain From the sick soul and the world-weary brain.

Effort is worth more Min the result of effort. Effort is within our own control; the result of our effort may not be. Therefore it is important that we should not relax effort in any direction to which duty points, no mat- ter how small the prospect of the desired re- sult, nor how many times we have already tried and failed of that result. For effort is its own reward, and it brings sure- results of its own, no matter what other desired results fail to appear. Not all are keen enough to recognise this; a young writer was, however, who said, in submitting a manuscript for pub- lication and in recognition of the uncertainty of its acceptance: "Anyway, I have had the discipline of writing it, which can't be taken away." That particular manuscript was ac- cepted; which only goes to show that the man who is willing to labour hard for the discip- line's sake Zone is likely to win something more than the discipline.

div.head: HOMELAND.
div.p: HOMELAND.

Still vine-embossed, with roof o'er-messed Near the old turnpike's &ending, The house appears where life's first years Were passed, 'with joy attending. Dear faces farr, fond hearts are there, That long to give me greeting, , • Yet for a while by this old stile I pause before th-e-- meeting. Ofh, treasures rare I know are there— A sister and a brother • The light of love all light above— The sweet smile of a mother. Love never parts from faithful hearts, _ _
No matter- what betide them: And stronger binds responsive minds, Though broadest seas divide them. I pause no more; I've reached the door; Loved ones are round Jme pressing;
Thank Heaven foeliss ! for jOy like-this ! For home ;Ind mother's blessing!
Beauty is God's handwriting; welcome it in every fair face, every fair sky, every fair flower; and thank for it—Him who is the fountain of all loveliness.
All the work that a man can do than Sean be vested by one night's sleep is good for him; but fatigue that goes into the next day is al- ways bad.
Difficulties are the hotbeds of high spirits
3fost men owe the richness of their gifts to the difficulties they have overcome.

"There is no time like the present," we nave all been taught to say in regard to tasks that should be undertaken and duties that claim our attention, but the old maxim is no less true as a statement of blessing and op- portunity. Never in all .the past centuries of mankind was there so good a time to live, to work and to enjoy as in this present which is ours. We are the heirs of all that has been won by the toils and struggles of the ages. Never was knowledge so great, liberty so nearly perfect, humanity so crowned and equipped "as now. Never were the forces of nature contributing so richly to man's need. Never were high endeavours and lofty ideals so sure Of finding room and welcome; never have the peoples of the earth had so fair an outlook for hope and happiness. There has been no time like the pregent.
• No reward of patient endeavour can ever be too great to shower upon a loved mother.
OLD MOTHERS.
I love o:d mothers—mothers with white hair And kindly eyes, and lips grown softly sweet With murmured blessings ocer sleeping

babes. There is something in their quiet grace That speaks the calm of Sabbath afternoons; A knowledge in their deep, unfaltering eyes That far outreaches all phitoeophy. Time, with caressing touch, about them
weave
The --silver-threaded fairy-shawl of age, While all the echoes of forgotten songs Seem joined to lend a sweetness to their
speech. Old mothers—as they pass with slow-timed
step, Their trembling hands cling gently to youth's
strength ; Sweet mothers—as they pass, one sees again Old garden-walks, old rose 6, -and old lovee-
It is not in the abundance of worldly things that the richest harvest of content is gathered.

When a thing is particularly hard to do, it is likely to be particula-rly well worth doing. This is worth remembering the next time that difficulty and opposition stare us in the face. Easy things are within the reach of anyone; they offer neither inducement nor challenge to people of power. The prizes of life are protected by difficulty. Therefore obstacle, to a strong man, simply spells- inducement. The line of greatest resistance is the line inat often leads to the richest end.
Why comes temptation, but for man to meet And master, and make crouch beneath his feet, And so be pedastalled in triumph.

We should never lee behind no anywhere in life, in any experience, anything that is good and true. George Eliot said, "I decire no future that will break the ties of the past." We are not living wisely if we are . loslng anything out of our hands as we go an. In nature, nothing .is ever really lost. When wood is burned its form is 'changed, but 110 particle of it is wasted. The bloscom : is not lost when it falls off to make room for the coming of the fruit. The lovely things af childhood are rot lost when they are given up for the things that displpee them. Whatever is beautiful stays in the life always—only the outward form changes or perishes. We never can lose our frienda. They may leave us ns to their visible pre- sence, passing from us that we cannot see them any more; but what they were to us is ours for ever; what they did for us—the im- pressions they left upott us, the lesson i they taught us, the touches they put upon our characters, these we never can lose.

RUNCORN AND WIDNES.

The florist's boy had just swept some broken and withered flowers into the gutter, when a ragged urchin darted across the street. He stooped over the pile of mangled flowers, and looking them carefully through, came at last upon a rose, seeming,ly.in better condi!ion than the rest ; but as he tender y picked it. up the petals fluttered to the ground. He stood quite still, and his I:ps quivered perceptibly. The florist's bny, who been looking at him severely, felt • that his face was softening. " What's the matter with you ?" he ashed. The ragged. little follow choked as he answered: " It's for my mother. She's ill • and she can't eat nothin', an' I thought if she'd a flower to smell it might make her feel better."

"Just you wait a minute." said the florist's boy, as he disappeared. When he came out upon the pavement he held in I:ls hand a beautiful, half-opened rose, which he carefully wrapped in tissue paper. He had meant to put that rosebud on his mother's grave, and yet he knew he had done the better thing. " She'll understand," he said to himself, " and I know this will please her most."

div.head: PARABLE.
div.p: A PARABLE.
One night a man took a little taper out of a drawer, lighted it, and began to ascend a long, wißding stair. "Where are you going?" said the taper.

_ "Away high up," said the man, "higher than the top of the house where we sleep." ."And what are you going to do?" said the taper. "I am going to show the ships out at sea where the harbour is," said the man. "For we stand here at the entrance of the harbour, and some ships far out on the stormy sea may be looking for our light even now."
"-Alas! no ship could -see my light," said the little taper; "it is so very small." "If your light is small,' said the man, "keep it burning bright and leave the rest to me."
Well, when the man got up to the top of the lighthouse he took the,latle taper, and with it lighted the great lamp.; that stood ready with their polished reflectors behind them.
You who think your little light of so small account, can you not see what. God may do with it? Shine—and leave the rest to him.
"I CAN SMILE."

Every act, every occupation, is fun of great possibilities; so also is every life, even the poorest. There was a little girl, an invalid, of whom I once heard. She wanted to knit woollen comforters for the poor factory folks who passed daily by the window near her conch, but the hand movement was too tiring for her; so the wooden pins were taken away —laid, as was their tiny mistress, "on the shelf." Just at first she fretted; then a thought came to her: " I can't work for the dear poor people," she said, "but I can smile at them, and p'raps that will make them feel baler when their backs ache."
-4_ GOD'S FLOWERS.

The author of "The Cry of the Children," says that, last summer, a little girl, ten 2,-cars old, who for the past two years had helped her mother to supply a large warehouse with artificial roses, was taken into the country for a short holiday by one of those admirable societies which are giving the East-End children glimpses of rural life and a few days of fresh air, both of which are too often unknown to the little toilers.

On the morning of her arrival, the child was taken round the garden of the cottage where she was to stay. She had never seen growing flowers before, and although her wonder was excited by the petals of the pansies—she thought they were_t_reel velvet "—and the scent of the pinks and the sweet peas, her eyes continually wandered toward a large rose-bus !1 that grew against the side of the house. It was one mass of blossoms, and her interest at last overcoming her shyness, she suddenly darted away from the lady who was showing her the garden, and ran to the rose-tree.

"These are 'much better than even mother can make," she said, rubbing the petals of an over-blown flower critically between her thumb and forefinger; an I don't believe my Aunt Sal, who is the best rose-'and at-'s factory, could touch 'cm. My ain't they lovely ? " Then she sighed regretfully, " I sha'n't ever be able to make roses like these 'ere. We ain't got no time to stick 'cm together like this." She was silent for a little while, still rubbing the petals gently, and the lady took the oppor- tunity to say something about the perfection of nature's handiwork. "Do you think as God is riled with us for making them there roses so bad 2 " the child asked, in a tone of anxiety.

Young as she was, the brand of the worker who fights hourly with starvation had entered into her soul, and during the whole of her visit she could not overcome her awe and wonder at the beauty of the roses "as God. made."
'What is that of which the common sort is the best ?—Sense.

NOTHING LIKE THE GOOD OLD TONGUE.

A certain late professor was an accomplished ;inguist. One day he was in a train when an official who knew him entered his compart- ment, and asked him to come out to the second-class to try and find out where a certain stupid foreigner was going. The official had attacked him in all the foreign tongues he knew,- but could get no other response than a stupid stare. The professor went to the carriage. The passenger sat in his scat looking very much bewildered and disturbed. The professor went at him in French, then in German, then in the languages of Scandinavia, Egypt, Italy, Spa:n, and practically every other on the face of this green -earth. Still the passenger sat mum as an owl, whi!e the look of bewilderment deepened on his face. The professor was nonplussed, and was about returning in defeat to his own seat, when the man looked wearily out of the window and remarked sadly to himself:— By gosh, I wish I was at home." He could speak nothing but English. • WHY lIE COULDN'T SEE HIM.
" I'd like to see Mr. Wexworth," said the man at the front door.

" I am sorry," replied the woman of the hens; " but you can't see him—" " He isn't ill, is he?" " No, sir; but--" " Then I think he'll see me. Tell him, if you please, that Willis Higgamore is here." " I should like to oblige you, but—" "Pardon me for being persistent, madam— you are Mrs. Wexworth, are you not ? " " I am."

" Pardon me for insisting, Mrs. Wexworth, but your husband and • I are old and intimate friends. I dare say he is busy. In the old days when we were thrown together often he was always busy. A professional man has to be saving of his time. But I repeat that I am quite sure he will see me. I shall not detain him long, but while passing through the town where he lives I could never forgive myself if I didn't call and say How do you ? ' if nothing else." • " Yial will excuse me ifl say-" "Your pardon, again, madam • but will you oblige me by telling him I would like to see him 1"
" I can't. He has been dead four years. I tried several times to tell you, but you wouldn't —certainly. No offence. Good day, sir."
AN ARCHITECT BISHOP.

A certain bishop, so Tuns the story, not long afLer he was appointed to his see, became dis- satisfied with certain arrangements in his p4lace, and called in an architect of eminence to ad- vise him as to the alterations that could be made.

The architect heard What was needed to be done, inspected the building throughout, and then drew up a report of the expense that would be entailed by the required work. On receiving the statement of the expenditure which would inevitably be involved, the bishop decided to . allow things to remain as they were. But before the architect left his lordship said:

" I shall be glad if you will tell me now for how much I shall draw a cheque on hccount Of the trouble you have taken. " I thank your lordship—a hundred guineas," was the disconcerting reply. "A hundred guineas ? " _

" Yes, my lord, that is my fee." " I3ut, sir, many of my curates do not receive so much for a whole year's services!" "That may be very true, my lord; but you will remember that I happen to be a bishop in my profession."
What yoke is most easily carried ?—The yolk of an egg.
" Louise, did I sing' Home, Sweet Home' with the necessary expression ? " " Yes, indeed, Isabel ; the way you sang it made everybody in the room feel like going home."

INLAND CORRESPONDENCE. The term "Inland Correspondence" means cor- respondenee posted within the United Kingdom, including the Isle of Man and the Channel Islands. "Inland Correspondence" is divided into the following classes: (a) Letters (d) Newspapers (b) Postcards (e) Parcels (c) Halfpenny packets Not only letters, but any document or article (with a few trifling exceptions) which can be trans- mitted by post at all, may be sent by letter post, the only limitation being that of size. TATUM POST. The prepaid rate of postage is as follows Not exceeding 4 ozs. in weight ... Id. For every additional 2 0z5.... id. A letter posted unpaid is chargeable on delivery with double postage; a letter insufficiently paid, with double the deficiency. No letter may exceed two feet in length, one foot in width, or one foot in depth:

div.head: POST-CARDS.
div.p: POST-CARDS.

The prepaid rate of postage on every post-card is one half-penny, and on every reply post-card one penny. A post-card posted unpaid is chargeable oa delivery with one penny. Cards used as post-cards must be made of ordinary card-board, not thicker than the material used for the thickest official post-card. They may not exceed 51 inches in length by 31 inches in width, or be less than 31 inches in length by 21 inches in width. A gummed label (not to exceed 2 inches long and f2-inch wide) bearing the address may now be affixed to the address side of card. If any of the Tales relating to a post-card be infringed, the card will be treated as a letter. HALFPENNY PACKET POST.
_ The Halfpenny Packet Post can be used only for packets not exceeding 2oz. in weight. Printed matter, Bcc., not in the nature of a letter, may be transmitted by this method.

NEW6PAPER POST. The prepaid rate of postage on a registered news- paper, including any supplement thereto, whether posted singly or with others is id. Newspapers not registered at the General Post Office are treated in the pcst like any other printed matter.

PARCEL POST. The postage on a parcel must be prepaid. Mark each parcel Parcel Post." A parcel must not be posted in a letter box, but presented at the counter of a post office, and the sender should see that the weight, size and postage are in order before leaving. PARCELS (FOREIGN AND COLONIAL). Parcels are accepted for parcel post to most foreign countries under conditions similar to the inland regulations, except that for customs require- ments the contents must be declared. The customs charges can be prepaid or collected on delivery. The postage varies to different countries and must be prepaid. MoNEY ORDERS (INLAND.) The postal authorities cannot issue a single money order for more than £4O, and will only cash them , at the money order office at which they are made payable, unless they are crossed, when they can be paid through a bank. No fractional part of a id. can be contnined in a money order. The rates of poundage are :-Not exceeding £l, 2d.; £3, 3d.; £lO, 44.; £2O, 64.; £3O, Bd. ; £4O, 104. By paying an additional 2d. and cost of the telegram of advice, a money order can be telegraphed under certain restrictions. MONEY ORDERS (FOREIGN AND COLONIAL.) The maximum amount for which a money order may be issued for places abroad varies in each particular place. The poundage rates are :-Not exceeding £1,34. ; £2, 6d. ; and above That, 3d. for each additional £2 or portion of it. A fee of 64. in addition to the ordinary poundage, together with cost of telegram of advice, enables money orders to be telegraphed to certain places abroad. POSTAL ORDERS. .Ixtrann.bie at any naoney order office in the United Kingdom, and possess the advantage over money orders that they can be cashed at any money order office. If crossed, they can be paid into a bank. They are issued for fixed amounts, rising by Gd., from od. to £1 Is. The poundage fees are :-Id. up to 2s. 6d.; Id. up to 155.; lid. up to 21s. Before parting with a postal order, - always fill in the name of the person to whom the amount is to be paid. Each order is numbered, as is also the counterfoil attached, which latter should be retained and name of payee filled in. The Post- mauter-General will entertain no further claim after an order is once paid. Stamps to the amount of 54. can be affixed to make up odd sums. TELEGRAMS (INLAND). The Postmaster-General possesses,almost entirely, the privilege of transmitting,collecung and deliver- ing telegrams in the United Kingdom. The charge for a telegram is a minimum amount of 6d. which covers 12 words, and an additional id. itar each extra word. This charge includes delivery within the postal district if sent out for delivery from a head telegraph office, but if from a sub-office then within three miles only, beyond which a charge of 3d. per mile is made from the office door. All charges are, as far as possible, prepared by affixing stamps to telegram form. Address of person receiv- ing a telegram has to be paid for, but sender's name if written on back of form need not be. Five figures count as one word. The cost of a reply may be prepaid. Telegrams can be repeated on payment of half the original charge, which extra payment is refunded if error is detected. Telegrams may be posted in wall or pillar boxes, or handed to rural postmen, and are wired as soon as received at the nearest telegraph office. Late fees secure attention, in certain cases, to telegrams banded in after the usual hours. The cost of registering an abbrevi- ated address, which must consist of two words, is £1 is. On Monday, Mr. Henry Grice, Runcorn's oldest tradesman, and the only sadler in the town, died at the advanced age of seventy-seven years. On t4unday night Mr. Thomas Ford, who had been cemetery superin- tendent for over forty yea rs,died at the cemetery lodge. He was seventy-three 3ears of age. His death ren ovcs a familiar figure from the town. Ho was a valued officer of the district council.

Warrington Fall at Hull. Warrington were narrowly beaten at Hull on Satur- day after a hard game. If Brooks had been in his usual place the result might have been different, for the international half was much missed. Dowell was also an absentee, but Warringtou had a strong side avail- able. Rogers, Cattrell, Connell, and Dechan; Anderson and Jones ; Herridge,Holder, Boylen, Walton, Major, and Fulton. Warriegton : Tilley ; Fish, Dickenson, Taylor, and Treharne; Lloyd and Jenkins; Boardman, Thomas, Neill, Naylor, Belton, and Chester. Referee, Mr. T. H. King (Salford) ; touch-judges, Messrs. J. W. Mellor (Goole) and F. Wilson (York). Hull started and were soon on the attack through strong forward play. Warrington defended gallantly and a raking kick by Tilley enabled the visiting for- wards to recover their lost territory. Jack Fish put in a clever run on the left wing until he was badly fouled by Fulton, but Dickenson's kick failed to realise points from the penalty. In succeeding play Taylor, the home captain, was hard pressed, and alter Treharne had taken the ball from Anderson, a free mark to one of the visitors was taken by Fish, but nothing was scored. Hull were now on their mettle, and Anderson manceuvred his way in dexterous fashion through a crowd of opponents before passing to Connell. The latter held the ball a little too long, and was promptly brought to grief by Dickenson. Warrington were very eager hereabouts, and Tilley's clever punting helped to keep Hull's line in jeopardy. It devolved upon Anderson to again get his side out of difficulties, and aided by Taylors prodigious punts, the locals once again threatened. Dechan was bowled into touch by Fish when the Scots- man was getting up speed, and Cottrell threw away a ' fine opportunity by an impossible pass to Ned Rogers when the latter was standing practically unguarded. Warrington's defence never wavered under severe pressure, but it cannot be pretended that Hull's attack was too well directed. This, however, was improved later, after Hull had experienced several narrow squeaks. and it was due to Anderson that points were forth- coming after nearly half an hour's play. The wily Lancastrian put in a short punt from behind the scrimmage, and following up smartly, picked up and handed it to Herridge. The latter " bullocked " his way along, and finally passed to Major, who got over near the pants, for Ned Rogers to complete the move- ment with a capital goal. Near the interval the locals again got to work, and a dashing effort by Dechan saw Fish beaten. Ile allowed the ball to elude him on the line, and the ex-13radfordian was almost over when Tilley succeeded in just reaching the ball and making it dead. Warrington attacked just before the interval and Dickenson knocked on when almost over the line at the corner. Half-time: Hull, 1 goal 1 try (5 points) ; Warrington, nil. Warrington led off with an attack on resuming, but the combination at centre was not up to the mark. The Warrington forwards werenever the equal of the home six, but they kept the visiting backs from encroaching. A rush. headed by Ilerridge and Walton, looked ominous for Warrington until Tilley again made the ball dead. Rogers nearly landed a penalty goal. Hull I ept up the pressure, and there was no question about their superiority in the forward department. Towards the close the Warrington scruramagers pulled them- selves together and going on their own they gave Hull some anxious moments. Treharne made it One save, and then in combination with Taylor looked like pulling the game out of the fire. Taylor was going at top speed when he failed to take a pass which would have given him a try under the posts. Final : Hull, 5 points ; Warrington, nil. A SECOND DEFEAT FOR OLDHAM.

Oldham were the visitors to Runcorn on Saturday, and 3,000 peopie saw them meet with their second defeat of the season. Richardson commenced for Runcorn, and the visitors were at Once forced to. play on the defensive. A free kick eventually brought relief, and Longworth got the Runcorn end. Jolley, Watton, and Butterworth, however, soon transferred play to the Oldham half, where Butterworth was almost over. After some keen play Padbury dribbled over the Oldham line, but 0. Smith sent the hall dead, and directly after Butterworth got over only to be ordered back. At half-time the score sheet was blank.

After the interval Walter broke away with a dribble, and when near the Oldham lino Moran sent the ball across to Kennedy, who opened the score with a fine try, Padbury failing with the goal kick. On resuming, play was of a bustling description, Llewellyn, G. Smith, and Tyson getting to the Runcorn line, where several scrummages ensued. Harrison, however, found relief with a kick into touch at the Oldham quarter-flag. W.. Dixon, G. Smith, Llewellyn, and B. Dixon. gained some ground for Oldham, but shortly after Wood was in difficulties, and Oldham were penalised. Jolley placed a goal without difficulty. In the last few minutes Jolley got possession from the pack and smartly dropped a goal. Result :—Runcorn 2 goals and 1 try (7 points), Oldham nil. Teams : Runcorn—Harrison, back; Hughes, Butterworth, Unsworth, and Moran, three-quarter backs; Jolley and Watton, half Lacks; Walker, Padbury, Langley, Richardson, Dixon and Kennedy, forwards. Oldham—Wood, ; Tyson, G. Smith, Llewellyn, and B. Dixon, three-quarter lacks ; Avery and W. Dixon, half backs • W. Smith, Jardine, Topham, Long- worth, 'Wright,andNansen, forwards. Referee, Mr. J. Priestley, Salford. Touch judges, Messrs. T. Foulkes, St. Helens, and J. Dutton, Warrington.

div.head: BROUGHTON TOO GOOD FOR ST. HELENS.
div.p: BROUGHTON TOO GOOD FOR ST. HELENS.

These terms met at St. Helens before a good gate. St. Helens early cn had to defend, and following a round of passing, in which Hogg and Barr participated, thcr leather went to Flynn, who cleverly dropped a goal for the Rangers. After this St. Helens were seen to advantage. Manchester ran from his own " twenty- flve "and cross-kicked to Hill, who scored under the posts. J. Greenwood failed at goal. St. Helens were penalised for offside on their goal line, and C. James's kick gave the Rangers a point lead. Half-time score : Broughton Rangers 2 goals (4 points), St. Helens 1 try (3 points). On the restart Harry made a grand opening for Flynn who ran over near the posts, but C. James failed to con- vert. After end to end play St. Helens were once more penalised, and C. James sncceeded in piloting the leather over the bar. St. Helens livened up somewhat, and after a splendid dribble between Briers and Flanagan, Bradley, the late Keighloy forward, scored under the posts. J. Greenwood landed a goal. Broughton rallied in the closing stages, and 13eetham ran over, C. James again kicking a goal. On time I3arr ran the full length of the field and planted the leather between the posts. C. James kicked his fourth goal of the match. Result :—Broughton Burgers 5 goals, 3 tries (19 points), St. Helens 1 goals, 2 tries (9 points).
SWINTON v. WIDNES: THE GAME ABANDONED OWING TO FOG.

At Swinton before 4,000 spectators. This game proved a complete farce, as a heavy mist prevented play from Leing followed by the spectators, and eventually after twelve minutes' play in the second half, it was decided to abandon the proceedings, this rendering a re-play necessary. Simister had tried a sclore for Swin- ton Jones failing to improve ; while Carr put on one for Widnes, the score when the game was abandoned being a try each.

div.head: LANCASHIRE COMBINATION.
div.p: LANCASHIRE COMBINATION.
WARRINGTON " A " V. LEIGH SHAMROCKS.

These teams tried conclusions at Wilderspool on Saturday before a large crowd. The ground was in a hewry state, and daring the first half the forwards had all the game, the interval arriving with no score. Early in the second half the " Wirepallers " were smart on the attack and after Bradshaw had effected, a good run on the left Daintith scored cleverly. Leigh next had a turn on the attack, and after Mclntyre and Landor bad beaten the visitors back, passing led up to Cartwright again crossing, but 111cIntro failed at the place kick. Flny was.of a give•and-talie nature to the cicse and Warrington ran out winners by two tries (six points) to Leigh Sharnroclis, nil.

div.head: SMALL HOLDINGS TN CHESHIRE.
div.p: SMALL HOLDINGS TN CHESHIRE.

It Was announced on Tuesday. that Colonel France- Hayhurst, ei,e of the largest lnndowners in Mid- Cheshire, had offered the Small holdings Committee of the County Council 30 acres of land near the borough of Crewe for small holdings and that the committee had accepted his offer. LOCI Combermere, the owner of the Combermero estate,has written to the committee easing that since the passing of the Act he had done all he could to increase the number of small holdings on his estate ; while the Duke of Westminster, Lord Tollemache,_the Earl of Crewe, Air. James 'l'omkin- son, INI.P.,an i d other landowners n Cheshire have largely anticipated the Act by forming smallholdings wherever practicable.

div.head: GIPSY LIFE.
div.p: GIPSY LIFE.
Shocking Neglect Case at Viarringten.

IGravelennie Bettis, a gipsy, was charged at the Borough Police Court on Saturday with neglecting her five children, thereby causing them unnecessary suffer- 1 ing and injury to health. Mr. A. Browne prosecuted on behalf of the N.5.P.0.0. and stated that the woman was living on a a piece of waste land on Winvvick-road. She at one time lived with a man ramed Edwards, who, unfortunately tecarne a Innatio and was detained at a town in Wales. Since that date defendant and the children had been wander- ing-about the country from town to town. At Warring- ton they lived in a small tent on Winwick-road, and when Inspector Cox visited them he found the children huddled around a coke fire in n bucket. The defendant was away at the time, so the children were conveyed to the Workhour e where they were detained. Inspector Cox, of the local N.5.P.0.0., said tbe tent in which the woman and children livad was a very small one and was full of holes, through which the wind was blowing, and the coverings to the feet were of little or no use. They were in a deplorable condition and were living I ilte animal. The woman got her living by begging and telling fortunes in the suburls.They had a srualNeartwithout any name upon it, and when they were removed from one town they packed up their tent and went on to the next, lie sent, for Dr. Peacock° who had the children removed to the Workhouse. j Inspeccor Forster, of the Borough Police, spoke to ' arresting the prisoner who, when charged, made„no reply. I D. Pescocke said the children's clothes were very * dirty. The wiry.: (it was n very cold day) was blowing throu,,h the holes in the tent. There was practically no sells to their boots. In his opinion the children were caused unnecessary suffering. Ile had i them removed at once to the Workhouse. IThe prisoner said she did what she could for the children. ' She was sentenced to four months without hard labour, the children to be kept in the Workhouse until her release.
