Exhaustive inquiries have been made by the School Attendance Officers into the circumstances of the various families and the result is that the Committee have made a start by feeding 200 thoroughly necessit- ous cases. Children who suffer through parental neglect have not yet been dealt with. In considering the question of means, the authorities received con- siderable assistance from employers of labour and it was found that in some cases there had been misrepresentation of the financial position of those who desired that their children should receive the benefit of the Act. The Committee went into the matter with considerable care and it was decided that meals be provided in the following circum- stances, the amount being calculated upon the gross income of the family after deducting rent : (a) Where there are one or two children, the income to be not more than 3s. per head of the children. (b) Where there are three or four children, the income to be not more than 2s. Gd. per head of the children only. No child shall be fed free if the parent is in full employment and receiving the recognized local rate of pay for his class of work. Garven Cottage has been well arranged and equipped as the cooking centre. There are three departments—the store room, containing crockery, supplies, (I.ic. ; the cooking-room in which there are two gas boilers (one for porridge and cocoa and the other for soup) and four gas ovens for the cooking of hot-pots, puddings, &c.; and the washing-up department. For the conveyance, of the freshly -cooked food to the centres, there are large cans containing three compartments, and they are so con- structed that it is impossible for the food to get cold in transit. The bread is carried in boxes and the crockery in baskets, each bearing the initials of the particular centre for which it is intended. There is an adequate supply of crockery, and the equipment also includes a patent bread cutter and a potato peeler. Mr. Tbomasson has been appointed cook., There is a busy scene at the Cottage shortly after' eleven o'clock each morning when the food and utensils are dispatched to the centres. Some of Messrs. Maginn's vehicles have been requisitioned for the purpose and the work is most expeditiously done. Every care is taken to vary the meals ft-cm day to day. lime is the hill-of-fare for the school week just concluded : Tuesday : Split pea and vegetable soup, with bread • boiled rice and currant pudding. Wednesday: Meat and potato pie with bread; meal cake and cocoa. Thursday: Lentil soup with bread; bread and jam pudding. Friday: Porridge with treacle; bread and jam and cocoa. At the Education Office centre, there was a slight variation from the above menu, it being found more convenient to serve soup on Wednesday and hot-pot on Thursday. There have been curious incidents at some of the centres, throwing side-lights on the home conditions of the children. One case may be quoted. A little girl at a centre in one of the poorest parts of War- ringten could not be persuaded to partake of soup or rice pudding. The teachers marvelled, and at last the little one gave the reason. She wanted chipped potatoes! Lastly a special word of praise must be accorded to the day school teachers who have willingly agreed to

div.head: PENKETII.
div.p: PENKETII.

PEI% A. C. PARKER'S LECTURE.—In connection with the Christian Service Section of the Wesity Guild, a lecture was given in the Wesleyan Sunday School on Saturday evening by the Rev. A. C. Parker,late minister at Penketh, and now of Headingley College. The subject of his lecture was "Work in the Birmingham slums," slum life being illustrated with limelight views. Mr. J. G. Withinshaw presided over a large audience. A collection was taken at the close, when £3 2s. was collected and handed over to Mr. Parker to be devoted to the slum work. Mr. James Woodward and Mr. G. Bates manipulated the lantern. CHURCH GUILD TEA AND CONCERT.--In connection with St. Mary's Church Guild an excellent tea and con- cert were given on Monday evening to inaugurate the Great Sankey Women's Guild. There were about GO members of the guild present at Sankey Sunday school, and after tea,the chair was taken by the Vicar. At the concert various tableaux were interspersed with recita- tions and songs. The tableaux were as follows "Two strings to her bow," Miss Fairclough, Messrs. J. Jones and Kertland ; "The Daily Telegraph," Mr. Orford Johnson ; "Grace, disgrace, candlegrace," Misses Dixon and Houghton, and Mr. H. Pairclough ; "Suffragist at home," Miss Gorse and Mr. Kertland ; "Suffragist at roam," Miss Gorse, Mr. J. Jones and others; "Caught," Misses Gorse and Jones, and Mr. Johnson; " The seasons," Miss Dixon, Fairclough, Gilbert, and White. Two character songs were given " She's a lassie from Lancashire" and "I wouldn't leave my little wooden but for you," which were encored and had to be given again. Mr. W. H. div.head: Examiner, Saturday, January 16, 1909.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, January 16, 1909.
ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. Rugby Football. By `livaMt."

It is generally admitted that Warrington did as well as was expected at Hull, seeing that they had to make the journey without Brooks, the crack international half-back. True they were beaten, but as the margin was only 5 points to nil they obviously gave a good account of themselves on the defence. It has to be remembered that Hull have not been beaten on their own ground this season, and this was tke first occasion on which they have failed to run up double figures at the Boulevard. It was also Warrington's first experience of being nilled during the present campaign, and their first visit to the county of broad acres.

Hull have got together a big and clever team, and if it was not for their .unreliability away from borne they would be occupying a top place in the League. Both forwards and backs have plenty of weight and dash, and the Warrington men found that they had gat a severe task on hand. Anderson, the clever ex-Wigan half, had a lot to do with the home side's success as he made the opening for the only try, and was always a thorn in Warrington's side. Brooks would just have balanced matters behind the scram, and might easily have turned the scale in Warrington's favour. The Hull men had far more opportunities, but the third line was kept well in check by the Warrington centres and it was seldom the ball got smartly to the wings.

On the other hand, while the Warrington defence was excellent, the attack fell hr below expectations. Dickenson and Taylor both missed the easiest of scoring chances—one in each half —and Jenkins was the weaker of the two halves. Ile does not play any- think like the same game with Lloyd as partner, as with Brooks, so that the absence of the latter is ft double misfortune. Fish did not look over keenly for work, and seemed content to keep the burly Dechan from crossing the line. The Warrington men would rather hhve seen Fish display some of the Scotchman's impetuosity on the attack. Treharne and Tilley were two of the best backs and both prevented certain scores by the Hull men. Harry Taylor, who is getting into the veteran stage, turned out once more for Hull and played a marvellous game. He can still hold his own with any full back in Yorkshire.

There is an interesting fixture down for decision at Wilderspool to-day, when Wakefield Trinity are the visiting side. The clubs have only met about once in recent years, when Warrington lost a cup-tie at Belie Vue, Wakefield, with such players as Boscow, and Moores in the back division. Earlier recollections bring to mind a visit from the Trinity with Dicky Lockwood in their ranks. He was supposed to be past his best and getting fat, but he scored a remark- able try from centre and enabled the visitors to win. Since then the Wakefield men have had their ups and downs--mostly the latter. But to-day they are a strong club once more, and the team is fighting hard for a place in the first four. Much depends on the Watrington match from a Wakefield point of view, and the Trinity are sure to fight hard.

With Warrington at full strength I should have no doubt about the result, but the absence of Brooks, Jenkins and Dickenson through injury quite upsets the back division, and I am none too conadent of the homesters winning. Much will depend on the forwards. If they can reproduce the form which fl ittened out the Oldham pack, the team will do, for even moderate backs can play well behind winning forwards. For to-day at least the Warrington front rank must prove themselves a "terrible six."
The selected team is: Tilley, full back; Fish, Cartwright, Taylor and Treharne, three-quarters; Lloyd and Lees, half backs; Thomas, O'Neill, Dowell, A. Boardman, P. Boardman and Belton, forwards.

The selected Wakefield team is as follows : Metcalf° full back ; Bennett, Lynch, Sidwell and Simpson, threequarters ; Slater (captain) and Kershaw, half- backs ; Beaumont, Walton, Auton, Crossland, Rakes, and Taylor, forward. It is expected that Metcalfe will not play owing to a bereavement.

The " A " team should have visited Ince, but the latter will be engaged in a Cup-tie with Cadishead. A feature of interest is the selection of Elockenhall and Shugars. The latter is, I hear, back in town and he will be welcomed. llockenhall was playing at his best when he retired, but I am smewhat dubious about his wisdom in returning to the field after nearly two years absence, lie was always a useful player, and he may yet qualify for the premier team.

Several Warrington players will feel disappointed at the decision of the Union not to send a team to Australia during thc coming slimmer. The prospects of the tour seemed good a few weeks ago, but news has come to hand which makes it clear that a visit to New Zealand at any rate would be premature just now. Australia might find the necessary guarantees, but the Union naturally wish to tackle both Kangaroos and All Blacks on the same trip. I think at least two Warrington men would have been chosen, but they must needs bide their time. Brooks is lucky in having youth on his side.

At the same meeting of the Union on Tuesday an application was received from a Mr. Moko in Now Zealand offering to bring a Maori team over next season, but the offer was respectfully declined. We don't want the public to tire of touring combinations.
The Kangaroos lost another match on Tuesday,wben they played Batley in miserable weather before a .£4O gate. The "gallant youths "won by 12 points to 5. Australia were without Messenger and Deane.

The second test match will take place on the Newcastle United ground next Saturday. There are only two changes in the N.U. team, Lomas taking Dickensln's place at centre, and Silcock coming in for Mann, vrha is apparently unattached at present. The team is:

H. Gifford (Borrow) ; B. Jenkins (Wigan) and J. Lomas (Salford), centres ; W. Batten (Hunslet) and ' G Tyson (Oldham), wings ; E. Brooks (Warrington) and J.fhotnas (Wigan) half-backs;W. Jukes(Hunslet), R.Higson (ffunslet), W.Longworth(Oldharn), A. Smith (Oldham), A. Robinson (halicia), and R. Silcock (Wigan) forwards. Reserves : W. Young (Leeds) ; W. T. Davies (Batley), centre ; W. Miller (Wigan), wing ; J. Lally (Widnes). F. Boylen (Hull), and R. Padbury (Runcorn).

Warrington will have to go to St. Helens without Brooks, whose international honours are costing the Club dear. The reserves strike me as being rather a peculiar lot. I should hardly have considered Lally and Wattle Davies as present-day stars.

div.head: Hockey.
div.p: Hockey.

Latchford re-commenced operations last Saturday with two victories. The first team at home easily beat Bankfield by 9-3. The visitors' forwards played well enough in mid-field but were weak in front of goal, whereas Latchford snapped up their chances. Travis scored four times, Spensley three times, and Banks twice. The defence was sound.
The second team went to Liverpool and thrashed Bankfleld 5-0, The state of the ground was in favour

of the heavy home forwards but the visitors set th pace after a while and popped on three goals before half-time. The back division played very well indeed, Kenworthy being especially good. The goals were scored by Warburton (2), Minarda (2), Booth (1).

The first team go to Widnes to-day with the follow- ing eleven :—Goal, NV. Unsworth ; fall backs, C. Plinston, T. Dixon; halves, F. Newell, J. B. Wilkinson, J. Albinson ; forwards, G. H. Heald, H. Parker, H. Scott, E. Banks, W. Spensley. Referee, Mr. NV. B. Cobb. Train from Bank Quay (low level) 1-55.

The second team meet Stockport " A " at Latchford with the following :---Goal, J. Appleton; backs, J. Wilkinson, W. IL Pickles; halves, A. Mil, A. Knight, F. Tole; forwards, H. Booth, A. Starkey, A. Allender, W. H. M inards, C. Hackney. Referee, Mr. H. Warburton. Bully-off 2.30.

div.head: Moody-Manners Opera.
div.p: The Moody-Manners Opera.

The visit this week of the Moody-Manners Opera Company to the Royal Court Theatre marks a red- letter day in the last two decades of its history,for it is now nearly twenty years since the original Carl Rosa Company graced the re-opening of the old Public Hall with a six night's run of works similar to those presented this week, and there has been little or nothing on the same lines during the long interval. It is pleasing to find that the public have supported Mr. Beecham's enterprise in no half hearted way. With the exception of " Lohengrin " and " Tann- hcuser "which are, of course, difficult of assimilation by audiences not possessing the acquired taste for Wagnerian opera, the performances have been well attended and public interest culminated on Wednesday in quite a rush to see Puccini's "Madame Butterfly" as to which highly favourable anticipatory opinions had been formed.

On Monday night Bizet's well-known opera, " Carmen," was presented in a most capable manner by a company in which :Miss Rosina Beynon took the lead as the fickle yet passionate Gipsy, the equally important character of Don Jose being enacted lsy Mr. Paul Weiss. Centreing, as the action does, around the intercourse of these two, it may be said unhesitat- ingly, that both parts were splendidly, if not quite equally well,portrayed. Miss Beynon played and sang from beginning to end with a whole-hearted self- forgetfulness which was electrical in firing enthusiasm. Mr. Weiss was unfortunately somewhat stiff in his acting and a little unsympathetic in his singing in the unfolding of the opera's strong situations. Yet later he thoroughly warmed to his work and in the tragic climax of the concluding scena, in which he and Miss Beynon have the stage to themselves both, he and she showed a degree of earnestness and abandon which not only carried conviction but made a profound impression upon the audience. The " Escamillo" of Mr. Chas. Moorhouse was in every way a satisfactory impersonation, his singing of the stirring Toreador's song having about it the true ring of the artiste. All the secondary parts were well done and the chorus and orchestra worked well together in an entirely adequate presentment of the work. Two Wagnerian operas figured in the list chosen by the patrons of the theatre and the first " Lohengrin "—was Produced on Tuesday evening before an audience which, while numerically dis- appointing, followed the performance with keen interest and discrimination and was often moved to enthusiasm. " Lohengrin "is a work which makes trying demands upon the half-dozen principals. The development of the story is left entirely with them and there are long drawn-out scenes—as at the beginning of the second act—in which two or three characters monopolise the stage, which would certainly become very tedious were they not in the hands of most, capable artistes. The Moody-Manners Opera Company is, however, so rich in talent that the ladies tlud ' gentlemen to whom tlql leading parts of "Lohengrin " ' were entrusted came throug4 their difficult task with distinction and held the close attention of the audience throughout. Mr. Charles Carter' in the I picturesque title part, was full of knightly ardour and devotion and his soulful singing created a great impression. Miss Enriqueta Crichton was eminently successful as Elsa, whose alternating moods of rapture and despair were finely realized. Her ' interpretation of the prayer which is one of the gems of the opera was touching and expressive. Mr. I Marshall Vincent as Frederick of Telremund and Miss Marie Louise Roger as o,triad, his wife, played the parts of bitter conspirators to the life, Miss Roger in ; particular infusing intense dramatic earnestness into her portrayal. Mr. William Anderson as the King and Mr. R. Carter as the Herald were well placed I and did full justice to their respective roles. The chorus sang magnificently and the manner in which they worked up to the impressive climax in the first act could hardly be improved upon. Brilliant orchestration is the feature of "Lohengrin," for,*after the manner peculiar to Wagner, the most beautiful motiven are,of course, given to the instrumentalists,— and the playing on Tuesday was wholly satisfactory. The mounting and dressing of the opera were on a lavish scale and the production was in every respect I fully in keeping with Moody-Manners' best traditions. None of the older operas have aroused quite so much interest as "Madame Butterfly," which was , performed in Warrington for the first time on Wednes- day, and moved a crowded house to not a little sad- ness and much enthusiasm. Miss Enriqueta Crichton sang brilliantly in the title role, and acted with a I delicacy and naivete combined with dignity which I won all hearts. She is a' on "practically through- out the three scenes, and the success of the opera was due almost entirely to her musical capacity, her personal charm, and unflagging energy. Mr. Charles Carter, as principal tenor, most adequately fulfils all I the requirements of his part as Lieutenant Pinkerton, the faithless husband of poor Butterfly. The duets , between Miss Crichton and himself were splendidly sung. Miss Rosina Beynon, as Susuki, the faithful servant of Madame Butterfly, plays up to the principal role most skilfully and at the same time invests her own part with ' considerable distinctiveness and attraction. The I remaining noteworthy performance was that of Mr. Marshall Vincent, as Sharpies, the United States !Consul at Nagasaki, who is put to the creel task of enlightening the fair Butte-fly as to her husband's perfidy in a scene of wonderful pathos and power. Puccini's music to the opera is quite modern in character, and marked by haunting melody and I picturesque orchestration. It was delightfully rendered by the very capable orchestra under the direction of Mr. Cuthbert Hawley. We only need to add that "Madame Butterfly " is handsomely staged to bring in any waverers who had merely thought of witnessing the matinee performance to-day. The , opportunity should not be missed by any who have inot yet seen the opera which has taken London by storm since its first production in 1905. Gonnod's "Faust" was given on Thursday even- ing before a well-filled auditorium. The principal parts of Faust and Marguerite were in the bands of Mr. F. J. Hargrave and Miss Raymond Ray ! respectively and, while the playing and singing of both were in many respects admirable, they scarcely reached the high level of the performances daring the esrlier part of the week. The Mephistopheles of Mr. William Anderson was replete with all the sardonic • exultation which so materially assists in making the part an easy success. But on the merits of the part ; itself Mr. Anderson may be congratulated on his conscientious acting and good singing. Without his powerful yet round-toned bass many of the fine ensembles, and especially the final trio in the prison scene, would have lacked much of the dramatic effectiveness which was often their most conspicuous feature. The parts of Seihel and Valentine were ably portrayed by Miss Beynon and Mr. Charles Moorhouse while the good singing, grouping and action of the ' chorus added greatly, as they always do, to the success of "Faust," the great Kerm esse chorus the Waltz and , the March being most picturesquely acted and sung. I. Last evening Wagner's " Tannhauser " was pre- sented with cons iderable success, the loading parts being in the hands of Miss Enriqueta Crichton, Messrs. Paul Weiss, Charles Moorhouse and William Anderson. I This (Saturday) afternoon Puccini's "Madame ! Butterfly " will be repeated and the week's repertoire will close this evening with Balfe's " The Bohemian Girl."

div.head: LOCAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: LOCAL PARLIAMENT.
CONSERVATIVE MINISTRY TAKES
OFFICE. Tariff Reform Forecasted in Kin g's Speech.

Tho Warrington Parliamentary Debating Society entered upon a new Session on Thursday evening and the large attendance at the meeting held in the Assembly Room at the Conservative Club betokened a marked revival of interest in the Society's doings. The newly-formed Conservative Ministry assumed the reins of office and there was quite a formidable array of talent on the Government Benches, beaded by the Prime Minister (Mr. %V. H. Stans/leld) and the Chancellor of the ExCheqtrer "(Councillor Fulton-Smith) The Liberals were present in strong force, on the Opposition benches, but to the regret of all Mr. Upson has, owing to pressure of other work, resigned the leadership. His place was temporarily occupied by Mr. J .F. Awbery. Most of the vacant places were in the Social ist, Nationalist, and Independent quarters of the House.

div.head: RE-ELECTION OF SPEAKER.
div.p: RE-ELECTION OF SPEAKER.
Pending the choice of Speaker for the Session, Mr. W. Mason took the chair.

The PRIME Mrmsrert (Nlr. W. H. Stansfleld) pro- pesed;the re-I.!eAon of Mr. C. Plinston to the ofhee, remarking that he had conducted the meetings with dignity, tact, and courtliness. Ile had been impartial to all sections of the House and his decisions had always been well founded, his knowledge of the-rules and procedure being unique. Mr. J. F. AWBERY (Leader of the Opposition, o tern), seconded and said Mr. Plinston had undoubtedly distinguished himself in the position. Mr. HEARNFI (Kilkenny S.) in supporting on behalf of the Nationtlists , said Mr. Plinston had been very careful of the interests of minorities.
Mr. NIGHTINGALH (Normanton), for the Socialists, ! said Mr. Plinston satisfied them by his impartiality and decisiveness of character.

Mr. S. WRIGHT (L, Derby) also supported and the resolution was enthusiastically passed. The SFR &KR n. briefly returned thanks and assured the members that his great object was the success of the Society, mad he would endeavour to be fair to all sides. (Applause). THE KING'S SPEECII. Mr. N. COlg. (Clerk of the Rouse) then read) the King's Speech as follows : Gentlemen,-1 hare again called you to the discharge of your varied and important duties. My relations with Foreign Powers continue friendly. The dreadful calamity which has befallen the subjects of his Majesty the King of Italy has evoked the sympathy of the whole civilized world, and I commend to your consideration the advisability of rendering immediate financial assist- ance to this friendly nation In its time of need. Affairs in the Ea-t have assa med a grave aspect. The action of Russia and Bulgaria has seriously disturbed the settlement made by the Treaty of Berlin and has accen- tuated the difficulties which have long troubled the signatory Powers in dealing with the Balkan States. My Government, in conjunction with the other pavvers Interested, is endeavouring to effect a peaceful and per- manent settlement. I regret that grave symptoms of unrest are being exhibited in parts of my Indian Empire, but I trust that these are only temporary, and that wise legislation and firm government will restore peace and tranquility to this part of my dominions. The SouthlAfrican Colonies have:sent delegates to a conven- tion sitting at Durban to discuss means of effecting a closer union of these. Colonies. I look forward to a successfullissue from these negotiations and am watching with interest what, I hope, will prove to be the beginning of a period of improved welfare for my Dominions in that part of Africa. The present unsettled condition of Ireland demands, and will no doubt receive, careful attention. I have under consideration the desirability of estab- lishing a Royal Residence in Ireland. Measures will be submitted to you having for their objects, the Federation of the Empire, the Preservation of our Trade, and the amelioration of the condition of the unemployed in this country. The Reform of the Poor Laws, and the placing of Old Age Pensions on a more satisfactory basis, will also occupy your attention. At an early date, a Bill dealing with Education in Elementary Schools will be introduced, which will endeavour to effeat a j ust and impartial settlement of this important question. Before the session closes efforts will be made to bring forward a measure providing for such a Reform of Parliament as may be necessary for the well-govern- ing of my dominions. I trust that care will be taken to maintain the prestige and efficiency of the means of National Defence.
May your deliberations tend to promote the safety, honour, and v. elfare of my dominions.

div.head: DEBATE.
div.p: THE DEBATE.

Mr. R. DONE (Newport, Parliamentary Secretary to the Board of Eda cation) in moving the adoption of the King's Speech, said that one of the first items in the programme was the measure for the Federation of the Eropiro. The Liberals had been very loud in their protestations that the Union Jack was as much their property as anybody else's—(Opposition "hear hears")— and that they were as desirous of promoting tbe good of his Majesty's dominions as any other party. There- fare the Government hoped they would have their sup- port in federating the Empire. At a recent Liberal meeting he saw displayed the motto "Free Trade with all the world." Well his Majesty's dominions were a most important part of the world and if the Govern- ment proposed a measure to bring about Free Trade in the Empire they would go far to realize the dreams of Cobden and Bright, who, if they were living to-day, would be averse to the present Liberal doctrines on the question of trade. (Opposition laughter.) The only step the Liberal Government had taken to realise the dreams of Cobden and Bright was to pass that measure of prohibition—the Patents Act. The ConservativtiGovernment preferred to do something of a sensible nature to consolidate the Empire. He was a Tariff Reformer because he was a Free Trader. (Laughter.) The Liberal party were not Free Traders but free importers. "Free Trade with all the world " was the Government's ultimate aim. The Liberal party were fond of accusing the Conservative party of being attached to the beer barrel. (Float, hear.) They could not, however, say that they were attached to the oyster barrel, like the Liberal party, for they had backbone in their programme. He would rather be attached to a beer barrel and have backbone than be in an oyster barrel and have none. (Laughter.) The present Old Ago Pensions Act required amending, as it was legisla- tion done in a panic. Mr. Done hinted that the measure of electoral reform would probably include reform of the House of Lords as well as a redistribution of seats. He concluded by expressing the hope that his party would not, like the Lilieral party, sacrifice their principles on the altar of expediency, or they would be bound to fail.

Mr. JOHN How Ann (St. Alban's, Mid-Herts, Solicitor General for Scotland) seconded, and contended that if we were to retain our position as tha foram ost com- mercial nation, there must be an alteration in the fiscal system. _ _

Mr. J F. AWBERY (Dover) prefaced his speech with an expression of regret at the resignation of Mr. Upson from the leadership of the party, and informed the House that he (Mr. Awbery) had come to the conclusion that as a public ofacial it would hardly be the correct thing for him to succeed Mr. Upson in such a militant position. He congratulated Mr. Stens&ld on his elec- tion as Prime Minister, and the Conservative party on the well-filled benches on their aids. He hoped the entrance of the Conservatives to power indicated that they would take a far greater interest in the affairs of the society thin they had done in the past.—Contirminz, Mr. Awbery characterised the debate on the King's Speech as a waste of time which might be given to the discussion of measures. The mover of the King's Speech had not attempted to defend the item contained in it, but had merely belaboured Liberals with all the( vigour he could command. It was much easier to criticise than to construct. (Laugh- ter.) For the first time, he believed, in English political history, they had no reference in the King's Speech of a Conservative Ministry, to economy. (Laughter.) After the extravagance which characterised the last Conservative administration, the Government had had the good sense not to peso as virgins in the matter of economy. (Laughter.) Upon what lines did they intend to deal with Ireland ? Was the establishment of a Royal residence there to be the root cure of all Irish troubles ? (Laughter.) To put that as one of the fore- most planks in the party programme was bringing politics down to a low level. He was particularly anxious that the House should have the opportunity of debating Free Trade. In order to place round this question the halo of sanctity, the position of Minister for the Colonies had been given to the member for West Birmingham the local Free Trade apostle—(great laughter)—he meant the local Tariff Reform apostle. It was to be hoped thab the right hon. gentle- man would place before them proposals which were not only sincere but sound, (Hear, bear.) He would utter a word of caution to the Government They had trifled with the q uestion before when they mere in power, with the result that they disturbed the serenity of their Cabinet. (Laughter.) They must not

0 expect on getting back to power to be united on the question. (Cries of" We are.") How were they going , to regulate the convictions of Unionists who might be returned as pledged free feeders. (A voice: "They are not returned.") Then they came to this humiliating spectscle—that because a powerful section of the Unionist party could not see eye to eye with those , who flogged the tariff reform horse, they were to be I banned from the deliberations of the party. He wanted the Government to take heed to the lessons of the past and to bear in mind the fact that up to now they had never had an emphatic or definite explanation of the attitude which the real leader of the party took in the matter. (Opposition cheers.) Any proposals savouring of class legislation would receive the 'strenuous opposition of the Liberal party. (Cheers.) IMr. W. H. STANSFIELD (Prime Minister) said the , last speaker had given them a sort of chamber lecture, Iwhich he ought not to have addressed to the Govern- ment. One would have thought it would be a great matter of pleasure to the Opposition if the Colonial Minister happened to introduce a Bill which broke up the Government side of the House. (Laughter.) They were prepared to risk it. (Ministerial cheers.) He claimed there was not a single measure of class interest in the King's Speech; on the contrary it foreshadowed legislation for the good of the whole community. The Government would endeavour to effect a just and impar- tial settlement of the Education question. The Liberals had raised up a nightmare by inflicting injustice on a great section of the community in this matter. With regard to the disaster in Italy, the Government pro- posed to devote a sum of £lOO,OOO to the relief fund. They had been twitted on making no reference to economy in the King's speech. They believed the truest economy was to spend wisely and they did not believe it was economy to starve the national defences, and they would certainly not do that. He would advise the present leader of the Opposition to cultivate the spirit of Mark Tapley, who was jolly under adverse circum- stances, and, to refer to another Dickens character, economy might "turn up" where he least expected it. (Laughter.) The Conservative Government left Ireland

, in a quiet condition. ("Oh, oh," from the Nationalists.) The Liberals had left them a legacy of unrest in that country. One thing he would tell them—the Govern- ment would not bring in a Home Rule Bill. They would rely upon administration. opening up the country, and cultivating trades. He had not the slightest doubt that a Royal residence in Ireland would do good. (Laughter.) The Irish were a warm-hearted nation and _ _ _

they were very fond of Kings—(laughter)—and if they could get the King and his Court in Ireland it would do a great deal to satisfy them. The Government would not send their prize humorist there to laugh Ireland into peace. Mr. Birrell was a great wit and scholar but he was a failure as a Minister. (Opposition laughter.) Mr. W. FURNESS (Bristol) said that when he looked upon the august assembly opposite he found a startling condition of things—there were more Government officials than members. (Laughter.) Having com- mented upon the personnel of the Government, Mr. Furness warned the Ministry that if they purposed to find funds for old age pensions by their pet scheme of tariff reform they would have keen, earnest and, be hoped, successful opposition. Tariff reform meant that if they taxed imported goods they were going to tax the poor and increase their burdens—in fact, they would increase the burdens of the commnnity generally Not only that, but they would increase the price of. everything they consumed or wore and thus restrict the output. Were they going to chain the Empire together by the lust for business and greed or would they be content to let it remain as it was—federated by love, kindred names and kindred blood, and the general respect held by the Colonies for the Mother Country. (opposition cheers). Mr. M. G. 111.1A.RNE (Kilkenny S.) announced that he would consider it his duty to move an amendment on the Home Rule question. He assured the Government that so long as they brought in measures for the improvement of the democracy they would have the hearty support of the Nationalists, but as soon as they introduced anything like class legislation they would fight them tooth and nail. The galaxy of talent on the Government benches would cost the tax payers a lot of money, for he had found that their salaries would total £93,325 per annum. (Die PFtRINIEER: "rhey are cheap at the price "and laughter.) "We are tired of Royal residences in Ireland "said 'Mr. Hearne "We had them before you had them in England. We don't want to be children to play with toy castles. We want to look at things as men and as a nation, with the aspirations of a nation." The Tories had been the heriditary enemies of the Irish cause in the past but anything they proposed for the betterment of the people would have the Nationalists' support. Alderman BRNNETT (Secretary for the Colonies) said he confessed frankly that he was very independent and democratic, and he had some misgivings as to whether his party would bring in a pragramme sufficiently democratic and advanced for him. (Laughter.) But when he attended their deliberations he found that most of them were as democratic as himself, and the King's Speech seemed to him so admirable that there was not a single line to which he could take exception. Mild complaints had been made as to the way the Government proposed to deal or not to deal with the Irish question. He for one was heartily sick of the Irish question. They bad been settling it for the last thirty years to his own knowledge. Mr. Gladstone once said—and if he bad carried out all the sensible things he had bald ho would not have ended his career undersuch a cloud of failure— (Opposition cries of" No," " No,") —that he was not pr epared to extend to Ireland anything that he was not prepared to extend on equal terms to any other part of the United Kingdom. Unluckily he did not keep to that. In any measure of Imperial Federation that he (Alderman Bennett) might introduce he would not pro- pose anything that ran counter to that great principle enunciated by Mr. Gladstone. Why Ireland should always be whining like a spoiled child he did not know. He would treat Ireland with simple justice instead of giving her special treatment, and he did not believe in continually yielding to outrage and terrorism which ought not to influence sound statesmen. As to the Education question, they did not believe in preferential treatment of any particular denomination. He was a Nonconformist and proud or the fact, but that did not say he was going to treat his friends of other denominations with anything less than justice. With regard to tariff reform, he was as absolutely sincere on that question as he had been on any question during his life,and he would make his proposals trs sound as possible. He believed they would commend them- selves to his colleagues, as they were all sensible fellows. (Laughter.) They could not govern nations by sentiment and be was surprised to find Mr. Farness falling back on that antedeluvian piffle about senti- ment in regard to federating the empire. The silken ties of sentiment were all very well but they were not business and they were not commonsense. There was no more illogical conglomeration of States on the face of the earth than the British Empire as it was at present. The Government would try to ' systematise those conditions and augment the ties of sentiment with a sound business arrangement which would be advantageous to all the parties concerned. (Government cheers). Mr. NIGHTINGALE (Normanton), then moved ' the adjournment of the debate. In committee the House decided against a proposal that ladies should be admitted to membership. 1 It was decided that in future the Society should meet on Tuesday instead of Thursday evening.

div.head: Warrington Ragged School.
div.p: Warrington Ragged School.

At the soup kitchen connected with the above school during the past fortnight, there has been distributed on the average 950 gallons of soup and over 850 loaves of bread per week. The arduous task of pre- paration has been entirely undertaken by the superintendent and founder of the school (Councillor James Skelhnd). Ile expresses his sincere thanks to thcse kind friends who by their material help have enabled him to alleviate the hunger of the starving hundreds who have crowded to the kitchen each day. Their wan faces and scent clothing spoke for themselves of the keen necessity for the soup they came to obtain—and none were turned away.—Mr. Smith has been extremely useful in maintaining order.—Meat has been given by G. and J. Bowcock, B. Cross, Cooper, and Councillor Singleton ; subscriptions from Miss Jackson (Sankey) and Rev. T. Miller.

div.head: (QUESTIONS FOR TARIFF REFORMERS.
div.p: (QUESTIONS FOR TARIFF REFORMERS.
XIII —lf Protection is true, why not cut ourselves off from the Colonies, in order that we may make more work by shutting out Colonial goods P

The Tariff Reformers say that all our troubles arise from untaxed imports. Yet they propose to allow imports to enter this country untaxed from the British Empire. But the British Empire covers about one-third of the world's population. What Tariff Reformers propose, therefore, is to• allow one-third of the world to continue to ruin us. Here are practical examples. The Tariff Reformers say that untaxed imprted hops are ruining the Kentish hop-grower. But hops are imported from the Colonies.
Tariff Reformers also say that untaxed imported doors and joinery throw British carpenters out of work. But joinery is imported from the Colonies.

Last year £21,000,000 worth of manufactured goods were imported untaxed from the Colonies and India. If Protection is true, the Colonies robbed British working men of £21,000,000 of work last year, and such robbery ought to be ended. L. G. C. IL

div.head: WARRINGTON FREE CHURCH COUNCIL. WEEK OF UNITED PRAYER.
div.p: WARRINGTON FREE CHURCH COUNCIL. WEEK OF UNITED PRAYER.
The animal week of united prayer in connection with the Warrington and District Free Church Council has been observed this week.

"THANKFULNESS." . The opening meeting was held in the Lecture Hall attached to the Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church on " Monday evening. The subject was " Thankfulness." , Mr. U. E. Parker presided over a moderate attendance - and read a letter from Mr. A. Mounfleld, who was ' announced as speaker, regretting that he could not attend owing to another important engagement which : he had overlooked when he cansented to attend that ' gathering. Mr. PARKER said the subject of praise and thanks- giving was one that should find a response in all hearts. The followers of Jesus Christ had a great deal to be thankful for and it was a reflection upon Christian ; people generally that they were not characterised by : joy and gladness and this gave rise to the idea that ~ there was nothing but graveness and solemnity associ- ated with religious life. Life undoubtedly had itS ' serious side but if their lives were devoid of joy and gladness it must b 4.3 because they had not realized f their high calling and the glorious inheritance ,1 to which they as children of God were heirs. 1 They ought to show that they really believed 1 they were sons of God and heirs to a great inheritance I which even here and now they could enter into and call their own. To some extent it was a question of" temperament but temperament and dispositioa of mind could be cultivated. Mr. Parker gave instances of the. - 1 cheerful spirit shown by people living in i poverty-stricken surroundings in the slums of Warring- . ton, who when asked if they would like to move to - another house said they were happy and content where , they were. He would urge upon those who professed to be followers of Jesus Christ that they should see things in their proper proportions. The great mis- , take often made was that people magnified small things and did not see the large and small things, as conspicuously as they should. The things which , I were the right of every Christian man and woman—the spiritual possessions—were great and glorious and if . people could only put the minor things which made their lives sad, dull and dreary, in their proper places and lay hold on the big things which made for gladness,. i the Christian life and character would bubble over with . joy and gladness. ,

"THE CHURCH UNIVERSAL. There was a great improvement in the attendance on Tuesday evening when the meeting was held in Bold Street Church parlour. Mr. J.C. HOLLAND presided and spoke of the great work of the Church throughout the world. Referring to the apathy and indifference often manifested in these days he expressed the hope that they would soon pass away and that there would be a splen- did revival of God's work everywhere. He thought sometimes they made a mistake in calculating succeSe more by numbers than by spirituality. Mr. P. I.Vvvvp, .Thvgg we the speaker. Ho said the Church was the essential agent of the Kingdom of God. Jesus Christ created the Church, and His Apostles founded individual Churches, not as societies of sympa- thetic souls but as distinct means of grace. We were indebted to every church. No one church and no one set of thinkers was responsible for our ideas and tendencies to-day, but we could gather from each church tomething that was helpful. Referring to the Free Churches, Mr. Jones said they owed a debt of gratitude to the men and women who had made it possible fo them to worship God in a free way. He spoke of the' sterling faith, how they were always in the forefront o the battle against intolerance and wrong, and said that although those pioneers were gone and forgotten, the - work they did remained. The speaker made reference to the report on the Free Church life and work la - Liverpool and to the apparent temporary depression in the attendance at the different places of worship, and went on to say that he questioned whether a quarter of the people of Warrington attended a place of worship on Sunday. It looked as if the gulf between the masses and the Church—already wide—was growing wider still. The Socialists and Labour men were generally throwing stones at the Christian churches, but they must remember that it was largely owing to the churches that these movements existed, for it wan the Church that had done so much to educate the , people. He believed the present slackness of attend- ance at the churches was only a temporary matter and that a time of revival would come. There were certain features of their work that would have to be . emphasised to attain that end. They must fight for a more practical obedience to the law of brotherhood.- The Fatherhood of God carried with it and involved the brotherhood of men and the lack of that feeling of brotherhood accounted for a great deal of the non- attendance at places of worship. Then there was the necessity for the church to take a greater interest in the social questions of the day. The age in which we lived was a Socialistic age and the questions that engrossed men's minds were not so much questions of law and of politics as of social conditions. It was the - duty of the Church to take an interest in everything - that concerned the uplifting and the welfare of the • people. The Church must also be more true to her great central work—the work of saving men.

div.head: "NATIONS AND RULERS."
div.p: "NATIONS AND RULERS."

A meeting was held on Wednesday evening in- , Emmanuel Church Institute at 8 p.m., and despite the inclement weather there was a crowded attendance. 1 The Rev. E.B. Keeling, Superintendent of the Wesleyan' Circuit, occupied the chair and Mrs/ Gillespie presided at the organ. The Rev. F. Vaughan was the speaker, the topic for the evening being Nations and Rulers." The speaker commenced by saying the will of God for individual' and nation was nothing less than divine indwelling while the ideal of the Christian was personal dealing with the true God. The measure of the realisation of this ideal was the measure of real progress of individual or nation. Mr. Vaughan then showed from the life of Israel from Egypt to Sinai that thay, as a people,were in actual enjoyment of six remarkable blessings and privileges before they had any personal dealings with God. At Sinai they were called "to meet with God', for a threefold purpose.—(l). to learn His will concern"' ing them, (2) their true relationahip to their fellowSt and then (3) that they might make an offering of tent that God might dwell among His people and be the pivot power of all their work.. The speaker pointed out that the inconsistencies of Lbw' day, the harrowing spectacles to be seen in enlightened) and intelligent social life, were due to the fact that God was permitted to figure in a creed, but denied s' place in the life. While this obtained the Church' t languished under the silvery mildew of helpless respect' ability and humanity cried in vain for its wrongs to he' righted by legislation. The need of the hour was personal dealings with God by rulers and those who made them. Much fervent prayer was offered, and a most helpft4 meeting was brought to a close, and the Benedictio' pronounced by Rev. E, B. Keeling. .

div.head: " FOREIGN MISSIONS."
div.p: " FOREIGN MISSIONS."

A meeting was held in the Wycliffe Memorial Halt- on Thursday evening, when the Rev. T. Miller spoke oa "Foreign Missions. The Rev. J. Yonge presided. Mr. MrLuia referred to the great difficulties whico' beset missionaries and described the various methode' which they adopted in their work. He also spoke of the great transforming power of Christianity. Last evening a meeting waa held at Golborne-stree Baptist Church, when the subject was "Home Life. The Rev. R. E. Letheren presided and Mr. James SW/ was the speaker.

ST. HELENS. PROFESSIONAL UNEMPLOYED. Four young men were charged at St. Helens on Satur- day with sleeping out at the brickworks. In one case it was said that the man had sevenpence in his possession and the Chien Constable sand that he belonged to the Iclass of professional unemployed. He had been forty- six times before the court, thirty-two of which were for 'sleeping out. The man' whose name was Daniel Smith, was sent to prison for two months' hard labour. TEMPERANCE WORK IN ST. HELENS. The annual meeting of the St. Helens branch of the British Women's Tempetance Association was held on Tuesday night at the Town Hall. Mrs. R Pilkington presided. Miss Glover, the hon. scoretary, detailed the work that had been done during the year, They had a visit from Mies Kershaw, and at various meetings obtained 420 pledges. The year began with a member- I ship of 118, rind concluded with a total rnerntership of I 141. The Y. branch had 2 xceetional year, having made 142 now members and five new brander, and as a result the Frances Willard memorial shield had been awarded to St. Helens. The post of treasurer had been accepted by Mrs. Best. The report was adopted and speeches followed. HOUSE COLLAPSE AT ST. HELENS. An alarming occcurrence happened on Sunday morn- , ing in Hamer-street, St. Helens, when part of tl e gable-end of the house No. 8 bulged out and fell upon , the sheds of a marine store yard which adjoins. The ! house is a good age, and the wall itself is a marvel of construction, consisting of "rubble," and being only , five or six inches thick. The gable is surmounted by an extensive chimney-stack, and the marvel is that the tine gable wall has stood the strain of the chimney- stack and the weather for so long. About a quarter to I eleven in the morning, about ton minutes after a lodger had gone to lie down on the I:3d in one of the upstairs I rooms, the wall gave way, but as it fell outward the ' lodger escaped injury. As it appeared possible that the I chimney-stack, Ac., would come down at any minute, I arrangements were made to erect a hoarding and prevent passers-by walking into danger. NEW ASSISTANT MEDIC:s.L OFFICER. Dr. Paterson, of Hereford, was on Wednesday appointed Assistant Medical officer of St. Helens. For I some time the post hee been filled by a lady, but she recently received an appointment under the Lancashire ; County Council, and the Corporation decided to have al male assistant rather than a lady doctor. Dr. Paterson ' is 29 years of age, and at present holds the position of assistant to the medical officer of health for the ' Herefordshire Combined Sanitary District. His ! qualifications are M. 8., D.P.H. (London), BSc. I (London), and L.R.C.P. He was foe some time junior demonstrator of physiology at St.' Bartholomew's Hospital, London. He had hold the appointment of assistant medical officer to the county , borough of Croydon, and also been the resident medical ' officer to the Croydon Isolation Hospital: The salary —-- for the new appenutment is £250, rising to £350.
